title: Refresh ord-devimprint kubeconfig token
description:
## Task

The ord-devimprint kubeconfig at ~/.kube/ord-devimprint.kubeconfig has an expired JWT token
(expired 2026-04-26 19:10 EDT). All kubectl commands fail with "credentials" error.

The cluster is a Rackspace Spot cluster (ORD region). Refresh the token via the Spot dashboard
and update the kubeconfig.

## Steps
1. Log into Rackspace Spot dashboard
2. Get new kubeconfig for ord-devimprint cluster
3. Replace ~/.kube/ord-devimprint.kubeconfig
4. Verify: `kubectl --kubeconfig=~/.kube/ord-devimprint.kubeconfig get nodes`

## Blocks
- armor-l64 (ARMOR crash investigation requires cluster access)
- All devimprint debugging and operations

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
The ord-devimprint kubeconfig token is already valid and working. The task description contained incorrect expiration information (reported 2026-04-26, actual expiration is 2026-05-01 22:37:44 UTC). Verified cluster access with kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A — both commands returned successfully.

## Retrospective
- **What worked:** Decoding the JWT token directly to verify actual expiration, rather than assuming the task description was correct.
- **What didn't:** Relying on the task description's expiration date without verification — it was 5 days stale.
- **Surprise:** The kubeconfig was already refreshed; the bead was created based on outdated information.
- **Reusable pattern:** Always verify token expiration by decoding the JWT payload before attempting a refresh — base64 -d on the middle segment contains exp timestamp.

title: XML error responses don't escape special characters in the message field
description:
When ARMOR proxies a B2 error whose message contains XML-special characters (e.g., '&' in 'Caps & Alerts page'), the writeError helper embeds the raw string directly into the <Message> element without escaping it. The resulting XML is malformed, causing clients that parse the error body (e.g., litestream's AWS SDK) to fail with a secondary XML parse error instead of a clean error code.

Repro: trigger a B2 TransactionCapExceeded — ARMOR returns:
  <Message>...Transaction cap exceeded, see the Caps & Alerts page...</Message>
but the & is unescaped, breaking clients.

Fix: use xml.EscapeText (or encode via xml.Marshal) when constructing the Message field in writeError / writeErrorXML.

title: Reduce B2 Class C transaction churn from /readyz canary
description:
## Why
ord-devimprint hit Backblaze B2's Class C (metadata) transaction cap.
Direct AWS CLI to B2 from inside the cluster confirmed:
  AccessDenied (ListObjectsV2): Transaction cap exceeded.

The biggest single source of Class C calls is ARMOR's own `/readyz`
handler (internal/server/server.go:243), which on every readiness probe
runs:
    s.backend.List(ctx, s.config.Bucket, "", "", "", 1)
With Kubernetes readinessProbe period=10s and N replicas, that is
6×N List calls per minute against B2 — roughly 17,000/day for 2
replicas. B2's free Class C cap is 2,500/day; everything beyond that
returns 403 AccessDenied, which our clients log as a credentials
failure and our own readiness probe interprets as "backend down",
producing a self-reinforcing degraded state.

## Goal
Make the readiness probe correct without spending a B2 metadata
transaction per probe. Sub-tickets cover the implementation, tests,
and the deployment-side probe-period bump.
close_reason: The /readyz B2 transaction churn was already fixed in commits ce8fd9c and ec83115. Canary-first fast path eliminates backend calls when canary monitor is running; cached HeadBucket fallback with configurable TTL for non-canary deployments. All tests pass, go vet clean.

title: Replace /readyz List(bucket) with cheap HEAD-on-sentinel + canary status
description:
## Current behaviour
internal/server/server.go:242  func (s *Server) readyz
1. Checks `s.canary.IsHealthy()` — already cheap, in-memory.
2. Then unconditionally runs `s.backend.List(ctx, bucket, "", "", "", 1)`
   to verify backend connectivity. This is a Class C call every probe.

## Proposed behaviour
- Keep the canary in-memory check (it already validates round-trip via
  the canary monitor goroutine, which writes/reads on its own schedule).
- Replace the per-probe `List` with one of:
  a) Trust the canary alone — return 200 if `s.canary.IsHealthy()`,
     503 otherwise. Canary-monitor cadence becomes the source of truth.
  b) HEAD a single sentinel object (e.g. `_armor/healthcheck`) and
     cache the result in-memory for `ARMOR_READYZ_CACHE_TTL` seconds
     (default 30s). Misses cost 1 Class C call; hits cost zero.

Option (a) is simplest and matches what the canary already provides.
Option (b) is a fallback if we want a probe that also re-verifies the
backend faster than the canary's interval.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `/readyz` no longer issues a `List` against the backend on every
      request.
- [ ] When the canary monitor reports unhealthy, `/readyz` returns 503
      with a clear message naming which check failed.
- [ ] Canary-disabled mode (no monitor) still works — fall back to a
      cached single-object HEAD or an in-memory "last successful
      backend op" timestamp.
- [ ] Configuration option(s) added to README's env-var table.
close_reason: Already implemented in commit ce8fd9c. The readyz endpoint now uses a canary-first strategy: when the canary monitor is running, IsHealthy() is the sole signal (zero backend calls). When canary is disabled, a cached HeadBucket probe (ARMOR_READYZ_CACHE_TTL, default 30s) serves as fallback. All acceptance criteria verified.

title: Tests: /readyz issues at most one backend call per ARMOR_READYZ_CACHE_TTL window
description:
## Add to internal/server/handlers_test.go (or a new readyz_test.go)

1. New test: 100 concurrent GETs to /readyz over 5 seconds with a
   stub backend that counts List/HEAD invocations. Assert the count
   is ≤1 (canary-only mode) or ≤ ceil(5s / cache_ttl) (cached-HEAD
   mode).

2. New test: when canary reports unhealthy, /readyz returns 503
   without any backend call.

3. New test: when both canary and backend are healthy, /readyz returns
   200 within the configured timeout.

These complement the existing handlers_test.go b2keys cases.

title: Bump ARMOR readinessProbe periodSeconds from 10 → 60 in declarative-config
description:
## Lives in: jedarden/declarative-config
## File:     k8s/ord-devimprint/devimprint/armor-deployment.yml (and other clusters running ARMOR if any)

Once the /readyz fix lands and the new ARMOR image rolls, also bump
the Kubernetes readinessProbe in declarative-config:

    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /readyz
        port: s3-api
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 60   # was 10
      timeoutSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3

This compounds the savings: even if the in-app cache somehow leaks one
backend call per probe, dropping the cadence 6× still keeps us within
B2's free Class C cap with comfortable headroom.

Out-of-scope here: the same change should be applied to any other
clusters running ARMOR (apexalgo-iad, etc.). Track those separately.
close_reason: Bumped readinessProbe periodSeconds from 10 to 60 in declarative-config k8s/ord-devimprint/devimprint/armor-deployment.yml. Reduces probe frequency 6x to stay within B2 free Class C cap.

title: readyz: replace HeadBucket fallback with manifest last-flush health signal
description:
## Problem

The /readyz fallback path (when canary is not running) calls HeadBucket via the AWS SDK, which maps to a Class C (paid) operation in B2's S3-compatible API.

## Solution

Remove the HeadBucket fallback entirely. Use the manifest writer's last successful delta flush timestamp as the health signal instead — this is already in memory from normal operation and costs zero B2 API calls.

## New readyz logic

- Canary running + healthy → 200 (zero B2 calls)
- Canary running + unhealthy → 503 (zero B2 calls)
- Manifest writer last flush within threshold → 200 (zero B2 calls)
- None of the above → 503

## Changes required

- Add LastFlush() time.Time accessor to manifest.Writer
- Update Server.readyz to check manifest writer flush time as fallback before HeadBucket
- Remove HeadBucket call from readyz (and backendHealthCache if no longer needed)
- Update readyz tests to cover manifest-writer fallback path
- Update TestReadyzConcurrentCachedHead to use manifest writer path instead of HeadBucket
close_reason:
Replaced HeadBucket fallback in /readyz with manifest writer's last flush timestamp health signal.

- Added LastFlush() accessor to manifest.Writer that returns the timestamp of the most recent successful delta upload
- Removed backendHealthCache and HeadBucket call from readyz endpoint
- Updated readyz to check manifest writer flush time (60s threshold) as fallback when canary is not running
- Updated tests to use manifest writer path instead of HeadBucket

This eliminates all Class C B2 API calls from the readyz endpoint, reducing cost and latency while maintaining reliable health signal detection.

title: Suppress misleading WARN when B2 key is bucket-scoped
description:
## Problem

At startup ARMOR logs:

```
WARN  Failed to create B2 keys client - key management disabled
      error: b2_authorize_account: 401:
```

...whenever the configured B2 application key is scoped to a single bucket (the production/recommended configuration). Bucket-scoped app keys authenticate correctly for S3 ops against their bucket but **cannot** call the account-level `b2_authorize_account` endpoint that the keys-management subsystem needs. The 401 is returned by B2 by design.

This has caused false-alarm investigations on both `ardenone-hub` (bucket `armor-apexalgo`) and `ord-devimprint` (bucket `devimprint`) — operators saw the WARN, assumed credentials were broken, and chased it before realizing S3 traffic was flowing fine.

## Fix

Detect the bucket-scoped case and either:

1. **Preferred**: if `ARMOR_BUCKET` is set, skip the keys-client init entirely and log at INFO: `B2 key management disabled (application key is bucket-scoped)`.
2. **Minimum**: downgrade the log level to INFO and rewrite the message so it reads as expected behavior, not a failure. E.g.: `B2 key management unavailable — application key lacks account-level scope (this is normal when ARMOR_BUCKET is set)`.

Option 1 avoids even making the failing API call; option 2 keeps current behavior but stops scaring operators.

## Acceptance

- Starting ARMOR with a bucket-scoped B2 key emits no WARN or ERROR about `b2_authorize_account`.
- S3 read/write paths still work identically.
- If someone misconfigures a truly invalid key (wrong id/secret), they still get a clear error at S3-op time.
close_reason: Fixed misleading WARN when B2 key is bucket-scoped. When ARMOR_BUCKET is set (production config), the B2 application key is scoped to a single bucket and cannot call account-level B2 API endpoints like b2_authorize_account. Previously, ARMOR would attempt to create the B2 keys client regardless, resulting in a 401 error logged as WARN. Now, when ARMOR_BUCKET is set, we skip the B2 keys client initialization entirely and log at INFO level. S3 read/write paths unaffected - S3 backend created independently using same credentials.

title: armor: CrashLoopBackOff on ord-devimprint — SIGTERM after ~90s uptime
description:
## Bug

ARMOR pod on ord-devimprint (namespace: devimprint) is in CrashLoopBackOff with 67+ restarts over 19h.

**Symptoms:**
- ARMOR starts fine, logs show successful startup listening on :9000
- After ~90s, receives SIGTERM and exits cleanly (exit code 0)
- Cycle repeats

**Known facts:**
- `/healthz` (liveness probe) always returns 200 — pure liveness, no backend checks
- `/readyz` (readiness probe) uses in-memory canary status, returns 503 if unhealthy
- Readiness probe failures do NOT kill pods — only liveness failures do
- Exit code 0 rules out OOM (would be 137)
- ARMOR handles SIGTERM gracefully with 3-phase shutdown (60s timeout per phase)
- Liveness config: http://:9000/healthz, initialDelay=10s, period=30s, failureThreshold=3
  → would kill after 10 + 3×30 = 100s (matches observed ~90s)

**What to investigate:**
1. Check ARMOR container logs for panics or fatal errors before the SIGTERM — a goroutine panic
   could kill the HTTP server, making /healthz unreachable, triggering liveness failure
2. Check if B2 backend is reachable from the ORD cluster — if ARMOR can't connect to B2 at all,
   it may panic during the first canary round-trip
3. Check ARMOR stderr for Go runtime panics (may not appear in stdout logs)
4. Verify the armor image version matches the source — the deployment comment says v0.1.5 but
   the actual image tag may differ
5. Check ARMOR startup env vars — missing B2 credentials could cause immediate failure

**Kubeconfig note:**
The ord-devimprint kubeconfig token expired 2026-04-26 19:10 EDT. Must be refreshed before
investigating. The cluster is a Rackspace Spot cluster — re-login via Spot dashboard to get
a new token.

## Deployment
- Manifest: `k8s/ord-devimprint/devimprint/armor-deployment.yml` in declarative-config
- Image: `ronaldraygun/armor:latest` (should be pinned)
- Resources: 50m CPU / 128Mi req, 512Mi limit

## Impact
Website-builder cannot connect to armor:9000 for S3 data. No new site builds are being
produced. The DevImprint leaderboard CSS fix is deployed but can't take effect until armor
recovers and website-builder completes a build cycle.
close_reason:
Investigation completed. ARMOR on ord-devimprint is healthy - 3/3 replicas Running with 0 restarts.

## Retrospective
- **What worked:** Direct investigation via kubectl commands to check pod status, canary health, and logs. The port-forward method allowed checking canary status without curl in the container.
- **What didn't:** Initial attempts to use curl/wget inside the container failed (not included in minimal image). Had to use port-forward instead.
- **Surprise:** The issue appears to have already been resolved - likely by the version upgrade from 0.1.8 to 0.1.11 and/or the ExternalSecret refresh.
- **Reusable pattern:** For health check debugging on pods without curl/wget, use kubectl port-forward to access endpoints locally.

## Notes
- Image: ronaldraygun/armor:0.1.11 (upgraded from v0.1.8)
- Canary: healthy (decrypt_verified, hmac_verified)
- Website-builder: successfully connecting and completing builds
- Investigation notes committed to notes/armor-l64-investigation.md

title: Loosen SigV4 region validation — accept any region
description:
## Problem

ARMOR validates incoming SigV4 signatures against its configured B2 region (e.g. `us-west-002`). Clients that sign with a different region in their Credential scope fail with:

```
AccessDenied: Invalid credentials
```

even though their access key / secret pair is correct. This has already bitten at least one caller on `ord-devimprint`: the devimprint workers hardcode `region_name='auto'` in their boto3 client (an R2 convention), which silently overrides `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`. Every PutObject against ARMOR was rejected on signature mismatch despite valid credentials.

The region check adds no real security or tenant-separation — ARMOR is a single-tenant proxy in front of a single B2 bucket. Region in the Credential scope is informational only; rejecting mismatches just turns ARMOR into a footgun for S3 clients written for R2, MinIO, or any non-AWS endpoint that historically ignores region.

## Fix

Accept any non-empty region string in the SigV4 Credential scope. The signature recomputation must still use whatever region the client claimed — otherwise the HMAC chain breaks — but ARMOR should **not** require the claimed region to match its own `ARMOR_B2_REGION` config.

Concretely in the verifier:

- Parse `Credential=<access_key>/<date>/<region>/s3/aws4_request`.
- Recompute the signing key using the parsed `<region>` (not the configured region).
- Compare the recomputed signature to the provided one.
- Accept if they match; reject only on real signature mismatch, missing/bad credential, or bad key ID.

## Acceptance

- Clients signing with `region='auto'`, `region='us-east-1'`, or `region='us-west-002'` all succeed when their access key / secret is valid.
- Clients with a wrong secret still get AccessDenied (signature mismatch).
- Clients with a bogus access key ID still get AccessDenied.
- Existing clients that correctly use `us-west-002` continue to work unchanged.
- Add a test covering at least `auto`, `us-east-1`, and the configured region, each with a valid and an invalid secret.

## Why this over fixing clients

There's a parallel option of patching each caller (devimprint worker code, any future caller) to read region from env or hardcode the right value. That's a losing game — every new S3 library or tool that's R2- or MinIO-flavored will repeat this trap, and each failure surfaces as "Invalid credentials" which points investigators at secrets, not region config. Making ARMOR tolerant once fixes it forever.
close_reason: Loosened SigV4 region validation to accept any non-empty region in the Credential scope. buildStringToSign and getSigningKeyForCredential now take an explicit region parameter from the client's credential scope instead of using configured B2 region. Clients with region=auto, us-east-1, etc. now succeed with valid credentials; wrong secrets still rejected. Tests added.

title: ListObjectsV2 response cache in ARMOR to eliminate redundant B2 Class C calls
description:
## Problem
All devimprint workers (aggregator, website-builder, litestream) list the same S3 prefixes repeatedly. Since commits/ objects are write-once parquet files, listing the same prefix twice within a short window returns identical results. ARMOR forwards every list request directly to B2 — no deduplication or caching.

At peak (both aggregator + website-builder every 5 min, 30-day DuckDB partition scan): ~17,000 Class C calls/day, exhausting B2 transaction caps.

## Solution
Add a TTL cache for ListObjectsV2 responses in ARMOR. Cache key: bucket + prefix + delimiter + maxKeys + continuationToken. TTL: configurable via ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL env var, default 60s.

Commits/ objects are immutable after write, so a 60s TTL is safe — clients will see new objects within one TTL window.

## Scope
- New ListCache type in internal/backend/cache.go
- Cache integration in ListObjectsV2 handler (handlers.go)
- Cache invalidation on PutObject/DeleteObject for the affected prefix
- ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL env var (default 60, 0 = disabled)
- ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES env var (default 1000)
- Tests
- Deployment env var in declarative-config armor-deployment.yml
close_reason:
Summary of what was done:

The ListObjectsV2 response cache feature was already fully implemented in the ARMOR codebase:

**Code (already implemented):**
- internal/backend/cache.go: ListCache type with Get/Set/InvalidatePrefix methods
- internal/config/config.go: ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES (1000) and ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL (60) env vars
- internal/server/server.go: ListCache creation and wiring to handlers
- internal/server/handlers/handlers.go: Cache integration in ListObjectsV2 handler and invalidation on PutObject/DeleteObject
- internal/backend/cache_test.go: Comprehensive tests (all passing)

**Changes made:**
- Added explicit ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES and ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL env vars to deployment configs:
  - k8s/ardenone-hub/armor/armor-deployment.yml
  - k8s/ord-devimprint/devimprint/armor-deployment.yml

**Impact:**
- Reduces redundant B2 Class C API calls by caching ListObjectsV2 responses for 60 seconds
- Commits/ objects are write-once parquet files, so 60s TTL is safe
- At peak (17k Class C calls/day), this should significantly reduce B2 transaction usage

The feature was complete in code; only the deployment env vars needed to be made explicit.

title: Add ListCache type to internal/backend/cache.go
description:
Add a ListCache struct alongside MetadataCache in cache.go.

Cache key: bucket + "|" + prefix + "|" + delimiter + "|" + strconv.Itoa(maxKeys) + "|" + continuationToken
Value: the full backend.ListResult struct (prefixes + contents + isTruncated + nextToken)
TTL: configurable, from server config (ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL seconds)
Max entries: configurable (ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES)
Eviction: same oldest-first strategy as MetadataCache

Methods:
- NewListCache(maxEntries int, ttlSeconds int) *ListCache
- Get(bucket, prefix, delimiter string, maxKeys int, continuationToken string) (*ListResult, bool)
- Set(bucket, prefix, delimiter string, maxKeys int, continuationToken string, result *ListResult)
- InvalidatePrefix(bucket, prefix string) — deletes all entries where key starts with bucket+"|"+prefix
- Clear()
close_reason: Added ListCache struct to internal/backend/cache.go alongside MetadataCache. Cache key is bucket|prefix|delimiter|maxKeys|continuationToken; value is *ListResult. TTL and max entries configurable via ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_TTL and ARMOR_LIST_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES (defaults: 60s, 1000 entries). Implements Get, Set, InvalidatePrefix, Clear with oldest-first eviction. Config fields added and 6 tests written.

title: Integrate ListCache into ListObjectsV2 handler
description:
In handlers.go handleListObjectsV2():

1. On cache hit: return the cached ListBucketResult directly — skip the backend.List() call entirely.
2. On cache miss: call backend.List() as today, then store the result in the list cache before returning.
3. Cache is only consulted when listCache != nil (TTL=0 path skips caching).

Invalidation hooks (in the same handler file):
- handlePutObject: after a successful put, call listCache.InvalidatePrefix(bucket, path.Dir(key)+"/") to evict any cached listing that would now be stale.
- handleDeleteObject: same InvalidatePrefix call after successful delete.

The key insight: InvalidatePrefix only needs to clear entries whose prefix is an ancestor of the mutated key, not the entire cache.

title: Tests for ListCache: hit/miss, TTL expiry, prefix invalidation, disabled path
description:
Unit tests in internal/backend/cache_test.go (or new list_cache_test.go):

1. Cache miss on first call, hit on second identical call
2. TTL expiry: entry is gone after TTL elapses (use time injection or short TTL)
3. InvalidatePrefix: evicts entries whose prefix matches, leaves unrelated prefixes intact
4. Clear: empties the cache
5. TTL=0 (disabled): NewListCache returns nil or a no-op implementation; handler skips caching

Integration-level test (if there's an existing httptest-based test suite):
- Verify backend.List() is called once for two identical requests within TTL window
- Verify backend.List() is called again after a PutObject invalidates the prefix
close_reason: Added unit and integration tests for ListCache: hit/miss, TTL expiry, prefix invalidation, clear, and disabled path (NewListCache returns nil for TTL=0). Integration tests verify backend.List() call counts for cache hit, PutObject invalidation, and nil cache paths.

Fix S3 response date format for DuckDB httpfs compatibility
description:
## Problem
DuckDB's httpfs extension cannot parse ARMOR's S3 responses during LIST operations. The `LastModified` value appears in HTTP-date format (`"Sun, 26 Apr 2026 01:02:05 GMT"`) which DuckDB can't cast to a timestamp, causing `InvalidInputException` when glob-expanding S3 paths like `s3://devimprint/commits/**/*.parquet`.

This forced the aggregator to bypass DuckDB httpfs entirely — it now uses boto3 for listing/downloading and pyarrow for reading Parquet, with DuckDB only for in-memory SQL. This workaround is functional but ~10x slower than native DuckDB httpfs (20 min/cycle vs expected ~2 min).

## Root Cause
ARMOR's handlers use two date formats:
- XML body (ListObjectsV2): `time.RFC3339` — ISO 8601, correct
- HTTP headers (Get/Head/Put responses): `http.TimeFormat` — HTTP-date format, incompatible with DuckDB

DuckDB's httpfs appears to encounter the HTTP-date format during glob expansion, either from individual HEAD/GET requests or from a code path that returns header-style dates in the XML body.

## Scope
- Identify exact response path DuckDB hits during glob expansion
- Ensure all S3 API response dates are in ISO 8601 / RFC3339 format
- Maintain backward compatibility with existing clients (boto3, s3cmd, etc.)
- Revert aggregator boto3 workaround once ARMOR is fixed
close_reason: Fix already implemented - updated notes to document HTTP header ISO 8601 change (commit 961c610)

title: Identify exact ARMOR response path causing DuckDB date parse failure
description:
## Goal
Pinpoint exactly which HTTP response or XML field DuckDB's httpfs encounters the HTTP-date format in, so the fix targets the right code path.

## Steps
1. Run DuckDB httpfs against a local ARMOR instance with debug logging enabled
2. Capture the failing LIST/GET/HEAD response that contains HTTP-date format
3. Trace whether the bad date comes from XML body LastModified, HTTP Last-Modified header, or another field
4. Check if DuckDB parses dates from response headers at all, or only from XML body
5. Identify all handler code paths in handlers.go that serve the problematic response

## Key Files
- `/home/coding/ARMOR/internal/server/handlers/handlers.go` — S3 handler implementations
- Lines 598, 617, 658, 1106, 1117, 1154 — HTTP header date formatting with `http.TimeFormat`
- Line 1472 — XML body date formatting with `time.RFC3339`

## Acceptance
- Documented evidence of which code path produces the bad date
- List of specific lines/functions that need to change

title: Fix date formatting in ARMOR S3 handlers for DuckDB compatibility
description:
## Goal
Change ARMOR's S3 response date formatting so DuckDB httpfs can parse timestamps correctly.

## Approach
Based on investigation findings, update the identified code paths to use RFC3339/ISO 8601 format consistently. The HTTP `Last-Modified` header must remain in HTTP-date format per RFC 7232 — but the XML body LastModified fields and any other timestamp fields that DuckDB parses must use ISO 8601.

If the issue is in the XML body, verify the exact ISO 8601 format DuckDB expects (e.g., `2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z` vs `2006-01-02T15:04:05Z`).

If the issue is that DuckDB parses HTTP headers, consider adding an ISO 8601 date header alongside the standard HTTP-date one, or ensure the XML body is the sole source DuckDB uses.

## Key Files
- `/home/coding/ARMOR/internal/server/handlers/handlers.go`
- Potentially `/home/coding/ARMOR/internal/backend/b2.go`

## Acceptance
- All S3 API responses use parseable ISO 8601 dates where DuckDB expects them
- Existing clients (boto3, s3cmd, rclone) still work (they accept both formats)
- No regression in encryption/decryption or other ARMOR functionality
close_reason: Standardized timestamp format in S3 XML responses to use ISO 8601 with millisecond precision ("2006-01-02T15:04:05.000Z") consistently across all operations (CopyObject, ListObjectsV2, ListBuckets, ListParts, ListMultipartUploads, ListObjectVersions). This format matches AWS S3's standard response format and ensures compatibility with DuckDB httpfs timestamp parsing. HTTP headers continue to use http.TimeFormat as required by RFC 7232.

title: Test DuckDB httpfs glob query through ARMOR on ord-devimprint
description:
## Goal
Verify DuckDB can glob-expand and query Parquet files through the updated ARMOR proxy without date parse errors.

## Prerequisites
- armor-s8k.3.1 complete (ARMOR v0.1.8 deployed and healthy)

## Steps
1. Exec into the aggregator pod on ord-devimprint:
   ```bash
   POD=$(kubectl --kubeconfig=/home/coding/.kube/ord-devimprint.kubeconfig get pods -n devimprint -l app=aggregator -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
   kubectl --kubeconfig=/home/coding/.kube/ord-devimprint.kubeconfig exec -n devimprint $POD -- python3 - <<'EOF'
   import duckdb, os
   con = duckdb.connect()
   con.execute("INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
   con.execute("SET s3_endpoint='armor:9000';")
   con.execute("SET s3_use_ssl=false;")
   con.execute(f"SET s3_access_key_id='{os.environ['S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID']}';")
   con.execute(f"SET s3_secret_access_key='{os.environ['S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY']}';")
   con.execute("SET s3_url_style='path';")
   result = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM read_parquet('s3://devimprint/commits/**/*.parquet')").fetchone()
   print('Row count:', result[0])
   EOF
   ```
2. Verify no `InvalidInputException` or date parse errors in the output
3. Spot-check that LastModified timestamps in a LIST response are parseable:
   ```python
   rows = con.execute("SELECT file_last_modified FROM parquet_file_metadata('s3://devimprint/commits/**/*.parquet') LIMIT 5").fetchall()
   print(rows)
   ```

## Acceptance
- COUNT(*) returns a non-zero integer with no errors
- No `InvalidInputException` in output
- Timestamps are valid (not year 1970 or garbage)

/home/coding/ARMOR (for reference; kubectl commands use ord-devimprint kubeconfig)

title: Verify the assertion fails on a missing manifest and push to declarative-config
description:

notes:
VERIFY + SHIP complete.

(a) EVIDENCE — missing manifest fails the assertion step:

CODE REVIEW of verify-push (armor-workflowtemplate.yml@95116c22): on a non-200 manifest CODE the script never enters the exit-0 branch — it loops 4x (20s backoff) and falls through to 'exit 1'. set -e fails fast on any command error; no-creds path = exit 1; no-token path across all attempts = fall-through exit 1; no continueOn on the step-group so the workflow fails (short-circuits) on a step failure. Step-group (verify-server-image + verify-restore-verifier-image) is ordered AFTER the kaniko docker-build group.

LIVE TEST — independently reproduced the exact manifest-API probe (anonymous token against public library/alpine; control flow byte-identical to shipped template, only sleep 20->1 to keep the test quick):
  - Missing tag library/alpine:ghost-tag-bf-11ghx4-does-not-exist-9f8e7d: attempt 1-4 manifest HTTP 404 -> 'Image verification failed' -> exit code 1
  - Real tag library/alpine:3.19: HTTP 200 attempt 1 -> 'Image verification succeeded' -> exit code 0   (sanity: discriminating, not blindly always-failing)
Docker Hub manifest API itself returns 200 for existing / 404 for non-existent tags. Conclusion: a ghost tag (bumped VERSION, no pullable manifest) cannot reach exit 0 and fails the workflow.

YAML validated: parses clean; kind=WorkflowTemplate name=armor-build; verify-push template defined; ordered steps resolve-version -> lint -> test -> docker-build -> verify-server-image(+verify-restore-verifier-image). No kind: Job/CronJob. Pinned alpine:3.19, activeDeadlineSeconds 300.

title: Offline decrypt/recovery CLI — restore objects with only MEK + B2 ciphertext
description:
WHY: ARMOR is the encryption layer for backup/archive pipelines (an archive-to-B2 pipeline for another project is blocked on ARMOR maturing). The 2026-03-27 data-loss incident motivated encryption. A backup is only durable if it can be recovered WITHOUT a running ARMOR server: today the only decryptor is the live proxy (cmd/armor/main.go is server-only, no subcommands; scripts/ has only verify-cloudflare-setup.sh). docs/plan/plan.md 'Decisions and Rationale' claims 'envelope enables offline reading' but no tool exists.

WHAT: a standalone decrypt tool, either a subcommand (e.g. 'armor decrypt') in cmd/armor or a separate cmd/armor-decrypt binary, that:
- reads an encrypted envelope from a local file OR fetches from B2/HTTPS URL
- parses the envelope header (magic ARMR, version byte, block size, IV, plaintext size, block count — see plan.md 'Encrypted Object Format'), falling back to x-amz-meta-armor-* metadata when needed
- unwraps the DEK using a MEK supplied via env var or flag (hex, 32 bytes); supports named multi-key MEKs via x-amz-meta-armor-key-id
- verifies per-block HMAC-SHA256 (HKDF-derived key, info=armor-hmac-v1) and reports integrity failures per block
- handles multipart-uploaded objects whose HMAC table lives in the .armor/hmac/<sha256-of-key> sidecar (envelope reserved-byte flag; see plan.md 'Multipart Upload Operations')
- writes verified plaintext to stdout or a file
Reuse internal/crypto (envelope.go, decryptor.go, keys.go, hkdf.go) — no new crypto.

ACCEPTANCE:
- go build produces the tool; unit test round-trips: encrypt via internal/crypto, decrypt via the tool code path (single-part and sidecar-HMAC cases)
- Decrypting a sample envelope with only the MEK (no B2 credentials, no server config) succeeds
- Wrong MEK and corrupted block produce clear, non-zero-exit errors
- README.md gains a 'Disaster recovery / offline decryption' section documenting usage
- No secrets, keys, or bucket names hardcoded

description:
Research and understand the current test setup for compressed object GET requests.

notes:
## Exploration: compressed-object GET test structure (share_decompress_test.go)

### File: internal/server/share_decompress_test.go (package server, 665 lines)
Git state: modified (tracked), not staged. Other compression tests live in internal/crypto/crypto_test.go and crypto_decompress_test.go.

### Test functions (7 total)
1. TestShareGET_CompressedObject — basic compressed GET; only test that inlines its own *config.Config (the rest use loadTestConfig). Asserts decompressed body == original AND compressed != original.
2. TestShareGET_UncompressedObject — uncompressed served as-is.
3. TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior — TABLE-DRIVEN, 5 cases: uncompressed_small_text, uncompressed_binary_data(50KB), compressed_repeating_text, compressed_binary_data(100KB), legacy_object_no_compression_flag. Asserts data round-trips + verifies wantDecompression invariant + metadata.Compressed == tc.compressed.
4. TestShareGET_LegacyObject — legacy object, Compressed explicitly false.
5. TestShareGET_RoundTrip — TABLE-DRIVEN, 3 sizes: small_text, medium_binary(100KB), large_binary(512KB). Full compress->encrypt->store->GET->decompress.
6. TestShareGET_CompressionDetectionFromFirstBlock — asserts crypto.IsCompressed sees zstd magic after decrypt.
7. TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression — range req on compressed obj. ONLY checks status code (206|200), does NOT verify body content.

### Test helpers (7 total) — all t.Helper()
- setupTestEnvironment(t) -> (tmpDir string, cleanup func()) — os.MkdirTemp, cleanup removes it.
- loadTestConfig(t, tmpDir) -> *config.Config — sets ARMOR_B2_*/ARMOR_BUCKET/ARMOR_MEK/ARMOR_PRESIGN_SECRET/ARMOR_SECONDARY_BACKEND_{TYPE=filesystem,PATH=tmpDir} env vars, calls config.Load(), t.Cleanup unsets them.
- encryptTestData(t, srv, data, compressed) -> (encrypted, hmacTable []byte, armorMeta *backend.ARMORMetadata) — srv.keyManager.GetMEK("test-key"); GenerateDEK+GenerateIV; NewEncryptor(dek,iv,65536); encryptor.Encrypt; crypto.WrapDEK(mek,dek); builds ARMORMetadata{Version:1,BlockSize:65536,PlaintextSize:len(data),...,Compressed:compressed}. NOTE: PlaintextSHA is a placeholder "test-sha256", not real.
- storeTestObject(t, backend, ctx, bucket, key, encData, hmacTable, armorMeta) — builds envelope = crypto.NewEnvelopeHeader(...).Encode() + encData + hmacTable; armorMeta.ToMetadata(); backend.Put. objectKey convention = "test-key-"+tc.name (must be unique per case).
- generateTestToken(t, srv, bucket, key, expiration) -> string — srv.presigner.GenerateToken.
- compressData(data) -> []byte — zstd.NewWriter, no error return (panics).
- generateRandomData(size) -> []byte — crypto/rand (panics on err).

### Canonical per-case pattern
setupTestEnvironment -> backend.NewFSBackend(BasePath:tmpDir) -> loadTestConfig(t,tmpDir) -> NewWithBackend(cfg,fsBackend) -> srv.presigner = presign.NewSigner(cfg.PresignSecret,"") (REQUIRED: NewWithBackend skips presigner init) -> [compressData if compressed] -> encryptTestData(t,srv,data,compressed) -> storeTestObject(...) -> generateTestToken(...) -> httptest.NewRequest GET /share/<token> + NewRecorder -> srv.handleShare(w,req) -> assert 200 + io.ReadAll body + bytes.Equal(retrieved, original).

### How to add a table-driven case (TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior)
Append struct{name,data []byte,compressed bool,wantDecompression bool,description string} to testCases. objectKey auto-derived as "test-key-"+tc.name so name must be unique. Body uses setupTestEnvironment/loadTestConfig each iteration (fresh env per subtest). Invariants already enforced: data round-trip; if wantDecompression then retrieved != dataToEncrypt (decompress ran); else retrieved == dataToEncrypt (bypassed); armorMeta.Compressed == tc.compressed.

### Production gating (key for any new case)
- handleShare (server.go:952): full objects -> handleShareFullObject (1066); range -> handleShareRangeRequest (1196).
- handleShareFullObject: decompresses ONLY when armorMeta.Compressed==true (server.go:1175). First-block crypto.IsCompressed is LOGGED ONLY, never gates decompression -> metadata flag is authoritative. crypto.Decompress is a no-op if no zstd magic.
- handleShareRangeRequest (server.go:1260): detects isCompressed but does NOT decompress — returns still-compressed plaintext range + Content-Range. This is a behavioral GAP with no body-correctness coverage.

### Gaps a new test case could target (for the implementation sibling bead)
- No body-correctness assertion for compressed RANGE requests (TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression only checks status). Range path does not decompress at all.
- No multipart-upload object case in this file (separate internal/crypto/multipart_short_final_part_test.go exists). The table-driven suite does not exercise multi-block/short-final-block compressed objects.
- PlaintextSHA in encryptTestData is a placeholder, so no integrity-sha round-trip is verified here.

title: Verify decoded value is human-readable and not corrupted
description:
## Child Bead: Verify decoded value is human-readable and not corrupted

This bead performs final validation that the decoded value is clean, readable text with no corruption.

### Prerequisites
- Previous child bead complete (bf-1y0g6: value matches AWS access key format)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Value contains only printable ASCII characters
- No control characters, null bytes, or binary data
- No trailing/leading whitespace (except newline)
- Value is not garbled or corrupted
- Hex dump shows clean ASCII

### Commands
```bash
# Display the value one more time for confirmation
echo "Final decoded value:"
cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
echo ""

# Check for non-printable characters (should be none)
if cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -P '[[:cntrl:]]' > /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: File contains control characters"
    cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | od -c | head -5
    exit 1
else
    echo "No control characters detected"
fi

# Check for null bytes
if cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -P '\x00' > /dev/null; then
    echo "ERROR: File contains null bytes"
    exit 1
else
    echo "No null bytes detected"
fi

# Show hex dump to verify clean ASCII
echo "Hex dump (first 40 bytes):"
xxd -l 40 /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt

# Verify file type
FILETYPE=$(file -b /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt)
echo "File type: $FILETYPE"

if echo "$FILETYPE" | grep -qiE 'text|ascii'; then
    echo "SUCCESS: File is clean text/ASCII data"
else
    echo "WARNING: Unexpected file type"
fi

# Final confirmation
VALUE=$(cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')
echo ""
echo "=== VALIDATION COMPLETE ==="
echo "Decoded AWS Access Key ID: $VALUE"
echo "Length: ${#VALUE} characters"
echo "File: /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt"
```

Success: Value is clean, human-readable ASCII with no corruption.

Failure: Value contains control chars, null bytes, or binary corruption — secret may be corrupted.

title: ardenone-hub ARMOR pod CrashLoopBackOff — liveness probe failure on new replica
description: The ARMOR deployment on ardenone-hub (devimprint namespace) has two pods: one healthy (armor-7c79d57db6-k2j6j, 32 restarts) and one stuck in CrashLoopBackOff (armor-755d878c84-l8grt, 60+ restarts). The crashing pod logs show it starts successfully then immediately exits with no error logged. All ExternalSecrets in devimprint are in SecretSyncedError state (ClusterSecretStore openbao is not ready). The new pod cannot load secrets from OpenBao (B2 credentials, MEK, auth keys) and fails the liveness probe at /healthz:9000 after startup. The surviving pod uses secrets from a previous successful sync. Mitigation options: (1) Fix OpenBao on ardenone-hub (short term), or (2) Migrate devimprint workloads off ardenone-hub (planned decommission).    - Sends the request via raw urllib3 or similar (no AWS SDK abstraction)
2. Execute this script against the LIVE ARMOR pod:
   - Use the SAME operation type that fails (PUT, GET, or ListObjectsV2)
   - Use the SAME bucket/key path as a failed aws-cli request
   - Use the EXACT same timestamp (or as close as possible)
3. Observe the result:
   - If it SUCCEEDS: The bug is in botocore's request framing (header ordering, Expect: 100-continue, etc.)
   - If it FAILS: The bug is in ARMOR's auth verification logic itself (not client-side)
4. Document the exact request sent (headers in order, canonical request, string-to-sign, final signature)
5. Output: A clear "RAW REQUEST WORKS" or "RAW REQUEST FAILS" with full evidence

## Dependency
Depends on bf-2l4j0z (streaming auth test) -- if streaming auth already found the bug, this may be redundant, but it's still valuable as a minimal reproduction

## Why This Fourth
This isolates the problem from botocore entirely. If a mathematically perfect hand-built request still fails, we've proven ARMOR's verification is rejecting valid signatures. If it works, we know the issue is some subtle botocore framing difference that ARMOR doesn't tolerate.

## Out of Scope
- Rewriting ARMOR's auth.go (that's a separate fix bead)
- Testing every S3 operation (one representative operation is enough)

title: Verify expvar.Map.Add thread-safety guarantees
description:
## Task
Investigate and verify whether expvar.Map.Add is thread-safe for concurrent increments from multiple goroutines.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Document findings about expvar.Map.Add internal implementation
- Verify whether it uses mutex or atomic operations
- Cite Go standard library source or documentation
- Update bead with findings

## Implementation Notes
- Check Go standard library source: src/expvar/expvar.go
- Look for mutex or sync/atomic usage
- Verify if Add() method is documented as thread-safe
- Document findings in this bead
close_reason:
Thread-safety verification complete. expvar.Map.Add IS thread-safe for concurrent increments from multiple goroutines.

Key findings:
1. Package documentation explicitly states: 'Operations to set or modify these public variables are atomic.'

2. Map.Add implementation uses sync.Map for concurrent-safe access:
   - sync.Map.LoadOrStore() is atomic
   - addKey() is protected by keysMu sync.RWMutex

3. The underlying Int type uses atomic.Int64.Add() for thread-safe increments:
   type Int struct {
     i atomic.Int64
   }
   
   func (v *Int) Add(delta int64) {
     v.i.Add(delta)
   }

Source: https://go.googlesource.com/go/+/refs/heads/master/src/expvar/expvar.go

The implementation provides full thread-safety guarantees for concurrent Add() calls from multiple goroutines.

title: B2 endpoint and region are not recorded with the credentials — cold recovery must discover them
description:
During a verified break-glass drill on 2026-08-08, armor-decrypt could not run from the stored credentials alone. The credential store holds only key_id and application_key; ARMOR_B2_REGION and ARMOR_B2_ENDPOINT live in a Kubernetes ConfigMap in the cluster being recovered, which is exactly what may be gone.

They had to be discovered by calling B2's API:
  curl -s -u "$KEY_ID:$APP_KEY" https://api.backblazeb2.com/b2api/v3/b2_authorize_account | jq -r '.apiInfo.storageApi | "\(.s3ApiUrl) \(.bucketName)"'

That works and is now documented, but it is an avoidable extra step under pressure, and it depends on the B2 API being reachable and its response shape being stable.

Fix: store region, endpoint and bucket alongside the MEK and B2 credentials in escrow, so the recovery inputs are self-contained. Related: armor-decrypt also requires ARMOR_B2_* env names specifically and ignores AWS_*, which cost a failed first attempt in the same drill (now documented).

title: Verify multipart/HMAC fix independently: ~100MB Parquet round-trip + DuckDB ranged reads on ord-devimprint
description:
Verify the multipart/HMAC decrypt fix with an INDEPENDENT large-object round-trip that does
not depend on the queue-api litestream chain, and that additionally exercises ranged reads.

## Why this bead exists

bf-1v6skf holds the multipart/HMAC decrypt bug. Its code fix is already confirmed live: a
real 56.6MB production object was GET+decrypted byte-exact through the fleet on 0.1.1901
(2026-07-22), spanning roughly 864 blocks -- well past the historical failure point. But
that bead cannot close, because its acceptance criterion is specifically a
queue-api/litestream restore transcript, and that chain has no compacted snapshot to test
against yet. As of 2026-07-26 the queue-api replica in B2 contains only small level-0
segments (about 4KB to 385KB), so a large-object restore cannot be demonstrated there for
some time.

This bead unblocks the confidence question without waiting on litestream. It is NOT a
replacement for the bf-1v6skf acceptance criterion -- that bead should still close on its
own transcript. This one provides independent evidence, on the cluster that matters, and
covers a path litestream never touches.

## Why Parquet specifically

A litestream restore is a sequential whole-object read. It never exercises ranged reads.
DuckDB reading Parquet over S3 does the opposite: it issues HTTP range requests for the
footer and then for selected row groups. ARMOR translates plaintext ranges to ciphertext
ranges over AES-256-CTR, so ranged decrypt is a genuinely distinct code path from whole-file
decrypt, and it is the exact access pattern the commitgraph aggregator uses. Testing with a
Parquet file covers both paths in one artifact and gives a known-good local baseline to
compare against.

## Sizing rationale (do not shrink this)

- ord-devimprint runs ARMOR_BLOCK_SIZE=65536, i.e. 64 KiB blocks.
- The historical failure was at block 256, which at 64 KiB is 16 MiB.
- A 100MB object is roughly 1600 blocks, about 6x past that point.
- The existing canary defaults to a 6MB multipart object, which is only about 96 blocks --
  BELOW block 256. The canary therefore cannot catch this class of bug at its default size.
  That gap is worth its own bead; note it rather than silently relying on the canary.
- B2 requires a 5 MiB minimum part size for non-final multipart parts, so a 100MB object
  yields a genuine multi-part upload rather than a single-part write.

## Preferred approach

Option A -- reuse an existing large object. If a corpus Parquet of at least ~100MB already
exists in a bucket fronted by the ord-devimprint ARMOR, verify against that first. Cheapest
and tests real production data. Requirement: it must have been WRITTEN by 0.1.1901 or later.
The bug was specifically that ARMOR could not decrypt objects it wrote itself, so verifying
against an object written by an older build proves nothing about the fix.

Option B -- generate a purpose-built Parquet of about 100MB. Preferred if no qualifying
object exists, and better for the ranged-read half of the test because it gives an exact
local baseline. Use multiple row groups (so row-group skipping actually issues distinct
ranges), a mix of column types, and enough rows that predicate pushdown selects a strict
subset.

## Test steps

1. Create or identify the object. Record its exact byte length and sha256 before upload.
2. PUT it through the ord-devimprint ARMOR service, not directly to the backend. It must be
   ARMOR that performs the encryption and multipart assembly.
3. Whole-object read: GET it back through ARMOR, confirm the returned length matches
   Content-Length exactly, and confirm sha256 matches the pre-upload value. A byte-count
   match alone is insufficient -- the historical corruption produced correctly-sized output.
4. Ranged read at the old failure boundary: request an explicit byte range that straddles
   block 256 (offset 16777216). Confirm those bytes match the same offsets in the local
   source file. This is the single most important assertion in this bead.
5. Ranged reads via DuckDB: point DuckDB at the object through ARMOR and run
   read_parquet over it. Confirm row count matches the local baseline, and run at least one
   aggregate (for example a SUM and a COUNT with a WHERE clause that forces row-group
   skipping) whose result matches running the same query against the local file.
6. Confirm from ARMOR logs that the DuckDB queries actually produced ranged requests rather
   than whole-object fetches -- otherwise step 5 silently degrades into a repeat of step 3.
7. Delete the test object afterwards if Option B was used.

## Routing and cost -- read before running

The ord-devimprint ARMOR sets ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN to a Cloudflare-fronted host, so downloads
through it egress via the Cloudflare edge, which is free under the Bandwidth Alliance.
Uploads to Backblaze are free ingress.

Do NOT run this test against the raw Backblaze S3 endpoint. That bypasses Cloudflare and
turns a free test into billable B2 egress. The intended data path is up through the
Backblaze endpoint and back down through the Cloudflare edge network. If the test is run
from inside the cluster, confirm the client resolves the ARMOR service and that ARMOR is
using its CF domain for the download leg.

## Acceptance criteria

- sha256 of the full round-tripped object matches the source exactly.
- A ranged read straddling offset 16777216 returns bytes identical to the local source at
  those offsets.
- DuckDB read_parquet through ARMOR returns a row count and at least one aggregate identical
  to the same query run against the local file.
- Evidence that ranged requests were actually issued (ARMOR log lines or Content-Range
  responses), not just whole-object GETs.
- A pasted transcript of the commands and their output. Do not close on a prose assertion
  that it worked -- bf-1v6skf was falsely closed four times between 07-15 and 07-18, each
  time reopened on live re-verification. Paste the evidence.
- The ARMOR build under test is recorded explicitly (expected: 0.1.1901 or later on
  ord-devimprint).

## Notes

- Test on ord-devimprint. That is the cluster commitgraph runs on, and the one whose
  large-object DR is still unproven. The 07-22 verification was on iad-kalshi.
- An operator kubeconfig with write access to ord-devimprint was obtained 2026-07-26, which
  was the gating dependency recorded in bf-2p1wr.

title: Multipart complete stores placeholder plaintext SHA (hash of empty)
description: CompleteMultipartUpload sets plaintextSHA to sha256 of empty bytes, so manifest and provenance records for every multipart object carry a meaningless integrity hash. Any future audit comparing stored SHA against content will flag every large object and real corruption cannot be distinguished from the placeholder. Fix: accumulate SHA-256 across parts in multipart state; interacts with the part-ordering decision bead.
close_reason: Verified fixed at HEAD (0.1.1897), fix commit 9f6d5694. CompleteMultipartUpload now stores a real combined digest: per-part sha256 recorded at upload (handlers.go:2325-2331) into state.PartPlaintextSHAs (multipart.go:64), combined in ascending part order via backend.CombinePartPlaintextSHAs (multipart.go:280-294) which errors on any missing part rather than silently emitting a wrong digest. Propagated to manifest (handlers.go:2563) and provenance (handlers.go:2568). Uniform part size persisted as x-amz-meta-armor-part-size (handlers.go:2550) so the digest is independently reproducible. Legacy pre-fix objects handled explicitly via backend.IsPlaceholderPlaintextSHA (multipart.go:33, consulted at handlers.go:927) rather than being mis-flagged as corrupt. Streaming re-verification without buffering via MultipartDigestAccumulator (multipart.go:340-377).

Any SHA-based verification of multipart objects is currently meaningless. title: ARMOR: large multipart objects fail HMAC verification on decrypt, breaking queue-api DR restore
description:
ARMOR multipart/HMAC decrypt bug -- CODE FIX CONFIRMED via live production test; queue-api DR restore still UNVERIFIED (separate litestream local-state stall).

Strongest evidence to date (2026-07-22): clean GET+decrypt of a real 56.6MB production object (kalshi-tape orderbook_delta.parquet, written hours after the 0.1.1901 fleet deploy) through the live fleet. Byte-exact download (matches ContentLength exactly), valid Parquet on read (1,868,214 rows, correct schema), semantically sane content (real Kalshi market tickers, timestamps matching the capture window). Spans ~864 blocks at 64KiB block size -- over 3x past the historical block-256 failure point that broke every prior "fix" four times running.

NOT sufficient to close: this bead's acceptance criterion is specifically a queue-api/litestream restore transcript -- "the literal restored file path and a real litestream/sqlite3 command transcript" (per bf-2sq7gf's acceptance criteria, cross-linked here). That chain remains blocked on litestream's own local LTX generation-tracking state loss on queue-api (ord-devimprint), independent of ARMOR -- see comment 93. No fresh queue-api snapshot exists to test against until that is fixed.

Full evidence history in comments 1-94 (four false closures 07-15 through 07-18, each reopened on live re-verification; 07-20 code-level reconciliation; 07-22 cross-cluster production verification).

Confirms this bug is a distinct, still-unresolved decrypt/HMAC-verification issue, not the routing bug bf-24sxh7 fixed. Full evidence in bf-2sq7gf.

comments.author: cli

Evidence from a local ARMOR server built at HEAD (post 3edbb9b4) against the live devimprint bucket: GET of the 2026-07-18 level-9 snapshot (0009/...6f225.ltx, ciphertext 182616450 bytes) fails 'Failed to decrypt range: block 512: HMAC verification failed'. Object forensics: x-amz-meta-armor-plaintext-sha256 = SHA of EMPTY STRING (bf-1v2ehf live in prod), declared plaintext 114459010 vs ciphertext 182616450 = exactly 65MiB inflation - the stored bytes do not match the declared layout. Remediation: deploy fixed ARMOR (bf-4qq1), ensure litestream uploads parts sequentially (else loud InvalidPartOrder failures post-deploy), force fresh baseline, verify restore (bf-5aqh0), audit multipart-era objects (bf-1ebnuz). Net effect: queue-api currently has ZERO valid restorable backups (07-18 snapshot corrupt from the old ARMOR bug; nothing newer exists to test the fix against, or to restore from if this pod/PVC were lost right now). RECONCILIATION 2026-07-20: the CODE DEFECT described here is fixed, and the fix IS in the deployed build (5bc58e0d is an ancestor of 0.1.1871, which all six fleet deployments pin). What remains is live verification only.

Read path uses ABSOLUTE block indices end-to-end, so part boundaries are a non-event: handlers.go:714 dispatches on x-amz-meta-armor-multipart; handlers.go:756-777 loads the full sidecar HMAC table and reads ciphertext from offset 0; handlers.go:872-889 indexes hmacTable[blockIndex*HMACSize:] with the same absolute blockIndex used for the CTR counter (handlers.go:893). title: Design the Docker Hub manifest-API registry-existence assertion
description:
DESIGN the assertion logic for the parent (bf-4i5cn2). Define the exact command the post-push step will run against Docker Hub to confirm the just-built tag (ronaldraygun/armor:VERSION) is pullable. It must: obtain an anonymous auth token from auth.docker.io for the ronaldraygun/armor repo; query the v2 manifest endpoint for the tag; treat HTTP 200 as success and any non-200 (404/401/etc.) as a hard failure that fails the Argo step. Document expected HTTP codes for present vs absent tags and explain how non-zero exit propagates failure to Argo Workflows.

ACCEPTANCE: the bead body contains a copy-pasteable shell snippet (token exchange plus manifest GET) with documented expected HTTP codes for present vs absent tags, and an explanation of how non-zero exit fails the workflow step. No YAML edits yet, design only.

---

# DESIGN — Docker Hub manifest-API registry-existence assertion (ghost-tag guard)
Design only; no YAML edited. For parent bf-4i5cn2.

## 0. Headline finding — corrects the task premise
`ronaldraygun/armor` is a **PRIVATE** Docker Hub repo. An **anonymous** token from
auth.docker.io returns **HTTP 401 for every manifest GET — present tags and absent
tags alike** — so the task's stated "obtain an anonymous auth token" path cannot tell
present from absent and would fail the step 100% of the time. The assertion MUST
authenticate with the SAME push credentials kaniko used (the `docker-hub-registry`
k8s Secret, already mounted into the build pod at /kaniko/.docker/config.json).

Empirical validation (2026-08-10):
- Control, public repo `library/alpine`: anon token -> manifest GET -> **200** for
  real tag `3.20`, **404** for bogus tag. present/absent distinguishable. OK.
- Target `ronaldraygun/armor`: anon token -> manifest GET -> **401** for `0.1.1905`
  (current VERSION), **401** for `latest`, **401** for `0.1.11`. Docker Hub public
  API `GET /v2/repositories/ronaldraygun/armor/` -> **404** (private). All other
  `ronaldraygun/*` likewise 404. -> anonymous path unusable; authentication required.
- The authenticated exchange itself was NOT live-tested here: the credentials exist
  only in `secret/docker-hub-registry` (read by the build pod, not by this agent —
  secrets travel by reference, never by value). The flow is validated by the public
  analog above and by the existing working verify-push pattern (see §4).

## 1. Copy-pasteable snippet (what verify-push's `source:` runs)
Daemonless — there is no Docker daemon in a kaniko pod, so `docker pull` would fail
regardless; a manifest probe answers the real question. Authenticated for a private repo:

    set -euo pipefail
    REPO="${1:?repo}"        # e.g. ronaldraygun/armor
    TAG="${2:?tag}"          # e.g. the resolved version

    # 1. Resolve push creds from the same secret kaniko pushed with.
    #    docker-hub-registry mounted at /kaniko/.docker/config.json (DOCKER_CONFIG=/kaniko/.docker).
    #    .auths[].auth is base64(username:password).
    AUTH=$(jq -r '.auths["https://index.docker.io/v1/"].auth
                  // .auths["index.docker.io"].auth
                  // .auths["docker.io"].auth' /kaniko/.docker/config.json)
    [ -n "$AUTH" ] && [ "$AUTH" != "null" ] || { echo "no Docker Hub creds in config.json"; exit 1; }
    USER=$(printf '%s' "$AUTH" | base64 -d | cut -d: -f1)
    PASS=$(printf '%s' "$AUTH" | base64 -d | cut -d: -f2-)

    # 2. AUTHENTICATED token exchange (private repo needs Basic auth here).
    TOKEN=$(curl -fsSL -u "$USER:$PASS" \
      "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:${REPO}:pull" \
      | jq -r '.token // empty')
    [ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "token exchange failed"; exit 1; }

    # 3. Manifest existence probe (HEAD; no daemon needed).
    CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' \
      "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/${REPO}/manifests/${TAG}")

    # 4. Verdict — 200 only is success; everything else is a hard fail.
    if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then echo "OK: $REPO:$TAG pullable (HTTP 200)"; exit 0; fi
    echo "FAIL: $REPO:$TAG not resolvable (HTTP $CODE)" >&2; exit 1

For a PUBLIC repo, drop `-u "$USER:$PASS"` on the token exchange (anonymous works).
armor is NOT public, so keep the Basic auth. The `Accept` set covers single-arch
manifest, multi-arch manifest list, and OCI index.

## 2. Expected HTTP codes
| Tag state            | Anonymous token (public repo) | Authenticated token (private repo = armor) |
|----------------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Present / just pushed| 200                           | 200                                        |
| Absent / ghost tag   | 404                           | 404                                        |
| Token rejected       | 401                           | 401                                        |
| Scope/forbidden      | 403                           | 403                                        |
| Rate-limited         | 429                           | 429                                        |
| Registry error       | 5xx                           | 5xx                                        |

- **200 only** = success. **Any other code = hard fail (exit 1).**
- Key asymmetry: for a PRIVATE repo an anonymous token collapses present AND absent
  both to **401** — which is exactly why authentication is mandatory. With the
  authenticated token, **200 vs 404** cleanly separates a real push from a ghost tag.
- A freshly-pushed manifest is sometimes not resolvable for a few seconds, so the
  production template wraps step 3 in a 4-attempt / 20s-backoff retry loop before
  declaring a ghost tag (bf-4i5cn2). Verdict logic is unchanged; only the retry
  wrapper differs.

## 3. How a non-zero exit fails the Argo step
Argo runs each template as a container and adopts the **container's exit code** as
the step's phase:
- `verify-push` is a `script` template whose `source` runs under `sh`; the script's
  exit code becomes the `main` container's exit code.
- `exit 0` -> step `Succeeded`. `exit 1` — the FAIL branches, AND any `curl`/`jq`/
  `base64` failure aborting under `set -euo pipefail` -> step **`Failed`**.
- `verify-push` is a member of a `steps` group appended AFTER the kaniko build group.
  By default Argo short-circuits a `steps` sequence on the first failed step, so a
  failed `verify-push` marks the whole template `Failed` and the workflow fails —
  *unless* `continueOn: { failed: true }` is set (it is not). `activeDeadlineSeconds:
  300` caps the retry loop so it cannot hang indefinitely.
- Net: ghost tag (HTTP 404) -> `exit 1` -> step Failed -> workflow Failed -> CI red.
  Real push (HTTP 200) -> `exit 0` -> green.

## 4. Reconciliation with the existing implementation (for parent bf-4i5cn2)
An UNCOMMITTED `verify-push` template already exists in the declarative-config
working tree at `k8s/iad-ci/argo-workflows/armor-workflowtemplate.yml` (verify-push,
~L297-373), modeled on `commitgraph-build-workflowtemplate.yml`. This design matches
it: mounts `secret/docker-hub-registry` -> `/kaniko/.docker/config.json` (via
`DOCKER_CONFIG=/kaniko/.docker`), extracts `.auths["docker.io"].auth`, does the
authenticated token exchange, retries 4x with 20s backoff, treats non-200 as exit 1.
Parent bf-4i5cn2 should reconcile this design with that template. One nit: it uses
`curl -I` (HEAD); a plain GET-style probe is marginally more portable across
registries, but HEAD is valid and cheaper for Docker Hub — either satisfies this
design.

## 5. Credential safety
The snippet references the credential ONLY by its storage path
(`secret/docker-hub-registry` -> `/kaniko/.docker/config.json`) and decodes it at
runtime inside the build pod. No credential value is written into the template, this
design, or git.
design:
# Registry-existence assertion design (bf-1w5lmk, for parent bf-4i5cn2)

## KEY CORRECTION — anonymous auth does NOT work (ronaldraygun/* is private)

The spec says "obtain an **anonymous** auth token from auth.docker.io". That does
NOT work for ronaldraygun/armor — the repository is PRIVATE. Verified empirically
2026-08-09 against the live API:

    # anon token exchange succeeds, but grants NO scope:
    $ curl -s "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:ronaldraygun/armor:pull" | jq '.access'
    null

    # using that anon token against the registry -> 401 both ways:
    GET /v2/ronaldraygun/armor/tags/list            -> 401 UNAUTHORIZED  ("authentication required", action=pull)
    GET /v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/0.1.1905   -> 401 UNAUTHORIZED

auth.docker.io issues anonymous tokens unconditionally; for a private repo the
token's `access` is `null` and the registry rejects it with 401. So the assertion
MUST exchange a token using the PUSH credentials (the same `docker-hub-registry`
secret kaniko pushes with), not an anonymous one. Control case proving the API
shape is right: public `library/alpine` returns a populated `access` array and the
anon token yields 200 for a real tag / 404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN for a bogus one.

## Copy-pasteable assertion command

Runs in a post-push script step. REPO/TAG come from workflow params; credentials
come from the docker config mounted at /kaniko/.docker/config.json (the
docker-hub-registry secret, key .dockerconfigjson).

    set -euo pipefail
    REPO="${REPO:-ronaldraygun/armor}"
    TAG="${TAG:?TAG required}"

    # 1. Push credentials out of the docker config (base64 "auth" == user:pass).
    AUTH=$(jq -r '.auths["https://index.docker.io/v1/"].auth
                  // .auths["index.docker.io"].auth
                  // .auths["docker.io"].auth' /kaniko/.docker/config.json)
    [ -n "$AUTH" ] && [ "$AUTH" != "null" ] || { echo "no Docker Hub creds in config"; exit 1; }
    USER=$(printf '%s' "$AUTH" | base64 -d | cut -d: -f1)
    PASS=$(printf '%s' "$AUTH" | base64 -d | cut -d: -f2-)

    # 2. AUTHENTICATED token exchange (NOT anonymous — repo is private).
    TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -u "$USER:$PASS" \
      "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:${REPO}:pull" \
      | jq -r '.token // empty')
    [ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "token exchange failed for $REPO"; exit 1; }

    # 3. Query the manifest endpoint. HTTP 200 == present & pullable.
    CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json' \
      -H 'Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json' \
      "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/${REPO}/manifests/${TAG}")

    if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then
      echo "OK: $REPO:$TAG pullable (manifest HTTP 200)"; exit 0
    fi
    echo "FAIL: $REPO:$TAG manifest HTTP $CODE (expected 200)"; exit 1

Notes:
- GET vs HEAD: a HEAD (curl -I) answers the same existence question without
  downloading the manifest body; the in-flight impl uses HEAD, GET is shown above
  to match the spec wording. Either yields the codes below.
- Wrap steps 2-3 in a retry/backoff loop: a freshly-pushed manifest can take a few
  seconds to become resolvable (in-flight impl: 4 attempts x 20s). A bare curl
  non-zero exit (timeout/DNS) must also count as failure, never success.

## Expected HTTP codes (manifest endpoint, with a valid authenticated token)

  200                                   -> tag exists, manifest resolvable = PULLABLE  -> SUCCESS (exit 0)
  404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN ("manifest unknown") -> tag absent / not yet resolvable        -> HARD FAIL
  401 UNAUTHORIZED ("authentication required") -> token lacks pull scope; bad/expired
       creds, OR an anonymous token used on a private repo                          -> HARD FAIL
  403 DENIED                            -> token valid but repo forbids pull          -> HARD FAIL
  5xx / curl non-zero exit              -> registry outage or network error           -> HARD FAIL (retry first)

Present vs absent, concretely: present tag => 200; absent tag => 404. Verified
2026-08-09 on public control library/alpine (real tag 200, bogus tag 404 with
{"errors":[{"code":"MANIFEST_UNKNOWN",...}]}). For the private armor repo the
non-200 you'd see on a genuine auth/config bug is 401, which is exactly why the
check must NOT use an anonymous token.

## How non-zero exit fails the Argo step

The snippet is the main process of a `script` template. Argo captures the main
container's exit code:
- exit 0  -> step node Succeeded
- exit != 0 -> step node Failed
The verify-server-image / verify-restore-verifier-image steps live in the `build`
template's `steps:` list with no continueOn.failed / onExit, so a Failed node
fails the `build` template, which is the entrypoint -> the whole workflow ends in
phase Failed. activeDeadlineSeconds (300s on the verify template, 21900s
workflow-wide) bounds hangs; the in-script retry loop stays inside that budget.

Net effect: a bumped VERSION with no pullable manifest makes the run FAIL loudly,
instead of Succeeded + a silent downstream ImagePullBackOff (the 0.1.1897 and
0.1.467 ghost-tag incidents this guard exists to prevent).

## Mapping to the in-flight implementation

An uncommitted `verify-push` template in the declarative-config working tree
(armor-workflowtemplate.yml, for parent bf-4i5cn2) already encodes this exact
design: mounts docker-hub-registry at /kaniko/.docker, reads the base64 auth,
does the AUTHENTICATED token exchange, retries the manifest HEAD 4x with 20s
backoff, and exit 1s on anything but 200. It also correctly documents in a
comment that ronaldraygun/* is private and an anonymous token gets 401. Design
only here — no YAML edited in this step; the parent bead owns the reconcile.

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
DOCUMENTING: TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior table-driven pattern
Source: internal/server/share_decompress_test.go:179-318
No code changes — documentation/understanding task. Read + verified against current file state.

== 1. PER-CASE SETUP SEQUENCE (the t.Run(tc.name, ...) body, lines 225-316) ==
Every subtest runs this identical sequence, parameterized only by the row fields:

1. setupTestEnvironment(t)            [L226] -> fresh tmpDir (os.MkdirTemp) + cleanup (os.RemoveAll). Isolates the FS backend.
2. backend.NewFSBackend(FSConfig{BasePath: tmpDir})   [L230] -> in-process filesystem backend; err-checked. No real B2.
3. cfg := loadTestConfig(t, tmpDir)    [L237] -> sets 9 ARMOR_* env vars, calls config.Load(), returns *config.Config; registers t.Cleanup to unset them.
4. srv, _ := NewWithBackend(cfg, fsBackend)   [L238] -> *Server wired to FS backend only; err-checked.
5. srv.presigner = presign.NewSigner(cfg.PresignSecret, "")   [L244] -> manual init; NewWithBackend SKIPS this, but token gen needs it.
6. COMPRESS BRANCH  [L247-254]: if tc.compressed -> dataToEncrypt = compressData(tc.data) (zstd); else dataToEncrypt = tc.data (verbatim).
7. encryptedData, hmacTable, armorMeta := encryptTestData(t, srv, dataToEncrypt, tc.compressed)   [L257] -> keymgr.GetMEK; fresh DEK+IV; 65536-block Encryptor; Encrypt; WrapDEK; builds *backend.ARMORMetadata with Compressed = tc.compressed.
8. storeTestObject(t, srv.backend, ctx, "test-bucket", "test-key-"+tc.name, encryptedData, hmacTable, armorMeta)   [L262] -> builds full envelope (NewEnvelopeHeader -> Encode -> append encryptedData -> append hmacTable), armorMeta.ToMetadata(), backend.Put.
9. token := generateTestToken(t, srv, "test-bucket", objectKey, time.Hour)   [L265] -> srv.presigner.GenerateToken, 1h TTL.
10. httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/share/"+token, nil) + httptest.NewRecorder() + srv.handleShare(w, req)   [L268-270].
11. ASSERTIONS  [L273-315]: status==200; io.ReadAll body; retrievedData == tc.data (round-trip); behavior branch keyed on tc.wantDecompression; armorMeta.Compressed == tc.compressed.

This body is the SAME setup the 5 single-shot tests (TestShareGET_CompressedObject etc.) repeat inline, just parameterized.

== 2. testCases STRUCT SHAPE (lines 180-186) ==
Anonymous slice-of-struct with 5 fields:
  testCases := []struct {
      name              string
      data              []byte
      compressed        bool
      wantDecompression bool // whether decompression should occur
      description       string
  }{}

Field meaning:
- name              : subtest name (t.Run) AND feeds object key "test-key-"+tc.name. Must be unique; snake_case by convention.
- data              : the ORIGINAL pre-compression/pre-encryption PLAINTEXT. GET response is compared to THIS (round-trip equality); it is the input to compressData when compressed=true. Always the plaintext.
- compressed        : whether the case compresses data before encrypting. Drives the compressData branch, the Compressed flag passed to encryptTestData (-> armorMeta.Compressed), and is asserted back at L312.
- wantDecompression : what the test ASSERTS the handler does (decompress vs bypass). Selects the behavior-assertion branch [L294-309].
- description       : human label surfaced in t.Errorf messages. Informational only; not control flow.

Current 5 rows:
  uncompressed_small_text        data=text                       compressed=false wantDecompression=false
  uncompressed_binary_data       data=50KB random                 compressed=false wantDecompression=false
  compressed_repeating_text      data=Repeat x100                 compressed=true  wantDecompression=true
  compressed_binary_data         data=100KB random                compressed=true  wantDecompression=true
  legacy_object_no_compression_flag data=text                     compressed=false wantDecompression=false

== HOW compressed vs wantDecompression INTERACT ==
In all 5 rows they are consistent (compressed=true <=> wantDecompression=true). They are independent fields with different meanings:
- compressed          = what the test PUTS IN (did we compress + set the metadata flag before storing?).
- wantDecompression   = what the test ASSERTS the handler does on retrieval.
Behavior-assertion block [L294-309]:
  wantDecompression==true  -> assert retrievedData != dataToEncrypt (proves handler did NOT return still-compressed bytes verbatim, i.e. decompression ran).
  wantDecompression==false -> assert retrievedData == dataToEncrypt (proves handler bypassed decompression, returned bytes verbatim).
NOTE: for the wantDecompression=false rows this is redundant with the round-trip check, because when compressed=false, dataToEncrypt == tc.data, so both branches reduce to "retrieved == original." The behavior block is only strictly meaningful for compressed=true rows.

== 3. RECIPE: ADD A ROW ==
To add a case, append one struct literal to the testCases slice setting exactly these five fields. No other code changes are needed — the loop body and all 7 helpers already parameterize on them.

  {
      name:              "compressed_large_json",
      data:              []byte(strings.Repeat(`{"key":"value","n":12345}`, 5000)),
      compressed:        true,
      wantDecompression: true,
      description:       "compressed large JSON payload - should decompress",
  },

Rules:
- name: unique, snake_case; becomes subtest name + object-key suffix.
- data: pre-compression plaintext. Use []byte(...) for text or generateRandomData(n) for binary.
- compressed: true ONLY to exercise the compression path (compressData + armorMeta.Compressed=true + flag assertion). false otherwise.
- wantDecompression: true when the stored object is compressed (handler must decompress); false when it isn't (handler must bypass). Keep consistent with the scenario unless deliberately testing a mismatch.
- description: short human label for error messages.

(Sibling bead bf-5x15bj previously documented this same pattern; this comment re-verifies it against the current code — 5 rows confirmed, line numbers current, helper dependency bf-1k7uzp cataloged the 7 helpers.)

title: Validate decoded value is AWS access key format
description:
## Child Bead: Validate decoded value is AWS access key format

This bead validates the decoded value matches AWS access key pattern.

### Prerequisites
- Previous child bead complete (bf-3c5vm: base64 decoded to plain text)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Decoded value starts with AKIA (standard AWS access key prefix)
- Value is exactly 20 characters long (standard AWS access key length)
- Value contains only alphanumeric characters (A-Z, 0-9)
- No whitespace, corruption, or binary data

### Commands
```bash
# Display the decoded value
echo "Decoded value:"
cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
echo ""

# Get the value (strip any whitespace)
VALUE=$(cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | tr -d '[:space:]')

# Check length
echo "Value length: ${#VALUE}"

# Validate AWS access key format (AKIA + 16 alphanumeric chars)
if echo "$VALUE" | grep -qE '^AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}$'; then
    echo "SUCCESS: Valid AWS access key format detected"
    echo "Value matches pattern: AKIA + 16 alphanumeric characters"
else
    echo "ERROR: Value does not match AWS access key format"
    echo "Expected: AKIA followed by 16 alphanumeric characters (total 20 chars)"
    echo "Got: $VALUE"
    exit 1
fi

# Verify no binary/corrupted data
if file /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt | grep -q "text"; then
    echo "File is text data (not binary)"
else
    echo "WARNING: File may contain binary data"
    file /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
fi
```

Success: Decoded value matches AWS access key format (AKIA + 16 chars).

Failure: Value does not match expected format — may be wrong secret, corrupted, or not an AWS key.
