The first test (TestShareGET_CompressedObject) does NOT use this and builds cfg by hand instead.

3) encryptTestData(t *testing.T, srv *Server, data []byte, compressed bool) ([]byte, []byte, *backend.ARMORMetadata)   [line 641]
   Pulls MEK via srv.keyManager.GetMEK("test-key"), generates a fresh DEK + IV, builds a crypto.Encryptor (blockSize hardcoded 65536), Encrypt()s data -> (encrypted, hmacTable), WrapDEK(mek, dek), and returns those plus an ARMORMetadata. COMPRESSION-RELEVANT: sets armorMeta.Compressed = compressed (the bool arg is the sole controller of the flag), and sets PlaintextSize = int64(len(data)). Subtlety: for the compressed path callers pass ALREADY-COMPRESSED bytes, so this PlaintextSize is the compressed length, not the original — despite the name. PlaintextSHA/ETag are dummy strings ("test-sha256"/"test-etag").

4) storeTestObject(t *testing.T, backend backend.Backend, ctx context.Context, bucket, key string, encryptedData, hmacTable []byte, armorMeta *backend.ARMORMetadata)   [line 698]
   Builds the on-disk ARMOR envelope = headerBytes + encryptedData + hmacTable, then backend.Put(). COMPRESSION-RELEVANT (envelope layout): header is built via crypto.NewEnvelopeHeader(IV, PlaintextSize, BlockSize, [32]byte{} placeholder-SHA) then Encode()'d to a fixed 64 bytes, and fullObject is the concatenation [header | ciphertext | hmacTable]. KEY DETAIL: the EnvelopeHeader struct carries only {Magic "ARMR", Version, BlockSizeLog2, IV, PlaintextSize, PlaintextSHA, Reserved} — there is NO Compressed field in the on-disk envelope bytes. The Compressed flag travels ONLY via object metadata: armorMeta.ToMetadata() emits x-amz-meta-armor-compressed=true when (and only when) armorMeta.Compressed is set. So decompression is signaled by (a) that S3 metadata key and independently (b) runtime zstd-magic detection on the first decrypted block — not by the envelope header.

5) generateTestToken(t *testing.T, srv *Server, bucket, key string, expiration time.Duration) string   [line 735]
   Thin wrapper over srv.presigner.GenerateToken(bucket, key, expiration); returns the token string. Requires srv.presigner to be set (callers manually assign srv.presigner = presign.NewSigner(...) because NewWithBackend skips it).

6) compressData(data []byte) []byte   [line 747]
   Pure zstd compression: zstd.NewWriter into a bytes.Buffer, Write(data), Close(), return buf.Bytes(). COMPRESSION-RELEVANT: this is the sole producer of compressed payload; its output carries the zstd magic bytes that crypto.IsCompressed detects. No t param, not a t.Helper — used in table-test data construction.

7) generateRandomData(size int) []byte   [line 759]
   Fills a size-byte slice with crypto/rand.Read and returns it. Source of incompressible binary blobs for the table tests; panics on rand failure.

Compression-relevant summary (the three that matter for the Compressed flag + envelope layout):
- compressData: produces zstd bytes (magic-byte source). Pure transform, no flag awareness.
- encryptTestData: the ONLY place armorMeta.Compressed is set (driven by its bool arg). Also sets PlaintextSize = len(input) = compressed length on the compressed path.
- storeTestObject: defines on-disk envelope = [64-byte header | ciphertext | hmacTable]. The header has no Compressed field; the flag travels via x-amz-meta-armor-compressed in object metadata (ToMetadata), with zstd-magic detection as a backstop. The header's PlaintextSHA is a zero [32]byte placeholder in tests (real SHA lives in metadata as a dummy string here).

title: Add complex real-world and error scenario tests
description:
## Scope
Add comprehensive tests for real-world configurations and complex error scenarios.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Test real-world config patterns with exclamation
- Test multiline scenarios with exclamation
- Test error code patterns in values (E001, D123)
- Test type name typos and case variations
- Test type-like strings in complex nested structures
- Verify extraction works correctly in realistic scenarios

## Implementation Notes
Focus on Sections 12-15 of type_like_string_false_positive_test.rs:
- Section 12: Complex Real-World Scenarios
- Section 13: Error Code-like Strings in Values

title: x-amz-request-id/RequestId/x-amz-id-2 marked complete in remediation docs but never implemented in production error path
description:
docs/header-remediation-plan.md (Part 10, Acceptance Criteria for v0.2.0) and docs/bf-1jjcp7-remediation-plan.md both mark these items complete:
- [x] P1-001: All S3 responses include x-amz-request-id header
- [x] P1-002: All S3 error responses include <RequestId> XML element
- [x] P2-002: All S3 responses include x-amz-id-2 header

The originating bead chain (bf-a5evuz -> bf-60v3ao -> bf-1kbuqm -> bf-2oq6du -> bf-1jjcp7, all closed "Completed") only ever produced investigation/specification/plan documents (S3 spec comparison, issue catalog, remediation plan) -- none of those beads is an implementation task, and none touches the real S3 handler code.

Verified directly against shipped code: internal/server/server.go's writeError() (the single, real, shared S3 error writer used by the actual HTTP handlers -- internal/server/server.go:~823-833) sets only Content-Type and writes <Code>/<Message> in the XML body. It sets no x-amz-request-id header, no x-amz-id-2 header, and the XML has no <RequestId> element. `git log --all --grep` for these terms turns up only investigation/analysis commits (efca54c7, ca887a7a, 07b59cae), never an implementation commit. The only places RequestId/x-amz-request-id/x-amz-id-2 appear anywhere in the Go source are test-fixture/mock files that are explicitly documented as such in their own header comments (internal/server/http_error_fixtures.go: "reusable test fixtures", internal/server/error_server_setup.go: "configurable test server infrastructure" -- neither is production code) plus their _test.go consumers.

Per the remediation plan's own severity assessment this was P0/P1 -- "breaks AWS SDK compatibility ... prevents request tracing ... makes support troubleshooting impossible" -- so this is a real, currently-shipped gap, not cosmetic. Worth also re-checking the remaining checklist items in the same doc (P2-001 Content-Type on B2 admin endpoints, P2-003 backend error propagation tests) which were not independently verified here and may have the same doc-says-done-code-says-no pattern.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Add request-ID generation wired into the real S3-facing handler chain in internal/server/server.go (not just the test-fixture files)
- x-amz-request-id set on every S3 response (success and error)
- <RequestId> element present in every S3 XML error response
- x-amz-id-2 set on every S3 response
- Verify via a live request against a running ARMOR instance (not just a unit test against the mock fixture files) that the headers actually appear
- Correct docs/header-remediation-plan.md / docs/bf-1jjcp7-remediation-plan.md checklists to match true status -- if this was deliberately deprioritized rather than actually shipped, flag that decision to a human instead of leaving the checklist reading as done

title: Multipart objects unreadable: GET path ignores multipart sidecar layout
description: Read path assumes single-PUT layout: header, data, embedded HMAC table. Multipart-completed objects are raw concatenated part ciphertext with no header and the HMAC table in a sidecar; a multipart marker is set in object metadata on complete. No reader-side code checks that marker, so every GET of a multipart object 500s with prefetch offset out of range; the Range path shares the assumption. Repro: TestMultipartFullCycleByteVerification in the handlers test package (file multipart_routing_test.go), skip-gated on this bead. Fix both full-object and range paths. See the upload-retrieval test matrix doc, rows U4 R4 R7.

title: Strengthen multipart integration test to verify actual content
description: tests/integration/integration_test.go TestMultipartUpload does a real 3-part 15MB multipart upload/download cycle but only asserts ContentLength matches expected size -- never reads back and compares actual bytes. Change it to seed each part with distinguishable, verifiable content and compare full downloaded bytes against what was uploaded. Add sibling test cases: a final part that is not a multiple of part size, and a single-part multipart upload. Confirm this test actually gates the image-build/CI pipeline that produces deployed images -- a content-correctness regression should never be able to ship.
notes:
REOPENED 2026-07-15: verified the prior completion is inadequate. internal/backend/multipart_integration_test.go (TestMultipartUpload and its three siblings) do real-looking multipart upload/download cycles and do compare byte-for-byte content -- but ALL FOUR run against mockBackendForMultipart (same file, ~line 555), a pure in-memory Go map that concatenates part bytes directly. It never calls internal/crypto (no Encrypt, no Decrypt, no HMAC verification anywhere) and never talks to a real S3/B2 endpoint. It is structurally incapable of catching any encryption/decryption/HMAC bug, including bf-1v6skf (the P0 currently open: large multipart objects fail HMAC verification on real GetObject). The docstring claims this test "gates the CI pipeline" against content-correctness regressions -- it does not and cannot, regardless of CI wiring (bf-180ohh verified CI wiring, not test validity).

Corrected acceptance criteria:
- Test must exercise ARMOR's real request path: either the actual running armor server (S3 API surface) backed by a real or realistic backend, or at minimum internal/crypto's real Encrypt/Decrypt/HMAC-verify functions wired into the multipart assembly -- not a map-based mock
- Must reproduce at the scale where bf-1v6skf actually failed (44MB level-9-snapshot-equivalent object, not just the existing 15MB/3-part mock scenario) -- the current mock tests would still pass even if real, since they never got near the actual failing block boundary
- Must assert full decrypt success AND HMAC verification success on GetObject/range-read, not just that stored bytes match a map lookup
- Should be added as (or alongside) a true integration test that hits ARMOR over HTTP with real crypto enabled, so a future "looks real but mocks the crypto layer" regression is itself structurally impossible

should be closed as not-applicable with a note pointing at what actually
shipped instead — do not implement speculative code ahead of the decision.

If and when ADR-010 does call for an ARMOR-side change: implement exactly
what it specifies, as narrowly scoped as the ADR describes. Given this
project's repeated history of relaxed-alignment changes causing real silent
multipart corruption (ADR-002/003/005), any accommodation must:

- Be opt-in / explicitly scoped to the affected client(s), not a global
  relaxation of ADR-005's contract.
- Preserve (or explicitly replace with something equally strong) the
  integrity guarantee that a misaligned part currently gives up by being
  rejected outright.
- Ship with a real test that exercises `internal/crypto` through the actual
  handler path at a realistic scale — not a mock-backend test, and not a
  test capped at a toy size. This project's bead history (bf-28rb and others)
  has repeatedly had "passing" multipart tests that didn't touch the real
  failure mode; don't repeat that here.

## Acceptance criteria

- Only proceed if ADR-010 calls for this.
- New/changed behavior is covered by a real-crypto-path test at production
  scale, `go test -race ./...` green.
- ADR-010 updated (or a short follow-up ADR added) documenting what
  actually shipped and why, so the next person reading ADR-010 doesn't have
  to reverse-engineer the final implementation from the diff.
- No cluster/`declarative-config` access needed or used here — deploying the
  fix to `iad-ci` and verifying it against live scheduled backups is a
  separate, ops-gated bead.

title: Genesis: ARMOR Phase 6 - Backup Restore Verification & Validation
description:
## Genesis Bead
Tied to plan: docs/plan/plan.md, Phase 6 (Backup Restore Verification & Validation)

## Overview
Prove that backups stored through ARMOR are actually restorable, continuously. Phase 5 (bf-4l7q) detects write-path corruption at upload time; this phase closes the other half of the 2026-06 incident: a backup existed, passed object-level checks, and was still unrecoverable when needed. "Verified" means a real restore through the read path with application-level assertions -- not object presence, not ContentLength, not canary health.

Concrete motivation, found 2026-07-14/15 while this phase still had zero bead coverage: bf-1v6skf / bf-24sxh7 confirmed that ord-devimprint's queue-api backup chain is currently unrestorable (multipart GET path bug), discovered only by manually running an actual restore test. This is exactly the failure mode Phase 6 exists to catch automatically and continuously, instead of requiring a human to notice and manually reproduce it.

**Scope:** every ARMOR deployment and bucket -- armor-apexalgo (live ACB content), ord-devimprint, and the three deployments never audited after the multipart bug (iad-ci, iad-kalshi, rs-manager).

**Boundary:** ARMOR proves restorability of what ARMOR stores. Estate-wide restore verification of non-ARMOR streams (CNPG/barman WAL, restic backup-home, Velero) was meant to belong to a separate standalone engine (previously scaffolded as "DRILL") -- that scaffold was deleted 2026-07-11 at user request and does not currently exist. Keep metric naming and bead conventions generically compatible with a future estate-wide tool, but do not block on or reference DRILL as if it exists today.

## Progress
- [ ] Restore-verification harness (dual-path: ARMOR read path + armor-decrypt direct-to-ciphertext)
- [ ] Application-level validity assertions per artifact class (SQLite, tar/gzip, Parquet)
- [ ] Multipart-era corruption audit of the 4 unaudited/at-risk buckets
- [ ] Restorability metrics and alerting
- [ ] Failure escalation via automatic bead creation
- [ ] Scheduled DR drill automation (armor-decrypt path)

title: Retract obsolete sequential-multipart-writer pinning guidance
description: bf-59unr3 and bf-4qq1 instructed that all ARMOR multipart writers (including commitgraph clone workers and litestream) be pinned to sequential, block-aligned, no-retry part behavior. ADR-005's uniform-part-size contract made that obsolete: out-of-order and concurrent parts are now supported, and retries are idempotent. Sweep docs/plan/plan.md, docs/adr/, README, and consumer-facing notes for that guidance and retract it, replacing with the actual ADR-005 client contract (uniform part size P pinned from part 1; only the final part may be short; non-aligned intermediate parts get 400). Leaving it in place discourages clients from using parallel uploads that now work.

Depends on bf-n0aor9 (request shape capture) -- we need the actual wire data to know if streaming is even used

The hypothesis list calls out streaming auth as a key suspect, but it's just speculation until we see real traffic. If this bead finds no difference, we rule it out. If it finds a difference, we've likely found the bug.

GOAL: Before checking the real candidate tag, lock down a manifest-API check method that reliably distinguishes pullable tags from ghosts, validated against the two known reference points: 0.1.1896 (must be HTTP 200) and 0.1.1897 (must be HTTP 404).

TASK:
- Decide which endpoint/auth path to use. Two candidates to compare:
  (a) Web-tier: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://hub.docker.com/v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/<tag>
  (b) Registry-tier: https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/<tag> with an anonymous pull token fetched from: https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:ronaldraygun/armor:pull (token is anonymous/public, NOT a secret).
- Run BOTH against 0.1.1896 (known-good, expect 200) and 0.1.1897 (known-ghost, expect 404).
- Pick the method that reproduces 200 and 404 correctly. If (a) works without a token, prefer it (matches the original bead's check). If it returns 401 for both, fall back to (b).

ACCEPTANCE: a single documented curl command (endpoint + any token step) that returns HTTP 200 for 0.1.1896 and HTTP 404 for 0.1.1897, with all four status codes recorded in a comment. This method is the input to split-child 3.
notes:
VALIDATED manifest-API check method for ronaldraygun/armor (input to split-child 3).

KEY CORRECTION TO TASK PREMISE: ronaldraygun/armor is a PRIVATE repo. Both candidate paths in the task assumed anonymous access; NEITHER works anonymously. Confirmed private three ways: (1) anon auth.docker.io token -> access:[] (control library/nginx -> access:[{pull}] and HTTP 200); (2) Hub API GET /v2/repositories/ronaldraygun/armor/ -> 404 "object not found" to anon (Docker Hub hides private repos); (3) authenticated token -> access:[{ronaldraygun/armor,pull}] and discriminates correctly.

STATUS MATRIX (both reference tags):
- Method (a) hub.docker.com/v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/<tag> [web-tier, no token]: 0.1.1896=404, 0.1.1897=404 -> REJECT. Not a real manifest endpoint (returns Cloudflare 404 HTML for both); cannot discriminate good from ghost.
- Method (b) registry-1.docker.io/v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/<tag> + ANONYMOUS token: 0.1.1896=401, 0.1.1897=401 -> REJECT. Private repo; anon token grants access:[] -> 401 for both.
- Method (b) registry-1.docker.io + AUTHENTICATED token: 0.1.1896=200, 0.1.1897=404 -> ACCEPT. This is the validated method.

VALIDATED COMMAND (credential by reference from ~/.docker/config.json; no secret inline; 200=pullable, 404=ghost):
  AUTH=$(python3 -c "import json;print(json.load(open('$HOME/.docker/config.json'))['auths']['https://index.docker.io/v1/']['auth'])")
  TOK=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Basic $AUTH" "https://auth.docker.io/token?service=registry.docker.io&scope=repository:ronaldraygun/armor:pull" | python3 -c 'import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["token"])')
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" -H "Accept: application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json" "https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ronaldraygun/armor/manifests/<TAG>"

Reproduced 200 (0.1.1896) / 404 (0.1.1897) on repeated runs. Token mint step is mandatory because the repo is private; the anon-token variant in the task brief returns 401/401 and must not be used.
close_reason: Validated manifest check method. Method (b) registry-1.docker.io with AUTHENTICATED token reproduces 0.1.1896=200 / 0.1.1897=404. Key correction: ronaldraygun/armor is a PRIVATE repo, so the anon-token variant (401/401) and web-tier method (a) (404/404) both fail to discriminate; a token-mint step using the local docker config credential is mandatory. title: ARMOR: hand-run restore test confirms bf-1v6skf still unresolved -- fresh snapshot fails HMAC verification (block 256), litestream restore produces empty output
description:
## Summary

Ran the actual litestream restore by hand (2026-07-16, ~15:26-15:37 UTC) against ord-devimprint's live queue-api backup chain, with correctly-paired armor-readonly credentials. This is the real end-to-end test that bf-5cfcb/bf-4f9i6 were supposed to perform and verify -- both were closed "Completed" but neither actually ran a working restore (see reference_armor_multipart_corruption_bug memory, 07-16 update). This bead documents a genuine, reproduced failure with fresh evidence.

## Method

- kubectl port-forward to svc/armor (devimprint ns, admin kubeconfig) on the box holding S3 creds, SSH-reverse-tunneled to lab where litestream + the existing scratch config live (scratch/fresh-restore/litestream-restore.yml, repo-relative)
- Fixed a stale/mismatched access-key-id in that config (did not match either current armor-readonly or armor-writer secret -- worth checking who/what wrote that stale value)
- Paired correctly with armor-readonly's actual auth-access-key/auth-secret-key (from k8s secret armor-readonly in devimprint ns)

## Result: restore fails

litestream restore -config litestream-restore.yml restored/queue.db:
- Dry-run plan succeeded: valid plan, 32 files, txid range 0000000000000001-000000000006c829, level-9 snapshot (73,400,320 bytes, created 2026-07-16T00:02:25Z -- TODAY, not stale data) down through level-0 WAL segments.
- Actual restore ran ~9 minutes then failed: Error: decode database: decode header: EOF
- restored/ directory ends up empty -- no queue.db produced, nothing to verify.

## Root cause isolated: same HMAC bug as bf-1v6skf, still live today

Direct raw S3 GET (bypassing litestream) of the level-9 snapshot object itself:

aws --endpoint-url http://localhost:19000 s3 cp s3://devimprint/state/litestream/queue.db/0009/0000000000000001-000000000006ac2a.ltx /tmp/x
=> download failed: An error occurred (InternalError) when calling the GetObject operation (reached max retries: 4): Failed to decrypt range: block 256: HMAC verification failed

- Object confirmed via head-object: ContentLength 73,400,320 bytes, LastModified 2026-07-16T00:02:25Z -- a fresh snapshot, not scarring from before bf-24sxh7 shipped.
- Identical failure signature (block 256: HMAC verification failed) to the original bf-1v6skf finding on 2026-07-14, on a completely different, brand-new object created after bf-24sxh7 (the multipart GET-path/sidecar fix) was closed 2026-07-15.
- Conclusion: bf-24sxh7 fixed the GET-path routing/sidecar-detection bug (a real fix, confirmed by its own test), but did NOT fix this separate HMAC-verification-on-decrypt failure for large snapshot-class objects. bf-1v6skf's own hypothesis section already called this out as a distinct read/decrypt-path bug, not the routing bug -- this is now confirmed still reproducing, unchanged, after the routing fix landed.

## Practical impact

queue-api's ord-devimprint backup chain is, right now, still NOT restorable. If the live pod/PVC were lost today, this data cannot be recovered from the B2/ARMOR replica.

## Also flagging: false-positive bead closures upstream

- bf-5cfcb (Execute litestream restore to scratch location) was closed Completed, but its own execution trace shows exit code 124 (timeout), zero litestream commands run.
- bf-4f9i6 (Verify restored database integrity) was closed Completed via a report that ran integrity checks against this repo's own .beads/beads.db (ARMOR's bug-tracker DB) instead of a restored queue.db -- no restored database has ever existed to verify.
- Both should be reopened; this bead supersedes them with genuine, reproduced evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- Root cause identified for why HMAC verification fails specifically at large/multipart-reconstructed object boundaries during decrypt (this bead's evidence: fails consistently at block 256 on a 73MB level-9 snapshot)
- Fix applied to internal/crypto's per-block HMAC verification for reassembled multipart objects
- A fresh snapshot restores successfully end-to-end via litestream restore, with sqlite3 PRAGMA integrity_check passing on the actual output file
- Do not close this or any parent bead based on a report that doesn't cite the literal restored file path and a real litestream/sqlite3 command transcript

## Related

- bf-1v6skf (parent P0, still blocked -- this is fresh evidence it remains unresolved)
- bf-24sxh7 (closed GET-path fix -- confirmed real but insufficient)
- bf-5cfcb, bf-4f9i6 (falsely closed, should be reopened)
- bf-2i3ipy (Phase 6 genesis, still blocked, 0/6)

title: Multipart canary fails with B2 EntityTooSmall: part size below 5MB minimum
description: Observed 2026-07-18 on every 0.1.1871 deployment (iad-ci, rs-manager, ord-devimprint): multipart_healthy=false with CompleteMultipartUpload 400 EntityTooSmall (Your proposed upload is smaller than the minimum allowed size). The multipart canary uploads a ~6MB object split into parts smaller than B2's 5MB minimum non-final part size. Fix internal/canary: use parts >= 5 MiB that are also block-aligned (multiple of 64KiB), e.g. two 5.25MiB parts (10.5MiB canary), keep sequential order. Add a unit test asserting canary part sizing satisfies both constraints. Note the small-object canary is healthy everywhere and a real 50MB sequential multipart round-trip through deployed ord-devimprint 0.1.1871 was verified byte-identical the same day, so this is a canary-implementation bug, not a data-path failure.

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
Test-function documentation for internal/server/share_decompress_test.go (7 test functions, lines 24–584).

ALL 7 TEST FUNCTIONS (one-line purpose each):

1. TestShareGET_CompressedObject (L24) — single-case — Stores a zstd-compressed object (compressed BEFORE encryption, Compressed=true), then GETs /share/<token> and asserts the response body byte-equals the ORIGINAL pre-compression data (i.e. the server decompressed correctly). Also asserts compressed bytes != original to prove compression actually occurred.

2. TestShareGET_UncompressedObject (L117) — single-case — Stores an uncompressed object (Compressed=false) and asserts GET returns the body byte-equal to the original, confirming no decompression path runs on uncompressed data.

3. TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior (L179) — TABLE-DRIVEN, 5 cases — Verifies decompression behavior across every object type, each carrying an explicit wantDecompression flag. Cases: uncompressed_small_text, uncompressed_binary_data (50KB), compressed_repeating_text, compressed_binary_data (100KB), legacy_object_no_compression_flag. Core assertions per case: (a) retrieved body byte-equals original pre-compression data; (b) when wantDecompression=true the output differs from the encryption input (decompression ran), when false it equals the encryption input (decompression bypassed); (c) armorMeta.Compressed == tc.compressed.

4. TestShareGET_LegacyObject (L321) — single-case — Stores an object with Compressed explicitly forced false (simulates pre-compression-metadata legacy objects) and asserts GET returns the body byte-equal to the original — legacy objects served unchanged, decompression path not triggered.

5. TestShareGET_RoundTrip (L383) — TABLE-DRIVEN, 3 cases — Exercises the full pipeline compress -> encrypt -> store -> GET -> decompress for varied sizes/types: small_text, medium_binary (100KB), large_binary (512KB). Core assertion: retrieved data byte-equals original (full round-trip integrity). Also LOGs (not fails) if compression did not reduce size.

6. TestShareGET_CompressionDetectionFromFirstBlock (L474) — single-case — Verifies compression is detectable from the first decrypted block via zstd magic bytes (crypto.IsCompressed true) on the compressed payload before storing, then asserts GET returns 200 with decompressed data byte-equaling the original.

7. TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression (L537) — single-case — Stores a 200KB compressed object, issues GET with Range: bytes=0-9999, and asserts the response status is 206 (Partial Content) or 200 — i.e. range requests do not break on compressed objects.

TABLE-DRIVEN vs SINGLE-CASE:
- Table-driven (2): TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior (5 cases), TestShareGET_RoundTrip (3 cases).
- Single-case (5): TestShareGET_CompressedObject, TestShareGET_UncompressedObject, TestShareGET_LegacyObject, TestShareGET_CompressionDetectionFromFirstBlock, TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression.

SHARED STRUCTURE: All tests build an in-memory filesystem backend, a Server via NewWithBackend, attach a presigner, then encrypt+store via the shared helpers (encryptTestData, storeTestObject, generateTestToken, compressData, generateRandomData). The table-driven tests are the broader-coverage ones; the single-case tests each isolate one specific behavior (compressed round-trip, uncompressed passthrough, legacy-compat, magic-byte detection, range requests).

This satisfies parent acceptance: "Current test structure documented".

title: Perform restore from litestream backup to scratch location
description:
Execute the actual litestream restore command to restore the queue-api backup from the new generation into the prepared scratch database location. Follow the disaster-recovery notes for the correct restore procedure.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Identified correct backup generation to restore from

notes:
RESTORE TEST EXECUTED 2026-07-14 (human, via ord-devimprint-admin.kubeconfig port-forward to svc/armor + litestream v0.5.14, correct version -- v0.3.13 predates the LTX format and silently reports zero generations, do not use it here). RESULT: FAILS, reproducibly, on a live confirmed cause -- NOT a credentials/environment issue anymore (bf-24hrg is resolved). Direct aws-cli GetObject on the level-9 snapshot object (queue.db/0009/0000000000000001-0000000000066562.ltx, 44908497 bytes, created 2026-07-14 00:02 UTC -- i.e. TODAY, well after all prior ARMOR version fixes) fails: InternalError Failed to decrypt range: block 256: HMAC verification failed. Isolated the scope: a level-3 compacted object (836559 bytes, same generation) downloaded cleanly and completely at normal speed -- so this is NOT a blanket ARMOR outage, it is specific to large snapshot-class objects, same failure class as the 07-13 finding on the old corrupt 598e9 snapshot (see reference_armor_multipart_corruption_bug memory) but now reproduced on a BRAND NEW snapshot. litestream restore itself does not surface this cleanly -- it hangs silently retrying (10+ min, ~4 bytes/sec of read syscalls via /proc/pid/io) rather than failing fast, which is what made this look like a credential/connectivity hang before the raw aws s3 cp isolated the real error. CONCLUSION: queue-api disaster-recovery capability is still broken today -- the multipart storage bug (last-part-wins) was fixed, but reading/decrypting large snapshot objects back still fails HMAC verification. This is a live ARMOR bug, not resolved by any version bump so far, and needs engineering investigation (likely multipart-boundary-related given the size threshold) rather than another restore retry.

- bf-65lbr4: Identify correct litestream backup generation for queue-api restore

title: Root-cause barman-cloud-backup InvalidPartSize failures + write ADR-010
description:
## Context

`queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` (CNPG PostgreSQL, both on `iad-ci`) are the
only two barman-cloud backup targets in the estate that write through ARMOR
(`endpointURL: http://armor.armor.svc.cluster.local:9000`). `queue-db` has
failed **every** scheduled base backup since 2026-05-26 (600+ consecutive
`InvalidPartSize` failures); `forgejo-postgres` has the same failure mode.
Background: [ADR-002](docs/adr/002-multipart-corruption-detection-gaps.md),
[ADR-005](docs/adr/005-out-of-order-multipart-uniform-part-size.md),
[ADR-008](docs/adr/008-multipart-part-size-error-clarity.md).

ARMOR's side of this is done and correct: ADR-005's uniform-part-size
contract is enforced live, and ADR-008 shipped a clear, actionable rejection
message (`InvalidPartSize: Part size N is not a multiple of the block size
(65536 bytes)...`) instead of a silent failure. **This bead is not about
ARMOR's behavior being wrong — it is about characterizing why
barman-cloud-backup cannot satisfy ARMOR's documented, deliberate contract,
and deciding what (if anything) should change.**

## A same-day "fix" already failed — do not repeat this mistake

declarative-config commit `c8aefe75` (2026-08-06 08:50 EDT) disabled gzip
compression on both clusters' base-backup data
(`barmanObjectStore.data: {}`), on the theory that barman's tar streamer
flushes to S3 in exact 65536-byte chunks when uncompressed, so every part
boundary would land on a clean multiple of ARMOR's block size. The commit
message and manifest comments describe this as "verified empirically."

**That verification does not hold.** Live pod logs pulled *after* the fix
was deployed and synced (2026-08-06T21:03-21:04Z, many hours after the
08:50 EDT deploy) show both clusters still failing on every scheduled
attempt:

```
queue-db:          Part size 11876352 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
forgejo-postgres:   Part size 4284416 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
```

Overshoot analysis: `11876352 = 65536*181 + 14336` and `4284416 = 65536*65 +
24576`. Both remainders (14336, 24576) are exact multiples of 512 (POSIX
tar's block size) but NOT of 65536. This means barman-cloud-backup's real
flush granularity is NOT the 65536-byte unit the fix assumed — the "verified
empirically" claim was based on an insufficient one-off test, not on watching
real scheduled runs. (One `forgejo-postgres` run did succeed once, at 15:04Z
the same day — almost certainly because that particular backup's total size
happened to stay under barman's flush threshold and never triggered
multipart upload at all, not because the fix works.)

Two earlier CLI-flag-level workarounds were also tried on
`forgejo-postgres` and both failed live: `--min-chunk-size=5MB` and
`--min-chunk-size=2GB` (attempting to force a single-part upload). The 2GB
attempt still produced one misaligned part — expected, since ADR-005
deliberately does **not** exempt a lone first-and-only part from alignment
(only a genuinely trailing part *after* an already-aligned first part is
exempt — this is a poison-detection safeguard, not an oversight, added after
this project's real history of silent multipart corruption; see ADR-005 and
the historical incidents it links).

## What this bead is

1. **Actually characterize barman-cloud-backup 3.19.1's real
   upload/flush behavior** (the version confirmed live in both pods'
   tracebacks: `/usr/local/lib/python3.9/dist-packages/barman/cloud.py`).
   Do this locally, inside this checkout — no cluster access is needed or
   should be used:
   - Install `barman-cloud-backup` (pip, throwaway venv) and read
     `barman/cloud.py`'s `CloudTarUploader`/`CloudUploadController` upload
     path directly rather than re-guessing from outside behavior.
   - Reproduce the failure locally: run a local `cmd/armor` instance
     against a local/mock backend, drive a `barman-cloud-backup`-shaped
     (or literal) multipart upload of a realistic PostgreSQL-base-backup
     tar stream through it, and confirm you can reproduce non-65536-aligned
     part sizes with overshoot patterns matching the real evidence above
     (i.e. remainder is a clean multiple of 512, not 65536).
   - Determine precisely what would need to be true (client-side config,
     patch, or none-of-the-above) for barman-cloud-backup to reliably
     produce ARMOR-compliant part boundaries with data of arbitrary,
     unpredictable size.

2. **Write ADR-010** documenting the root cause and a recommendation.
   Plausible directions to weigh (not prescriptive — pick based on what the
   investigation actually finds):
   - A client-side-only fix exists and is real (not another "verified
     empirically" mistake) — document exactly what it is and why it's
     provably reliable across arbitrary data sizes, including the
     boundary cases ADR-005 cares about (short-first-part poisoning).
   - No reliable client-side fix exists with the current barman-cloud
     version, and ARMOR needs a deliberate, narrowly-scoped accommodation
     (e.g. an opt-in mode with a different integrity mechanism for clients
     that can't guarantee alignment). If recommending this, be explicit
     about how it avoids reintroducing the exact class of silent corruption
     ADR-002/003/005 already fought and fixed once.
   - These two backup targets should stop writing through ARMOR's direct
     S3 endpoint entirely for base backups (e.g. route through Garage the
     way `apexalgo-iad`/`ardenone-cluster` already do, with ARMOR/B2 as a
     secondary off-site copy instead of the primary barman target).

## Acceptance criteria

- Local reproduction that matches the real observed failure pattern
  (misaligned part with a 512-but-not-65536-byte-multiple remainder),
  not a hand-wavy "should be similar" — cite the actual numbers.
- ADR-010 written and added to `docs/adr/`, referencing ADR-002/003/005/008
  and this bead's evidence.
- Do **not** close this bead on the strength of one successful test run —
  today's incident is the second time in this exact saga that a single
  passing attempt was mistaken for a fix (see forgejo's 15:04Z run above,
  and the four prior "fixed, still corrupts" cycles documented in ARMOR's
  own git/bead history for this general class of bug). If proposing a fix,
  the acceptance test must be multiple consecutive successful runs against
  data sizes that vary (don't let a single lucky size hide non-determinism).
- Do not modify anything outside this repository. This bead needs no
  cluster or `declarative-config` access — deploying/verifying any resulting
  fix against the live `iad-ci` clusters is deliberately out of scope here
  (tracked separately, ops-gated).

title: Escrow-proof drill: verify the OpenBao-held MEK decrypts current data, per bucket
description: MEKs live in OpenBao (secret/<cluster>/backblaze/armor style paths) and reach clusters via ESO. Nothing proves the OpenBao copy decrypts TODAYated data - an in-cluster rotation that skips OpenBao would silently invalidate the escrow. Code half (dispatchable): extend the restore-verifier DR-drill mode to accept the MEK from an external source (file/env distinct from the serving MEK) and report a distinct escrow_drill status/metric comparing escrow-MEK decryption of a fresh object against the serving path. title: Decode base64 file to plain text
description:
## Child Bead: Decode base64 file to plain text

This bead performs the actual base64 decoding of the file.

### Prerequisites
- Previous child bead complete (bf-3cdka: base64 file exists and is non-empty)

### Acceptance Criteria
- Base64 decoding succeeds without errors
- Decoded output is written to /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
- Decoded output file is non-empty
- No decoding errors (malformed base64, etc.)

### Commands
```bash
# Decode the value
base64 -d /tmp/litestream_key_id.b64 > /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt 2>&1

# Check exit code
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Decoding successful"
else
    echo "ERROR: Base64 decoding failed"
    cat /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt  # This contains error output
    exit 1
fi

# Verify output file is non-empty
if [ -s /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt ]; then
    echo "Decoded file is non-empty"
    ls -lh /tmp/litestream_key_id.txt
else
    echo "ERROR: Decoded output is empty"
    exit 1
fi
```

Success: Decoding succeeds, output file exists and is non-empty.

Failure: Decoding fails or produces empty output — base64 file may be corrupted or not valid base64.

title: S3 API lets clients read/write/delete internal .armor/ keys — add namespace guard
description:
GAP: docs/plan/plan.md ('ListObjectsV2 Size Correction', 'Passthrough Operations') specifies that .armor/ internal objects are invisible to clients, and internal/backend/b2.go does filter .armor/ keys from List (b2.go ~:308) and ListObjectVersions (~:1183). But there is NO guard on the object-level operations: internal/server/handlers/handlers.go contains no .armor prefix check, so any authenticated client can PutObject, GetObject, HeadObject, DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, CopyObject, or multipart-upload directly to .armor/* keys.

IMPACT: a client (or a compromised client credential) can tamper with exactly the state that provides ARMOR's integrity guarantees:
- .armor/chain/<writer>/* and .armor/chain-head/<writer> — forge or truncate the tamper-evident provenance chain
- .armor/manifest/<writer>/* — poison manifest delta files, which carry IV + wrapped-DEK entries used for decryption (see plan.md Phase 4)
- .armor/hmac/<sha256> — replace multipart HMAC sidecars
- .armor/rotation-state.json — corrupt in-progress key rotation
- .armor/multipart/*.state and .armor/canary/* — disrupt crash recovery and health checks

FIX: reject client S3 operations targeting keys with the .armor/ prefix (403 AccessDenied, standard S3 XML error via the existing error helper) in the S3 handler layer (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go), before backend dispatch. Internal code paths (provenance, manifest, canary, rotation, multipart state) go through the backend directly and must remain unaffected.

ACCEPTANCE:
- Table-driven tests in internal/server/handlers/handlers_test.go covering Put/Get/Head/Delete/DeleteObjects/Copy (both source and destination)/CreateMultipartUpload against .armor/ keys → 403 AccessDenied
- Canary, provenance, manifest, key rotation unit tests still pass (internal paths unaffected)
- ListObjectsV2/.armor filtering behavior unchanged
- README.md 'S3 API Coverage' notes the reserved .armor/ namespace

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
## GAP ANALYSIS: missing decompression test case

### The named gap
**Metadata-flag vs. actual-content divergence — specifically the "legacy-compressed" case: payload IS zstd-compressed but `ARMORMetadata.Compressed == false`.** No existing test covers a row where the flag and the actual plaintext disagree; in all 5 table rows + all standalone tests the two signals are kept aligned.

### Why this is the real gap (code evidence)
The handler computes TWO independent compression signals but only acts on ONE:
- `internal/server/server.go:1162` — runtime magic-byte detection `crypto.IsCompressed(decrypted)` (first decrypted block). Result is computed and **logged only** (`compressed_meta` vs `compressed_detected`), never used to gate behavior.
- `internal/server/server.go:1175` — `if armorMeta.Compressed {` is the sole decompression gate. It keys off the **metadata flag**, not the detection.

The detection at :1162 was clearly added precisely because flag and reality CAN diverge (objects compressed before the flag existed, or a client that sets the flag wrong) — yet no test exercises that divergence. It is dead/untriggered in the suite.

The table CAN'T express it: per the documented pattern (bf-5x15bj §2.5-2.6), the single `compressed bool` field drives BOTH whether `compressData()` runs (actual data state) AND the value written to `armorMeta.Compressed`. They are structurally coupled, so a divergence case is impossible to add as a row without splitting the field. The pattern's own note confirms it: "in all five existing rows wantDecompression == compressed."

(Note: the breadth case `compressed_large_repeating_text` already suggested in bf-5x15bj is NOT the answer — it is "more of the same," not an uncovered branch. The uncovered *scenario* is the divergence.)

### Current behavior under the gap (what the test would pin)
With compressed payload + flag=false:
- server.go:1175 gate is false → `crypto.Decompress` is never called
- `finalData = allDecrypted` = raw zstd-compressed bytes
- client receives `compressData(original)`, NOT `original` → **round-trip fails; silent corruption**
- The :1162 detection does NOT rescue it (it only logs). This is a latent regression risk worth pinning, and arguably a bug (detection should gate, not just log).

### Exact new test case — NEW STANDALONE FUNCTION (not a table row)

Placement decision: a new function, mirroring `TestShareGET_LegacyObject` (lines 321-380), which already does the post-`encryptTestData` flag override pattern. Justification:
1. The table's `compressed` field couples flag+data; expressing a divergence requires splitting the struct field for ALL rows — invasive and unjustified for one edge case.
2. The assertion semantics differ: this case must assert the *current (broken) behavior* (`retrievedData == compressData(original)`, i.e. decompression did NOT run), which the dual-assertion block (§3 of the pattern, wants `retrievedData == tc.data`) cannot express.
3. The precedent — `TestShareGET_LegacyObject` is already a standalone function for exactly this kind of "set the flag explicitly after encrypt" case.

Stub:
```go
// TestShareGET_LegacyCompressedPayload pins behavior for an object whose
// plaintext is actually zstd-compressed but whose metadata Compressed flag is
// false (a pre-flag / mislabeled object). The server gates decompression on the
// metadata flag (server.go:1175), not on runtime magic-byte detection, so it
// serves the raw compressed bytes and the round-trip does NOT reproduce the
// original. This documents that gap until detection gates decompression.
func TestShareGET_LegacyCompressedPayload(t *testing.T) {
	tmpDir, cleanup := setupTestEnvironment(t)
	defer cleanup()

	fsBackend, err := backend.NewFSBackend(backend.FSConfig{BasePath: tmpDir})
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to create filesystem backend: %v", err)
	}

	cfg := loadTestConfig(t, tmpDir)
	srv, err := NewWithBackend(cfg, fsBackend)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to create server: %v", err)
	}
	srv.presigner = presign.NewSigner(cfg.PresignSecret, "")

	originalData := []byte(strings.Repeat("Repeat pattern for compression. ", 100))
	compressedData := compressData(originalData)

	if !crypto.IsCompressed(compressedData) {
		t.Fatalf("precondition: test data must be zstd-compressed")
	}

	// Encrypt the ALREADY-COMPRESSED bytes but set the flag to false.
	encryptedData, hmacTable, armorMeta := encryptTestData(t, srv, compressedData, false)
	armorMeta.Compressed = false // legacy/mislabeled: flag says uncompressed

	ctx := context.Background()
	storeTestObject(t, srv.backend, ctx, "test-bucket", "test-key-legacy-compressed", encryptedData, hmacTable, armorMeta)

	token := generateTestToken(t, srv, "test-bucket", "test-key-legacy-compressed", time.Hour)
	req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/share/"+token, nil)
	w := httptest.NewRecorder()
	srv.handleShare(w, req)

	resp := w.Result()
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
		t.Fatalf("Expected status 200, got %d", resp.StatusCode)
	}
	retrievedData, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("Failed to read response body: %v", err)
	}

	// Pin CURRENT behavior: flag=false skips decompression, so the client gets
	// the raw zstd bytes (== compressedData), NOT originalData.
	if !bytes.Equal(retrievedData, compressedData) {
		t.Errorf("expected raw compressed bytes (decompression bypassed by false flag); got %d bytes that differ from both original and compressed payload", len(retrievedData))
	}
	if bytes.Equal(retrievedData, originalData) {
		t.Error("UNEXPECTED: round-trip succeeded despite Compressed=false — detection may now gate decompression; update this test")
	}
}
```
Fields/values summary:
- name: `TestShareGET_LegacyCompressedPayload` (object key `test-key-legacy-compressed`)
- data: `[]byte(strings.Repeat("Repeat pattern for compression. ", 100))`
- actuallyCompressed: true (via `compressData`); metaCompressed: false (forced)
- wantDecompression (asserted behavior): **false** — pins that the flag, not detection, gates decompression
- description: legacy/mislabeled compressed payload served raw because the flag gates decompression

### Secondary (lower-priority) gap, for completeness
The mirror divergence — flag=true but payload NOT compressed (no zstd magic). server.go:1175 calls `crypto.Decompress`, but `crypto.Decompress` (decryptor.go:315-317) re-checks magic and returns data **unchanged, no error** → graceful, client gets correct data. Worth a row/function eventually, but it is NOT corrupting, so it is second priority behind the flag=false case above.

### Conclusion
The missing case is the flag/data divergence, concretely "compressed payload + Compressed=false." It cannot be a table row (field coupling); it warrants a new standalone function that pins the current corrupting behavior and flips green only if detection is ever wired into the gate.

title: Identify a kubeconfig with exec and secret-read access to the commitgraph host cluster
description:
THIS IS THE CORE BLOCKER. The two access paths both need RBAC beyond a read-only proxy: Path A needs pod-exec on queue-api; Path B needs secret-read on commitgraph-b2-workers. Read-only proxies grant NEITHER. Find which kubeconfig grants each. This is the gate the prior 3 failures never got past.

Context: bf-1q3s0v documents that admin OIDC kubeconfigs (e.g. ord-devimprint-admin) expire roughly every 3 days and time out when stale. Expect some to be dead; the goal is to find a LIVE one.

Tasks:
- Against the host cluster identified in the previous child, test each admin/direct kubeconfig in ~/.kube/ (e.g. ardenone-manager, rs-manager, apexalgo-iad, ord-devimprint-admin, iad-ci, iad-options) for TWO operations:
  (a) secret-read: `kubectl <kubeconfig> get secret commitgraph-b2-workers -n commitgraph -o jsonpath='{.data}'` succeeds;
  (b) exec: `kubectl <kubeconfig> exec <queue-api-pod> -c litestream -n commitgraph -- echo ok` succeeds.
- Record, per operation, the kubeconfig path that works (exec-capable and secret-read-capable may be different kubeconfigs).

## Acceptance Criteria
- EITHER a working kubeconfig path is recorded for exec AND/OR for secret-read against the commitgraph cluster; OR
- if NONE work, a precise blocker report is produced naming exactly which kubeconfig is stale/expired and what needs refreshing (mirror the bf-1q3s0v self-service Spot-dashboard OIDC refresh pattern). That blocker report is itself a closable, actionable outcome.
- Result appended to scratch/commitgraph-b2-access.md.
notes:
Probed every ord-devimprint direct/admin kubeconfig for BOTH operations (host cluster = ord-devimprint, per bf-3hbw6f). Re-confirmed live pod queue-api-c5894c469-pzjsl, litestream container.

RESULT: BLOCKED — no kubeconfig grants secret-read OR exec. Auth fails at the API layer, so it blocks both ops identically.

Per-context matrix (timeout-bounded; stale Spot OIDC hangs):
- ord-devimprint-token / token-context (ngpc-user): secret-read=401 Unauthorized, exec=401 Unauthorized — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint-admin / apexalgo-ord-devimprint (ngpc-user-apexalgo static): 401/401 — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint / apexalgo-ord-devimprint (ngpc-user static): 401/401 — static token expired.
- ord-devimprint-admin / apexalgo-ord-devimprint-oidc (oidc exec): TIMEOUT/TIMEOUT — OIDC cache empty (~/.kube/cache/oidc-login/org_KsELolwAOxl3Zxfm has only 0-byte .lock files, no token blob) + no browser headless.
- ord-devimprint / apexalgo-ord-devimprint-oidc (oidc exec): TIMEOUT/TIMEOUT — same.
- ord-devimprint-observer (devpod-observer SA): 403/403 — read-only by design (never grants these; known).

Other-cluster kubeconfigs (apexalgo-iad, ardenone-manager, rs-manager, iad-ci, iad-options, iad-kalshi incl. default ~/.kube/config) are NOT candidates: commitgraph namespace is NotFound on all of them (recon matrix §1). No cross-cluster RBAC.

Root cause = authentication on ord-devimprint, not network (direct control plane answers; unauth curl returns http 403). API reachable, credential dead.

Remediation (operator self-service, mirrors bf-1q3s0v): Rackspace Spot dashboard -> ord-devimprint -> regenerate admin kubeconfig (overwrites ~/.kube/ord-devimprint-admin.kubeconfig). Then prime the OIDC token cache ONCE from a browser-capable machine (run any kubectl against it, complete login.spot.rackspace.com SSO) so the exec path works headless. The freshly-downloaded kubeconfig also carries a static ngpc-user token usable headless immediately but it is short-lived (the Aug-07 20:01 regen's static token was already Unauthorized by Aug-09, <~37h) — temporary unlock only. A single refreshed ord-devimprint-admin kubeconfig grants BOTH secret-read and exec (same cluster-admin OIDC identity); no per-operation split needed.

title: Key rotation test coverage: prove rotation works end-to-end, especially for multipart objects
description: Rotation (re-wrap DEKs via CopyObject MetadataDirective=REPLACE, resume state in rotation-state.json) has never been exercised against the current object formats and predates the multipart layout. Add tests proving, at the handler layer with real internal/crypto: (1) rotate a mixed prefix (single-PUT + multipart objects) to a new MEK; every object decrypts with the NEW MEK and FAILS with the old one; plaintext and ETags unchanged. (2) CRITICAL: rotation must preserve ALL x-amz-meta-armor-* metadata on multipart objects - especially the armor-multipart marker and wrapped-DEK - and must not touch the HMAC sidecar; a dropped marker silently makes every rotated multipart object unreadable (the exact bf-24sxh7 failure mode reintroduced by rotation). Assert marker+sidecar survive and the object round-trips after rotation. (3) Interrupted-rotation resume: kill mid-rotation, re-run, verify idempotent completion and no object left old-wrapped. (4) Non-ARMOR passthrough objects are skipped untouched. (5) Document (and assert a clear error for) the B2 CopyObject size ceiling - objects above it cannot be re-wrapped via CopyObject and must be enumerated by rotation as EXCEPTIONS, not silently skipped. (6) Document the operational runbook ordering in docs: new MEK written to OpenBao -> ESO sync -> rotate endpoint -> pod restart with new env - and note rotation via the admin API must never diverge from OpenBao (see bf-5m9nde for auth). go test -race green.

title: Root-cause barman-cloud-backup InvalidPartSize failures + write ADR-010
description:
## Context

`queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` (CNPG PostgreSQL, both on `iad-ci`) are the
only two barman-cloud backup targets in the estate that write through ARMOR
(`endpointURL: http://armor.armor.svc.cluster.local:9000`). `queue-db` has
failed **every** scheduled base backup since 2026-05-26 (600+ consecutive
`InvalidPartSize` failures); `forgejo-postgres` has the same failure mode.
Background: [ADR-002](docs/adr/002-multipart-corruption-detection-gaps.md),
[ADR-005](docs/adr/005-out-of-order-multipart-uniform-part-size.md),
[ADR-008](docs/adr/008-multipart-part-size-error-clarity.md).

ARMOR's side of this is done and correct: ADR-005's uniform-part-size
contract is enforced live, and ADR-008 shipped a clear, actionable rejection
message (`InvalidPartSize: Part size N is not a multiple of the block size
(65536 bytes)...`) instead of a silent failure. **This bead is not about
ARMOR's behavior being wrong — it is about characterizing why
barman-cloud-backup cannot satisfy ARMOR's documented, deliberate contract,
and deciding what (if anything) should change.**

## A same-day "fix" already failed — do not repeat this mistake

declarative-config commit `c8aefe75` (2026-08-06 08:50 EDT) disabled gzip
compression on both clusters' base-backup data
(`barmanObjectStore.data: {}`), on the theory that barman's tar streamer
flushes to S3 in exact 65536-byte chunks when uncompressed, so every part
boundary would land on a clean multiple of ARMOR's block size. The commit
message and manifest comments describe this as "verified empirically."

**That verification does not hold.** Live pod logs pulled *after* the fix
was deployed and synced (2026-08-06T21:03-21:04Z, many hours after the
08:50 EDT deploy) show both clusters still failing on every scheduled
attempt:

```
queue-db:          Part size 11876352 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
forgejo-postgres:   Part size 4284416 is not a multiple of the block size (65536 bytes)
```

Overshoot analysis: `11876352 = 65536*181 + 14336` and `4284416 = 65536*65 +
24576`. Both remainders (14336, 24576) are exact multiples of 512 (POSIX
tar's block size) but NOT of 65536. This means barman-cloud-backup's real
flush granularity is NOT the 65536-byte unit the fix assumed — the "verified
empirically" claim was based on an insufficient one-off test, not on watching
real scheduled runs. (One `forgejo-postgres` run did succeed once, at 15:04Z
the same day — almost certainly because that particular backup's total size
happened to stay under barman's flush threshold and never triggered
multipart upload at all, not because the fix works.)

Two earlier CLI-flag-level workarounds were also tried on
`forgejo-postgres` and both failed live: `--min-chunk-size=5MB` and
`--min-chunk-size=2GB` (attempting to force a single-part upload). The 2GB
attempt still produced one misaligned part — expected, since ADR-005
deliberately does **not** exempt a lone first-and-only part from alignment
(only a genuinely trailing part *after* an already-aligned first part is
exempt — this is a poison-detection safeguard, not an oversight, added after
this project's real history of silent multipart corruption; see ADR-005 and
the historical incidents it links).

## What this bead is

1. **Actually characterize barman-cloud-backup 3.19.1's real
   upload/flush behavior** (the version confirmed live in both pods'
   tracebacks: `/usr/local/lib/python3.9/dist-packages/barman/cloud.py`).
   Do this locally, inside this checkout — no cluster access is needed or
   should be used:
   - Install `barman-cloud-backup` (pip, throwaway venv) and read
     `barman/cloud.py`'s `CloudTarUploader`/`CloudUploadController` upload
     path directly rather than re-guessing from outside behavior.
   - Reproduce the failure locally: run a local `cmd/armor` instance
     against a local/mock backend, drive a `barman-cloud-backup`-shaped
     (or literal) multipart upload of a realistic PostgreSQL-base-backup
     tar stream through it, and confirm you can reproduce non-65536-aligned
     part sizes with overshoot patterns matching the real evidence above
     (i.e. remainder is a clean multiple of 512, not 65536).
   - Determine precisely what would need to be true (client-side config,
     patch, or none-of-the-above) for barman-cloud-backup to reliably
     produce ARMOR-compliant part boundaries with data of arbitrary,
     unpredictable size.

2. **Write ADR-010** documenting the root cause and a recommendation.
   Plausible directions to weigh (not prescriptive — pick based on what the
   investigation actually finds):
   - A client-side-only fix exists and is real (not another "verified
     empirically" mistake) — document exactly what it is and why it's
     provably reliable across arbitrary data sizes, including the
     boundary cases ADR-005 cares about (short-first-part poisoning).
   - No reliable client-side fix exists with the current barman-cloud
     version, and ARMOR needs a deliberate, narrowly-scoped accommodation
     (e.g. an opt-in mode with a different integrity mechanism for clients
     that can't guarantee alignment). If recommending this, be explicit
     about how it avoids reintroducing the exact class of silent corruption
     ADR-002/003/005 already fought and fixed once.
   - These two backup targets should stop writing through ARMOR's direct
     S3 endpoint entirely for base backups (e.g. route through Garage the
     way `apexalgo-iad`/`ardenone-cluster` already do, with ARMOR/B2 as a
     secondary off-site copy instead of the primary barman target).

## Acceptance criteria

- Local reproduction that matches the real observed failure pattern
  (misaligned part with a 512-but-not-65536-byte-multiple remainder),
  not a hand-wavy "should be similar" — cite the actual numbers.
- ADR-010 written and added to `docs/adr/`, referencing ADR-002/003/005/008
  and this bead's evidence.
- Do **not** close this bead on the strength of one successful test run —
  today's incident is the second time in this exact saga that a single
  passing attempt was mistaken for a fix (see forgejo's 15:04Z run above,
  and the four prior "fixed, still corrupts" cycles documented in ARMOR's
  own git/bead history for this general class of bug). If proposing a fix,
  the acceptance test must be multiple consecutive successful runs against
  data sizes that vary (don't let a single lucky size hide non-determinism).
- Do not modify anything outside this repository. This bead needs no
  cluster or `declarative-config` access — deploying/verifying any resulting
  fix against the live `iad-ci` clusters is deliberately out of scope here
  (tracked separately, ops-gated).
close_reason: Duplicate of bf-38uhih, which was dispatched and closed the same day producing ADR-010 (docs/adr/010-barman-multipart-incompatibility.md). No further root-cause investigation needed — ADR-010 documents the math proof (barman's write() overflow is a multiple of 512, never 65536) and the decision (reroute through Garage, not an ARMOR change).

description:

Deploying 0.1.1897 to any cluster would ImagePullBackOff fleet-wide — the same failure mode as the historical 0.1.467 ghost-tag incident (2+ days of unnoticed ImagePullBackOff). The fleet deploy was retargeted to 0.1.1896, which git merge-base confirms contains every runtime fix (0c6fc813 admin gating, b521651d ADR-005, 9f6d5694, 94d1a485, 5bc58e0d); 0.1.1897 would only add 3decc976 (key_rotation.go multipart-rotation-resume, 156 LOC).

Likely cause: the armor-build WorkflowTemplate runs go-test as a GATE before docker-build, and 3decc976 added 623 lines of new key_rotation tests — if any fail in CI, no image is published. Investigate the armor-build run for the 0.1.1897 bump (iad-ci argo-workflows; note podGC OnPodCompletion + short TTL, so logs may be gone — may need a re-run). Also note the resolve-version auto-bump quirk: because the current HEAD commit did not touch VERSION, re-triggering armor-build will compute 0.1.1898 (patch+1) and build THAT, not 0.1.1897.

ACCEPTANCE: a pullable ronaldraygun/armor image exists for HEAD's code (whatever the resolved tag), CI go-test passes, and the fleet can be bumped off 0.1.1896 to true-HEAD. Consider a post-build registry-existence assertion in the WorkflowTemplate so a bumped VERSION without a pullable image fails loudly instead of silently.

description:
ADR-012 decision 1 / Phase 7 credential provisioning — INVESTIGATION ONLY (read-only: no OpenBao writes, no key generation, no code changes).

Resolve the two ambiguities that have repeatedly blocked this work. For each of the four consumers determine (1) the exact OpenBao sub-path under the secret/rs-manager/iad-ci/armor family where its credential record will live, and (2) the exact well-formed ACL string in ARMOR's bucket:prefix[:actions] format (see internal/config/config.go parseACL / parseActions and internal/server/auth.go CheckACL).

Two consumers are NOT explicitly named in ADR-012 and MUST be pinned down here from source:
- CNPG/barman: ADR-012 says only "CNPG's backup prefix". Confirm the actual key-prefix from the CNPG backup job / barman config / stored paths (handler comments reference postgres/cnpg/...). Record the exact prefix string.
- restore-verifier: ADR-012 names no prefix. This consumer must READ across all consumer prefixes to verify restores, so its ACL is a MULTI-ENTRY read ACL (get+list on forgejo/, the cnpg prefix, ci-cache/, ...), NOT a single prefix. Enumerate every read entry it needs and no more.

The two explicit ones: forgejo -> *:forgejo/ ; ci-cache -> *:ci-cache/ (confirm the real bucket name; decide per ADR-012 decision 3 whether action verbs like put+list / get+list apply now, or whether this zero-code phase uses full-verb-per-prefix).

Deliverable: a mapping table recorded as a COMMENT on this bead — consumer | OpenBao path | ACL string | rationale (cite ADR-012 section + source file:line). Flag the strings.HasPrefix no-slash-boundary residual risk (e.g. forgejo/ also matches forgejo-other/) for each entry.

- CNPG prefix and restore-verifier multi-entry ACL resolved from source, not assumed

NAMING WART: an EXISTING OpenBao path rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/forgejo-backup is the declarative-config-backup writer (armor-externalsecret.yaml:43-46), NOT forgejo -- distinct path, but the name collides conceptually with this real forgejo consumer; recommend renaming that one to .../armor/declarative-config-backup when convenient.

2. CNPG/barman -- TWO clusters, TWO prefixes (ADR-012:35 "queue-db, forgejo-postgres"; the singular "CNPG's backup prefix" at ADR-012:79 is imprecise). Each cluster already has its OWN k8s Secret today (forgejo-backup-armor, queue-db-backup-armor), so provision TWO records (matches the per-cluster split + ADR-012 "destroy only its own prefix"). RECOMMENDED (least privilege):
   2a. forgejo-postgres | rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/forgejo-postgres | iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/ | barmanObjectStore.destinationPath s3://iad-ci/forgejo/cnpg/ (forgejo/cnpg-cluster.yaml:62); s3Credentials Secret forgejo-backup-armor. Decision-3 -> iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/:put+list.
   2b. queue-db | rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/queue-db | iad-ci:queue-db/cnpg/ | destinationPath s3://iad-ci/queue-db/cnpg/ (queue-db/cnpg-cluster.yaml:46); s3Credentials Secret queue-db-backup-armor. Decision-3 -> iad-ci:queue-db/cnpg/:put+list.
   REJECTED alt (one "CNPG" consumer): single path .../armor/cnpg with ACL "iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/,iad-ci:queue-db/cnpg/" -- a holder could cross-delete the other cluster's backups, which is exactly the cross-consumer leak ADR-012 exists to prevent.

3. ci-cache | rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/ci-cache | iad-ci:ci-cache/ | ADR-012:79 names ci-cache/. WARNING: ASPIRATIONAL -- "ci-cache/" appears in ZERO deployed manifests (grep across all of declarative-config + ARMOR repo hits only ADR-012 itself); build caches today use Docker registries (--cache-repo=ronaldraygun/cache in argo-workflows templates), not ARMOR. No writer pod/identity exists yet. The ACL string is well-formed for the future consumer but there is nothing to provision against today. ci-cache is a read+write cache, so the decision-3 form is NOT append-only: iad-ci:ci-cache/:get+put+list.

4. restore-verifier | rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/restore-verifier | iad-ci:forgejo/:get+list, iad-ci:queue-db/cnpg/:get+list, iad-ci:declarative-config-backups/:get+list, iad-ci:ci-cache/:get+list | Multi-entry READ ACL enumerating every consumer prefix and no more (ADR-012:79 "restore-verifier credential"; verifier scans the whole bucket internal/restoreverifier/verifier.go:1271 and skips .armor bookkeeping :1280, so NO grant for .armor/manifest). forgejo/ subsumes forgejo/postgres, forgejo/repos, forgejo/status, forgejo/wal, forgejo/cnpg (all textual sub-prefixes). TWO BLOCKERS the provisioning child must know:
   (a) The DEPLOYED restore-verifier does NOT authenticate to ARMOR at all: restore-verifier.yaml:6-8 says it "connects DIRECTLY to B2 (not through the armor proxy)"; its env (restore-verifier.yaml:76-90) carries only ARMOR_B2_ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET_ACCESS_KEY + ARMOR_MEK, no ARMOR_AUTH_*. verifier.go drives the B2 backend directly (v.backend Head/GetRange/GetDirect, verifier.go:1053,1089,1153). => An ARMOR ACL credential for restore-verifier is MOOT until/unless it is reworked to go through the armor proxy; today it needs B2 keys + MEK (full bucket read), which an ARMOR ACL cannot express.
   (b) DESIGN TENSION with the verifier's whole-bucket list: a prefix-scoped credential CANNOT do a no-prefix ListObjectsV2 (correctly DENIED -- ADR-012:22-24: list with no ?prefix from a scoped cred is denied). A migrated through-ARMOR verifier must iterate ?prefix= per granted entry rather than one whole-bucket list. The multi-entry ACL above is the correct grant set for that migrated shape.

== strings.HasPrefix no-slash-boundary residual risk (CheckACL auth.go:315: bare strings.HasPrefix(key, acl.Prefix), no delimiter/path-segment logic) ==
The trailing "/" on every prefix is LOAD-BEARING. WITH the slash, sibling bleed does NOT happen -- verified against the bytes: strings.HasPrefix("forgejo-other/x","forgejo/") is FALSE (byte 7 '/' vs '-'), so iad-ci:forgejo/ does NOT match forgejo-other/. The genuine residual risks:
- DROP the slash and the match goes unbounded: iad-ci:forgejo would match forgejo-other/, forgejox/, forgejoevil/. Same for every entry. RULE: never ship an ACL prefix without its trailing "/".
- NESTED-prefix reach (real, non-hypothetical): iad-ci:forgejo/ TEXTUALLY CONTAINS iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/ and forgejo/wal/. So the forgejo consumer's credential can read/overwrite the forgejo-postgres CNPG base backups at forgejo/cnpg/. Same namespace (forgejo owns its own postgres), acceptable per ADR-012, but it IS a cross-writer-identity reach -- the CNPG operator and forgejo-backup are different pods. The restore-verifier forgejo/:get+list entry inherits this same nested reach (intended: it verifies everything under forgejo/).
- forgejo-postgres iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/ and queue-db iad-ci:queue-db/cnpg/: no sibling leak (no other forgejo/cnpg* or queue-db/cnpg*), slash-dependent only.
- ci-cache iad-ci:ci-cache/: slash-dependent; would match ci-cachev2/ if the slash were dropped.

- File: internal/server/server.go

- share_decompress_corrupted_test.go: Corruption handling, error recovery  
- Integration tests: Full S3 lifecycle with byte-exact verification
- Range tests: HTTP 416 for compressed, HTTP 206 for uncompressed

notes:
## Analysis Complete

### Key Findings

**Settings that directly hide beads:**

1. exclude_labels (primary mechanism)
   - Current config: empty array
   - Default behavior applies: deferred, human, blocked
   - Any bead with these labels is filtered from candidate selection
   - Filtering occurs at both store and strand levels for safety

2. Status filtering (built-in, not configurable)
   - InProgress beads: Hidden (actively claimed by another worker)
   - Open beads with assignee: Hidden (stale assignments cause retry loops)
   - Cannot be disabled - prevents race conditions

3. split_after_failures (indirect effect)
   - Current: 0 (disabled)
   - When enabled, diverts beads with N+ failures to Mitosis strand
   - Does not hide beads, but changes processing path

**Settings that do NOT hide beads:**
- sort_order: Only affects candidate ordering, not visibility

### Documentation

Created comprehensive analysis: notes/pluck-settings-that-hide-beads.md

- All filtering mechanisms with code references
- Current ARMOR configuration analysis
- Combined filtering effects with examples
- Debugging and monitoring guidance

title: Add in-memory compressible round-trip test and compression test harness
description:
Stand up the handler-level PUT->GET compression test harness (a new handlers_compress_test.go in the handlers test package, package handlers_test) and lock in the ALREADY-WIRED in-memory (small-object) compress path as the verified baseline. Today the only compression coverage is the crypto-package unit tests (internal/crypto/compress_test.go); there is no handler-level proof that a real PUT with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true round-trips through a real GET. This is the baseline the rest of the split builds on.

Wiring under test (already present, do NOT modify production code): in-memory PUT opportunistic compress at handlers.go ~L354-377 (crypto.Compress, keep-only-if-smaller, header.SetCompressed) with the metadata Compressed flag at ~L414-425; GET decompression + X-Armor-Compressed response header at handlers.go ~L882-884 and ~L960-989. The in-memory/streaming routing threshold is 10MB at handlers.go L297/L303.

Deliver in that new test file (package handlers_test), reusing testSetup / handlers.New / mockBackend already defined in the existing handlers_test.go:
- Shared helpers: decodeStoredHeader (decode the 64-byte envelope header from the mock backend stored object), storedMetadata (parse stored ARMORMetadata), doPutGet (real HandleRoot PUT then GET, both must HTTP 200), compressiblePayload (N bytes of repeated JSON-manifest lines).
- Subtest compressible_inmemory: PUT a ~200KB compressible payload with cfg.Compress=true via the in-memory path; GET it back. Assert GET body byte-identical to plaintext; stored envelope IsCompressed()==true and header.PlaintextSize (the encrypted data region) strictly < len(plaintext); stored metadata Compressed==true; GET response carries X-Armor-Compressed: true.

Acceptance:
- go test ./internal/server/handlers/ compiles and passes; compressible_inmemory is green.
- No production-code change (this is the verified baseline).
- Label: split-child.

title: Extend canary monitor with multipart-path integrity check
description: internal/canary currently uses a fixed 1024-byte payload via direct backend.Put() -- structurally never exercises the multipart upload calls (create, upload part, complete), which is exactly where the 2026-06 corruption bug lived (see ADR-002). Add a second, longer-interval check (e.g. hourly, alongside the existing 5-min small-object check) that uploads a canary object sized just above the multipart threshold via real multipart S3 calls, downloads, and verifies byte-for-byte + HMAC + plaintext-SHA, reusing the existing Monitor's verification logic. Surface a distinct multipart_healthy status in the canary endpoint and Prometheus metrics so a multipart-specific regression is visible independently of the small-object check staying green.
notes:
Sharpened 2026-07-15 based on bf-1v6skf (P0, confirmed real bug): the multipart canary check this bead adds must not stop at "just above the multipart threshold." The actual failing object in production was 44,908,497 bytes (a litestream level-9 snapshot) and failed HMAC verification at block 256 on GetObject -- a smaller same-generation 836,559-byte compacted object read back fine. So the bug is scale-dependent in a way a single small canary object would miss entirely.

Corrected requirements:
- Canary must test at multiple sizes, including one well above 44MB (the confirmed-failing scale), not just "just over the multipart threshold"
- Must assert successful full decrypt AND HMAC verification on the read-back, matching exactly the failure mode found in bf-1v6skf (InternalError: Failed to decrypt range: block N: HMAC verification failed) -- a canary that only checks HTTP status code or ContentLength would not have caught this either
- Should log/alert with enough detail (failing block number, object size, generation) to make a future recurrence immediately diagnosable, since the litestream-based discovery path took significant manual investigation (raw aws s3 cp needed to isolate the real error after litestream itself hung silently retrying for 10+ minutes instead of failing fast)
- Related: bf-28rb (the existing multipart integration test) was found to use a fully mocked backend that bypasses internal/crypto entirely -- do not repeat that mistake here; this canary must hit ARMOR's real encrypt/decrypt/HMAC path, not a mock
close_reason: Already implemented: internal/canary runs a full multipart canary cycle (CreateMultipartUpload/UploadPart/Complete) with multipart_healthy status and metrics. Verified on main 2026-07-18.

title: Deploy+verify barman fix on iad-ci (queue-db, forgejo-postgres) + fix hourly ScheduledBackup cron bug
description:
## Why this is blocked, not open

This bead requires `kubectl` write access to `iad-ci` and push access to the
`jedarden/declarative-config` repo (a different repo from this checkout) to
actually deploy and verify anything. It is **not reachable from an
ARMOR-repo-scoped worker** and must not be picked up by one — set to
`blocked` deliberately, matching this project's established convention for
ops/credential-gated work (see e.g. the historical fencing of bf-4qq1,
bf-2t1f, bf-32ms, bf-5aqh0). A human, or an agent session with the relevant
kubeconfig and declarative-config write access, needs to pick this up
directly — not via `bf ready` dispatch.

## Background — read ADR-011, not ADR-010

ADR-010 (2026-08-06) originally recommended rerouting these backups to
Garage; that was reversed by explicit operator direction. **ADR-011**
(`docs/adr/011-barman-stays-on-armor-non-uniform-multipart.md`,
2026-08-07, supersedes ADR-010) is the current design: ARMOR's alignment
check was over-broad — part 1 and the presumed-final part never actually
needed block alignment (part 1 always starts at block 0; nothing follows
the final part). That exemption is **already shipped on main**
(`fc6c1a86`, `1f6e6934`) and, since both `queue-db` (~30MB) and
`forgejo-postgres` (~63MB) fit comfortably in a single multipart part
(S3's per-part ceiling is 5GiB), it resolves the outage **without** needing
non-uniform multipart support. That durable follow-on (for when these DBs
grow past one part) is tracked separately at `bf-57kgrx` and is **not** a
prerequisite for this bead.

## What needs to happen once unblocked

1. Deploy the current ARMOR main (containing `fc6c1a86`/`1f6e6934`) to
   `iad-ci`.
2. Configure both `k8s/iad-ci/queue-db/cnpg-cluster.yaml` and
   `k8s/iad-ci/forgejo/cnpg-cluster.yaml` in `declarative-config` with a
   barman `--min-chunk-size` large enough to force a single flush for each
   database's actual backup size (large enough that the whole backup fits
   before the first flush — the 2026-08-03/04 attempt at this failed only
   because the server-side part-1/final-part exemption didn't exist yet;
   it does now).
3. **Separately, fix the `ScheduledBackup` cron schedule on both
   clusters.** Both currently set `schedule: "0 4 * * *"` / `"0 3 * * *"`
   intending 5-field daily-at-4am/3am, but CNPG parses this as **6-field
   cron with seconds**, so it fires **hourly, at :04/:03 past every hour**
   (confirmed live 2026-08-06 and again 2026-08-07:
   `queue-db-daily-20260806140400`, `...150400`, `...160400`... one every
   hour). Per ADR-011: the fix is `0 0 4 * * *` / `0 0 3 * * *` (explicit
   leading `0` seconds field). Independently worth fixing regardless of
   the multipart issue — it's multiplying the failure/retry rate ~24x on
   single-instance CNPG clusters.
4. Verify by watching **real, live `Backup` objects** in both namespaces
   (`kubectl get backups -n queue-db`, `kubectl get backups -n forgejo`) —
   do not declare success from a manual/offline test or a single run.
   Given this saga's history (a same-day "verified empirically" fix on
   2026-08-06 turned out to still be failing hours later; ADR-011 itself
   notes its own fix is "committed but not yet confirmed in production"),
   require **multiple consecutive real `ScheduledBackup`-triggered runs**
   to complete successfully before treating this as fixed.
5. Add a short outcome addendum to ADR-011 (final deployed state, any
   deviation) — don't let this be the third unverified "fixed" claim in
   this saga's history.

## Acceptance criteria

- At least 2 consecutive real (not manual) `Backup` objects on each of
  `queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` show `status: completed`.
- `ScheduledBackup` cadence confirmed to actually be daily, not hourly
  (`0 0 4 * * *` / `0 0 3 * * *` or equivalent, live-verified against
  actual `Backup` object creation timestamps over 24h+, not just the
  schedule string).
- ADR-011 updated with the final, verified outcome.
