title: SigV4 auth rejects mathematically valid signatures from aws-cli while accepting barman-cloud with the identical credential
description:
## Symptom
aws-cli (via boto3/botocore) gets AccessDenied "Invalid credentials" on every
S3 operation (PUT, GET, ListObjectsV2) against iad-ci's ARMOR (0.1.1901),
even when using a credential independently confirmed correct in every way.
Meanwhile CNPG's barman-cloud WAL archiving succeeds continuously against
the SAME pod using the SAME credential pair at the SAME time.

## Evidence this is NOT a credential/ops issue (ruled out exhaustively)
1. Rotated ARMOR_AUTH_ACCESS_KEY/ARMOR_AUTH_SECRET_KEY at OpenBao
   secret/rs-manager/iad-ci/armor (MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY preserved
   unchanged, verified byte-identical before/after write).
2. Forced both consuming ExternalSecrets (armor-secrets ns armor,
   forgejo-backup-armor ns forgejo) to resync; confirmed via kubectl the
   K8s Secret objects held the new value.
3. Restarted the armor Deployment (kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt
   annotation via declarative-config, new pod armor-56586859c5-f6ph4).
4. Confirmed via `kubectl debug --target=armor` + reading /proc/1/environ
   on an ephemeral debug container that the LIVE running process's
   ARMOR_AUTH_ACCESS_KEY / ARMOR_AUTH_SECRET_KEY exactly match what was
   written to OpenBao — no drift, no staleness.
5. Independently hand-verified the SigV4 signature in Python (canonical
   request -> string-to-sign -> HMAC chain) against the confirmed-live
   secret key for a real aws-cli PUT request. The computed signature
   matched botocore's own computed signature exactly (both before and
   after rotation, i.e. reproduced twice with two different secret keys).
6. At the exact moment aws-cli was rejected, ARMOR's own logs showed
   Forgejo's barman-cloud-wal-archive PUTs succeeding (200) against the
   same pod, same rotated credential (visible in pg_stat_archiver +
   ARMOR request logs, 2026-08-02T23:43-23:46Z window).
7. Tried disabling aws-cli's newer default x-amz-checksum-crc32 header
   (AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required) in case that header
   was mishandled by buildCanonicalHeaders — no change, identical
   rejection with the plain 4-header (content-type;host;
   x-amz-content-sha256;x-amz-date) canonical request.

## What's provably true
- The stored/live credential is correct in every observable way.
- A mathematically correct SigV4 signature computed with that exact
  secret key is rejected by internal/server/auth.go's VerifyRequest path
  (confirmed via the generic "AccessDenied"/"Invalid credentials"
  fallback at server.go:703, which only fires when the returned error is
  NOT a *AuthError -- i.e. something outside the normal
  InvalidAccessKeyId/SignatureDoesNotMatch/etc. paths in auth.go).
- Something differs between the request shape aws-cli/botocore produces
  and whatever barman-cloud's S3 client produces, and ARMOR's
  verification is not equivalent across the two.

## Hypotheses not yet tested (starting points for whoever picks this up)
- barman-cloud may use STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD (chunked
  transfer with trailing signature) rather than a single upfront
  x-amz-content-sha256 -- server.go has special-case handling for that
  content-sha256 value (decoding aws-chunked bodies) that aws-cli's plain
  PUT never exercises. Worth checking whether the *auth* verification
  path (not just body decoding) treats streaming vs non-streaming
  requests differently in a way that only one of them satisfies.
- The deployed image tag (0.1.1901) may not be byte-identical to what's
  in the local git checkout used to read this code -- this repo has a
  documented history of ghost tags and deploy/source drift. Confirm by
  diffing the exact commit that built 0.1.1901 against HEAD before
  assuming the auth.go read during this investigation is what's actually
  running.
- Try a raw hand-built HTTP request (no botocore) with a manually
  computed signature, to rule out any botocore-specific request framing
  (e.g. Expect: 100-continue, header ordering/casing on the wire) that
  differs from what a packet-level equivalent-to-spec request would send.

## Impact
Any tool other than whatever barman-cloud uses currently cannot
authenticate to this ARMOR instance at all. Blocks the Massive/options
flat-file bulk sync evaluation (the reason this was found) and likely
any other rclone/aws-cli/DuckDB-based use of ARMOR fleet-wide, not just
iad-ci -- this is a shared codepath (internal/server/auth.go), not an
iad-ci-specific config issue.

Added two legacy-object cases to the TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior table-driven suite for objects without the x-amz-meta-armor-compressed flag (Compressed stays at its zero value false):

1. legacy_object_zstd_magic_prefix_no_flag — plaintext beginning with the zstd magic bytes (0x28 0xB5 0x2F 0xFD) but not actually compressed. Served byte-exact unchanged, proving the GET path trusts the absent metadata flag rather than content-sniffing.

2. legacy_object_multiblock_no_flag — a >64KB object spanning multiple encryption blocks. Proves multi-block reassembly honors the absent flag end-to-end and serves with no error.

Verified the core mechanic: ToMetadata() only writes the compressed key when Compressed==true, so compressed:false genuinely produces an absent key (true legacy behavior). Committed 81fb084a and pushed to origin.

title: Deploy 0.1.1897+ fleet-wide: ungated admin API exposes MEK export on all six deployments
description:
All six ARMOR deployments in declarative-config pin ronaldraygun/armor:0.1.1871. HEAD is 0.1.1897 -- 59 commits / 26 versions behind. The gap includes 0c6fc813 "gate admin API behind ARMOR_ADMIN_TOKEN" (bf-5m9nde), so the RUNNING FLEET still serves the admin key export, rotate and verify routes with no authentication.

EXPOSURE (verified 2026-07-20, not assumed): ARMOR_ADMIN_LISTEN is 0.0.0.0:9001 on every deployment, so any pod on the cluster network can hit the admin key-export route with the confirm parameter to exfiltrate the MEK, or POST to the key-rotate route with an attacker-supplied MEK to silently re-wrap every DEK. The only gate today is that confirm parameter. Scoped narrower than worst case: the sole ARMOR IngressRoute (iad-kalshi traefik armor-ingressroute) routes port 9000 (S3 API) only, NOT 9001 -- so this is cluster-internal pod-network exposure, not Tailscale-mesh or internet exposure. Still the highest-severity live gap, since the entire ARMOR security model rests on MEK secrecy and armor-apexalgo is a live ACB bucket.

DEPLOY PREREQUISITE -- do not skip: the fix is FAIL-CLOSED. When ARMOR_ADMIN_TOKEN is unset the admin API returns 403 and gated routes are disabled. The declarative-config manifests currently carry placeholder values. Provision a real per-deployment token into the referenced secret BEFORE or WITH the image bump, or dashboard key-rotate and the audit route break on rollout. The health, ready, canary and metrics routes stay token-free, so kubelet probes and Prometheus scrapes are unaffected.

Also lands with this bump: ADR-005 multipart ordering contract (b521651d), real combined plaintext SHA (9f6d5694), armor-decrypt multipart read path (94d1a485).

Per repo convention all changes go through declarative-config plus ArgoCD -- never kubectl apply. Never use the latest tag (note the iad-ci armor workflowtemplate line 188 pushes a latest tag; consumers correctly pin, but the tag push is worth revisiting).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Real admin token provisioned for every deployment (no placeholders remaining)
- All six deployments bumped to 0.1.1897+ via declarative-config commit, ArgoCD synced
- Verified post-rollout: unauthenticated admin key-export request returns 401/403; authenticated request succeeds
- All ARMOR consumers healthy through rollout (ord-devimprint is a 3-replica shared deployment)

description: Live verification 2026-07-19 of the bf-5tol4d implementation: a 50MB aws s3 cp with DEFAULT concurrency fails every time with InvalidPartSize - all 7 parts start concurrently, the short final part (least bytes) completes FIRST, P gets pinned to the final-part size and the first full-size part invalidates the upload. The implementation matched the original ADR spec; the spec rarity assumption was wrong - this is the COMMON case whenever part count fits the concurrency window (most files under ~80MB with aws cli defaults). Fix per the ADR-005 Amendment section (pushed): (1) pin P ONLY from part number 1; (2) a part arriving before part 1 has pinned P gets a retryable 503 SlowDown response with nothing stored - standard clients retry transparently; (3) keep the existing contradiction-poisoning as defense-in-depth for clients that never send part 1. ACCEPTANCE: 50MB aws-cli-DEFAULT-concurrency round-trip byte-identical (the exact failing repro); existing shuffled/sequential/retry tests stay green; a test where parts 2..N arrive before part 1 and succeed after SlowDown retries; go test -race green.

title: Wire HeadBucket connectivity probe into InitB2Backend
description:
Context: InitB2Backend in internal/backend/secondary_init.go has a doc comment (lines 99-104) that already CLAIMS it runs an explicit HeadBucket connectivity probe, but the implementation at line 153 returns NewB2Backend(ctx, b2Cfg) directly with no probe. NewB2Backend (internal/backend/b2.go:44) is lazy — it loads static credentials and constructs the S3 client but makes NO network call — so InitB2Backend currently succeeds offline for any syntactically valid config regardless of whether the endpoint is reachable or the credentials authenticate. This child adds the probe the doc comment already promises. Depends on sibling "Wire HeadBucket probe..." being done first... actually this IS that first step.

Acceptance Criteria:
- In InitB2Backend (internal/backend/secondary_init.go:128), capture the typed *B2Backend returned by NewB2Backend into a local instead of returning it directly at line 153.
- After successful construction, run a connectivity probe: call b2.HeadBucket(ctx, cfg.Bucket) (already exists at internal/backend/b2.go:526). This is the call where credential rejection and endpoint-unreachable failures actually surface (the AWS SDK defers auth to the first request).
- On probe failure return (nil, err) where err wraps the probe cause with high-level context, e.g. fmt.Errorf("b2 backend initialization failed: %w", err). Do NOT return the partially-constructed backend on probe failure.
- On probe success, return the constructed backend.
- NewB2Backend's own construction error (b2.go:54 "failed to load AWS config") must still propagate; wrap it the same way for consistency.
- Do NOT change validateB2Config or the defensive type-check guard.

Scope: implementation + error wrapping + nil-backend guarantee ONLY. Tests are the next two children.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED (commit 304a0122, pushed to origin): InitB2Backend now captures the typed *B2Backend from NewB2Backend into a local, runs b2.HeadBucket(ctx, cfg.Bucket) after construction, wraps both the construction error and the probe error with fmt.Errorf("b2 backend initialization failed: %w", err), and returns nil on probe failure so no partially-constructed backend escapes. validateB2Config and the type-check guard untouched. Verified empirically: a fake-cred config now surfaces 'b2 backend initialization failed: HeadBucket failed: ... api error Forbidden: Forbidden'. go build + go vet clean.

IMPORTANT FOR SIBLING TEST BEADS: the committed internal/backend/secondary_init_test.go::TestInitB2BackendFromConfig has TWO offline-success sub-cases ('valid config returns initialized B2 backend' and 'empty type allowed with valid B2 fields') that relied on NewB2Backend being lazy (fake creds KEYID/SECRET vs real endpoint s3.us-east-005.backblazeb2.com, wantErr:false). These now FAIL because HeadBucket makes a real network call and gets 403 Forbidden. The 6 validation/type-check sub-cases still pass. The success sub-cases need rewriting to point HeadBucket at a local mock S3 server (httptest) returning 200, plus a new probe-failure sub-case (403 -> nil backend, error containing 'b2 backend initialization failed'). This is the deferred test work.

Committed 304a0122, pushed to origin. All implementation acceptance criteria met; verified empirically (fake-cred config now surfaces the 403). Test work deferred to sibling beads per scope — note left on bead that TestInitB2BackendFromConfig's 2 offline-success sub-cases now fail by design and need a mock-server rewrite.

title: Full file lifecycle testing: real HTTP API path + write-through-delete coverage (canary bypasses handlers, no DELETE/LIST/overwrite verification)
description:
ARMOR's canary and integration tests never exercise the real, client-facing S3 HTTP API end-to-end -- and never test the full object lifecycle (write through delete). This is a genuine coverage gap distinct from the multipart/HMAC bug: the code path a real client (aws-cli, litestream, kalshi-tape's writer) actually hits is `internal/server/handlers` over HTTP; the canary (`internal/canary/canary.go` check()/checkMultipart()) calls `m.backend.Put`/`CreateMultipartUpload`/`UploadPart`/`CompleteMultipartUpload`/`GetRangeWithHeaders`/`Delete` DIRECTLY against the backend package, bypassing the HTTP handler layer, routing, auth/ACL enforcement, and the exact sidecar-detection logic that caused bf-24sxh7 (GET path ignoring the multipart marker). A regression isolated to the HTTP layer -- like bf-24sxh7 itself -- would not be caught by the canary as it exists today; it took a hand-run litestream restore to find that bug.

Additionally, no test (canary or integration) exercises the FULL file lifecycle. Confirmed gaps as of 2026-07-22:
- DELETE is fire-and-forget in both canary checks (`go func() { ... m.backend.Delete(...) }()`, cleanup errors silently swallowed) -- there is no assertion that delete succeeds, and no test that a deleted key actually returns 404/NoSuchKey on a subsequent GET/HEAD, or disappears from LIST.
- No overwrite/update-in-place coverage: writing the same key twice (a real pattern for litestream and other continuous writers) is never verified.
- No LIST coverage at all: nothing asserts an uploaded object appears in ListObjects, or that a deleted one stops appearing.
- Multipart Abort is only exercised as an error-handler side effect on failure paths, never as its own deliberate test -- and nothing verifies Abort actually removes the incomplete upload on the B2 side. ## Test Failure Analysis

test_detect_invalid_colon_at_start

### Test Case
Input YAML: :value

Expected: Invalid (should detect colon at start without preceding key)
Actual: Valid (no error detected)

The SyntaxValidator::validate_structure() method does NOT check for lines that start with a colon (:) without a preceding key.

Add validation in validate_structure() to detect and report an error when a line starts with a colon (after trimming whitespace).

## Test-structure exploration — synthesis (part 4/4, feeds bf-3exlq8)

### Test infrastructure already in place
Decompression tests run against a filesystem-backed storage fake (backend.NewFSBackend on a temp dir) injected into a real Server via the NewWithBackend factory, so no live B2/Cloudflare is needed. Helpers in internal/server/share_decompress_test.go do the full lift: setupTestEnvironment/loadTestConfig wire env-driven config; encryptTestData generates DEK/IV, encrypts, and returns an ARMORMetadata with the Compressed flag controllable; storeTestObject assembles the on-disk envelope (header + ciphertext + HMAC table) and Put's it; compressData zstd-compresses a []byte; generateRandomData makes payloads; generateTestToken mints a presign share token. At the pure-library layer, internal/crypto/crypto_decompress_test.go has its own compressData and drives crypto.Decompress / crypto.IsCompressed directly. A test can go raw bytes -> compress -> encrypt -> store -> token -> GET in a few lines.

### Scenarios already covered
- crypto.Decompress (unit): happy-path zstd roundtrip; uncompressed passthrough; empty; sub-magic-length short data; roundtrips small/medium/large up to 1MB; error cases (corrupted payload after magic, truncated stream, magic-only bytes, partial frame).
- crypto.IsCompressed: magic present/absent, empty, too-short, partial-magic.
- Share endpoint = server.handleShare -> handleShareFullObject, the BUFFERED path (collects all decrypted blocks then crypto.Decompress(allDecrypted) at server.go:1175): compressed object decompresses to original; uncompressed served as-is; table-driven mix (uncompressed text/binary, compressed repeating/binary, legacy-no-flag); explicit legacy object; full compress->encrypt->store->GET->decompress roundtrip at 3 sizes; first-block zstd-magic detection.
- Share range request: ONE test (TestShareGET_RangeRequestWithCompression) that checks only the HTTP status (206/200), NOT the returned bytes.

### Likely missing test case (handoff to bf-3exlq8)
No test exercises the STREAMING decompression path in handlers.handleFullObjectStream (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go:963-975) — the main authenticated S3 GetObject route that wraps an io.Pipe decryptor in zstd.NewReader and io.Copy's decompressed bytes to the client, sets X-Armor-Decompressed: true (line 846), and omits Content-Length for compressed objects (lines 837-839). Every existing compressed-decompression test routes through the SHARE endpoint's separate BUFFERED path (server.handleShareFullObject -> crypto.Decompress(allDecrypted)), so the streaming zstd-on-a-pipe code, its headers, and its chunked-transfer behavior are entirely untested. (Secondary smaller gap: the share range path, handleShareRangeRequest server.go:1196, only calls IsCompressed for logging and never decompresses — serving raw compressed bytes — and its single test asserts only status, not content.)

title: Support non-uniform multipart parts (per-part cumulative offsets)
description:
ADR-011. Barman emits parts of chunk_size + N*512, so part 2 contradicts the uniform P pinned by part 1 and is rejected. Until this lands, barman through ARMOR has a silent size ceiling: it works while a backup fits in one part and reverts to InvalidPartSize once it does not.

Three changes:
1. Per-part offsets from cumulative sizes rather than (N-1)*P. Requires all lower parts known, so defer an early-arriving part with the retryable 503 SlowDown already used for part>1-before-part-1. Uniform uploads keep the existing fast path.
2. CTR seek to an arbitrary byte offset (encryption is block-indexed today).
3. Boundary-block HMAC backfill at CompleteMultipartUpload: a block spanning two parts cannot be HMACed by either alone. Re-read each boundary block from the completed object there. At most numParts-1 blocks of 64KiB.

Preserves the on-B2 layout; no third format.

Given ADR-002/003/005's silent-corruption history, lands only with adversarial tests: mid-block boundaries at every offset residue, out-of-order arrival under deferral, retried part at a different size, completed object verified byte-identical end to end.

title: Deploy+verify barman fix on iad-ci (queue-db, forgejo-postgres) + fix hourly ScheduledBackup cron bug
description:
## Why this is blocked, not open

This bead requires `kubectl` write access to `iad-ci` and push access to the
`jedarden/declarative-config` repo (a different repo from this checkout) to
actually deploy and verify anything. It is **not reachable from an
ARMOR-repo-scoped worker** and must not be picked up by one — set to
`blocked` deliberately, matching this project's established convention for
ops/credential-gated work (see e.g. the historical fencing of bf-4qq1,
bf-2t1f, bf-32ms, bf-5aqh0). A human, or an agent session with the relevant
kubeconfig and declarative-config write access, needs to pick this up
directly — not via `bf ready` dispatch.

## What needs to happen once unblocked

1. Apply whatever client-side fix the investigation bead (and, if needed,
   its ADR-010-driven follow-on) actually determined works, to both
   `k8s/iad-ci/queue-db/cnpg-cluster.yaml` and
   `k8s/iad-ci/forgejo/cnpg-cluster.yaml` in `declarative-config`.
2. **Separately, fix the `ScheduledBackup` cron schedule on both clusters.**
   Both currently set `schedule: "0 4 * * *"` intending "daily at 4am," but
   CNPG's scheduler is actually firing **hourly, at :03/:04 past every
   hour** (confirmed live 2026-08-06: `queue-db-daily-20260806140400`,
   `...150400`, `...160400`... one every hour; same pattern on
   `forgejo-postgres-daily`). This is a 6-field-cron-with-seconds
   misinterpretation of the intended 5-field schedule, and it's
   independently worth fixing regardless of the InvalidPartSize issue — it's
   multiplying the failure/retry rate ~24x versus what was intended, on
   single-instance CNPG clusters.
3. Verify by watching **real, live `Backup` objects** in both namespaces
   (`kubectl get backups -n queue-db`, `kubectl get backups -n forgejo`) —
   do not declare success from a manual/offline test or a single run. Given
   this exact saga's history (see the investigation bead: a same-day
   "verified empirically" fix on 2026-08-06 turned out to still be failing
   in production hours later), require **multiple consecutive real
   `ScheduledBackup`-triggered runs** to complete successfully before
   treating this as fixed.
4. Update `docs/adr/008-multipart-part-size-error-clarity.md` (or ADR-010,
   once it exists) with the final outcome — currently ADR-008 says the
   client-side fix is "underway... not this ADR's concern"; that sentence
   should be corrected once there's a real, verified resolution instead of
   a second unverified claim.

## Acceptance criteria

- At least 2 consecutive real (not manual) `Backup` objects on each of
  `queue-db` and `forgejo-postgres` show `status: completed`.
- `ScheduledBackup` cadence confirmed to actually be daily, not hourly.
- ADR updated to reflect the real, verified outcome.

title: Decide and enforce: unsupported multipart part patterns must hard-fail, not corrupt
description: UploadPart derives each part CTR counter from arrival-order cumulative EncryptedBytes. Three patterns real SDKs use by default therefore corrupt silently: out-of-order or parallel part upload, part retry after network failure, and non-block-aligned intermediate parts. Decide: support them (derive counter from partNumber and fixed part size) or reject them with 400 plus documented client requirements. Then unskip TestMultipartSuspectPatterns in the handlers test package and cover all three. Matrix rows U6 U7 U8. Until then all ARMOR multipart writers including commitgraph clone workers must be pinned to sequential aligned no-retry part behavior.
close_reason: Verified resolved at HEAD (0.1.1897) via ADR-005 uniform-part-size contract (b521651d, amended 23dc1dcd). The bead asked to decide support-vs-reject; the decision was made and implemented — three of four patterns are now SUPPORTED, the fourth hard-fails. Out-of-order/parallel parts: offset derived from partNumber not arrival order (handlers.go:2287 startBlockIndex=((N-1)*P)/BlockSize), per-upload mutex (handlers.go:2124-2126), part>1 arriving before part 1 gets retryable 503 SlowDown with Retry-After storing nothing (handlers.go:2174-2180). Retry after failure: idempotent, deterministic CTR re-encrypt on same size; different size poisons + 400 (handlers.go:2200-2214). Non-block-aligned intermediate part: hard-fails 400 InvalidPartSize with actionable message (handlers.go:2194-2198). Nothing silently corrupts — poison-on-contradiction persisted (handlers.go:2243-2265, poisonUpload at 2356) and re-checked at Complete (handlers.go:2384-2388), plus complete-time backstop validation before any storage (handlers.go:2429-2458). TestMultipartSuspectPatterns is no longer skipped (multipart_routing_test.go:364), five subtests passing, and runs under -short. Matrix rows U6/U7/U8 covered. Documented residual (ADR-005): a client sending only a short final part and never part 1 loops on SlowDown until it gives up — loud failure, not corruption. Followup filed for retracting the now-obsolete sequential-writer pinning guidance.

comments.author: cli
comments.text: REOPENED 2026-07-18: hard-fail enforcement largely exists on main (InvalidPartSize for non-block-aligned intermediate parts, InvalidPart/InvalidPartOrder; out-of-order parts now SUPPORTED via cumulative-size CTR derivation). Remaining: verify+test the full suspect-pattern matrix from docs/upload-retrieval-test-matrix.md (retried parts, duplicate part numbers, gaps in numbering, single-part multipart), add any missing rejections, then close. See ADR-003.

comments.author: cli
comments.text: 2026-07-18 live verification sharpens the open decision: HEAD enforces sequential-only parts (InvalidPartOrder: Expected part 1, got part 7) - commit 3edbb9b4's cumulative-size derivation cannot support concurrent parts because a part's counter offset needs all lower part sizes. aws cli with default concurrency FAILS to upload; with max_concurrent_requests=1 a 50MB round-trip is byte-perfect. DECIDE: (a) true out-of-order support via uniform-part-size assumption or part-size registry, or (b) keep sequential-only, document client config (litestream, aws cli, SDKs) and ship compat notes. Either way add tests for: concurrent rejection, retried same part, duplicate part numbers, gaps at completion. ADR-003 updated with the enforced behavior.

title: Wire streaming PUT zstd compression and add streaming round-trip test
description:
NOTE: this is a DELIBERATE BEHAVIOR CHANGE. It contradicts the parent's blanket "no intended behavior change", which only holds for the already-wired in-memory path. Investigation during the split found the streaming PUT path has NO compression wired today, so the streaming round-trip case cannot pass without new wiring.

Finding: putObjectStreaming (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go L462-651) records plaintextSize as the data region (L524 NewEnvelopeHeader), computes envelopeSize from plaintext (L549), encrypts the raw temp file via encryptor.EncryptStream (L567), never calls crypto.CompressStream, never calls header.SetCompressed(), and omits the metadata Compressed field (L593-603). So a >10MB PUT is always stored uncompressed even with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true. crypto.CompressStream already exists (internal/crypto/compress.go L59) with unit coverage (compress_test.go).

Part 1 - Implement opportunistic compression in putObjectStreaming, mirroring the in-memory path (handlers.go L354-377): when h.config.Compress, compress the temp-file plaintext via crypto.CompressStream (streams src->dst, returns the compressed byte count; keep only when strictly smaller than plaintextSize). When kept: header.SetCompressed(); pass the COMPRESSED length (not plaintextSize) as the data-region size into NewEnvelopeHeader; recompute envelopeSize over the compressed size; set metadata Compressed=true; and feed the compressed bytes into encryption (note EncryptStream currently reads tmpFile directly - compress tmpFile into a second temp and EncryptStream over that, recompute blockCount/HMAC-table size over the compressed length). When not smaller, store uncompressed (current behavior). Preserve plaintextSHA over the ORIGINAL plaintext - GET verifies that digest against the decompressed bytes.

Part 2 - Add the streaming round-trip test (extends the harness from the prior children): subtest streaming_compressible - PUT an >10MB compressible payload (above the in-memory threshold at handlers.go L297) with cfg.Compress=true; assert X-Armor-Streaming: true on the PUT, GET body byte-identical to plaintext, stored envelope IsCompressed()==true and header.PlaintextSize < len(plaintext), metadata Compressed==true, GET X-Armor-Compressed: true. Also assert an incompressible >10MB payload round-trips stored UNCOMPRESSED (pass-through).

The GET path already decompresses flagged objects (handlers.go L960-989 + L882-884) - no GET change is needed; the flag set in Part 1 is what activates it.

Acceptance:
- go test ./internal/... passes; streaming_compressible green; the in-memory cases from the prior children still green.
- A streaming PUT with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true stores a flagged, strictly-smaller compressed object that round-trips byte-identical; an incompressible streaming payload passes through uncompressed.
- Label: split-child. Depends on the harness + pass-through children (split-child #1 and #2).

title: restore-verifier's ARMOR path never decrypts (guaranteed false-positive on every ModeDual check)
description:
restoreViaARMOR (internal/restoreverifier/verifier.go:1052) is wired to a raw B2Backend (constructed in cmd/restore-verifier/main.go, backend construction ~lines 162-173) with no crypto client — B2Backend.Get() (internal/backend/b2.go:112) never calls internal/crypto. Combined with B2Backend.Head()'s deliberate plaintext-size override for its other legitimate callers (b2.go:188-213), Get()'s GetRange(0, info.Size) fetches a meaningless truncated blob: the 64-byte envelope header followed by the first (plaintextSize-64) bytes of ciphertext, missing the ciphertext tail and the HMAC trailer entirely. This is SHA-256'd as ARMORSHA256 (verifier.go:991) and compared against the correctly-decrypted DirectSHA256 (verifier.go:1011) -- guaranteed mismatch for every real ARMOR-encrypted object, on every ModeDual run (the only mode runVerification(), the default periodic loop, ever calls), fleet-wide, independent of actual data integrity.

Confirmed via live investigation 2026-08-06: 10/10 real objects sampled from armor-apexalgo reported as SHA-256 conflicts; all 10 independently verified fully intact via a rebuilt cmd/armor-decrypt, and the exact false-positive ARMOR= hashes were reproduced byte-for-byte via a standalone program calling B2Backend.Get() directly with real production credentials. Full evidence: docs/bf-1ebnuz-corruption-inventory-armor-apexalgo.md. ModeDRDrill (verifyObjectDirectOnly) does not call restoreViaARMOR and is unaffected -- the real disaster-recovery guarantee is intact.

Fix direction (implementer's call, see ADR-009 docs/adr/009-restore-verifier-armor-path-never-decrypts.md for full discussion of both options and why a range-math-only fix is insufficient):
1. Give restoreViaARMOR a real ARMOR S3 client (new -armor-url/ARMOR_ENDPOINT config, separate backend/client pointed at the live proxy), matching the doc comment's original intent -- but introduces a live-ARMOR-proxy dependency this architecture currently avoids, so needs to degrade gracefully when no proxy is co-located.
2. Make the ARMOR path a second independent decrypt implementation via internal/crypto directly (the same package internal/server/handlers uses for real client GETs), rather than either reimplementing decryption a third time or silently skipping it -- keeps restore-verifier fully standalone.

Do NOT touch B2Backend.Head()/Get()'s existing size-override contract -- it's correct and load-bearing for its other callers; the fix belongs entirely in what restoreViaARMOR does with the backend it's given.

Add a regression test shaped like the reproduction in docs/bf-1ebnuz-corruption-inventory-armor-apexalgo.md: a real (or realistically mocked) ARMOR-encrypted object run through verifyObjectDual, asserting ARMORSHA256 == DirectSHA256 for known-good data.

Operational note: any historical armor_restore_verification_failures_total increase or near-zero runRatio gauge reading, on any bucket, predating this fix, should be treated as uninformative, not evidence of corruption. Check whether VERIFIER_ESCALATION is enabled anywhere and whether it auto-filed any beads off this false-positive signal -- those need identifying and closing as invalid once fixed.

title: armor-decrypt cannot read multipart objects: implements never-shipped reserved-byte layout
description: Verified 2026-07-18 against a real multipart object (devimprint litestream snapshot) with armor-decrypt built at HEAD: fails with 'decode envelope header: invalid ARMOR magic'. Root cause: cmd/armor-decrypt assumes every object starts with a 64-byte envelope header and detects sidecar HMAC via header.Reserved[1]==0x01 (the ADR-era design that never shipped), and its sidecar loader only reads a LOCAL file path. Real multipart objects per ADR-003 are headerless raw ciphertext with x-amz-meta-armor-multipart=true metadata and the HMAC table in a B2 sidecar object under the .armor hmac prefix keyed by sha256 of the object key. Consequence: the ARMOR-server-is-gone DR recovery path does not exist for exactly the object class that matters (large backups). Fix: in decryptB2, dispatch on the metadata marker (like handlers.go GET path): skip header decode, read data from offset 0 for plaintext-size bytes, fetch sidecar from B2, use absolute block indices; for local-file mode accept a sidecar JSON file alongside. Add tests with a real multipart fixture (headerless + sidecar), including the corrupted case. See ADR-004 Known defect note.
close_reason: Verified fixed at HEAD (0.1.1897), fix commit 94d1a485. All four bead claims confirmed: dispatches on metadata marker (main.go:525 isMultipart via x-amz-meta-armor-multipart, branching main.go:533-540) with the old header.Reserved[1]==0x01 detection removed; no 64-byte header assumed (main.go:642-650 reads from offset 0 for PlaintextSize bytes); sidecar fetched from B2 not just local disk (main.go:653 via backend.NewMultipartStateManager(...).LoadHMACTable — same manager the server uses, so the wire format cannot drift); absolute block indices (main.go:557). Local-file mode gained a -sidecar flag. Tests: buildMultipartFixture (main_test.go:129) drives TestRoundTripLocalMultipart, TestRoundTripLocalMultipartCorrupted, TestDecryptLocalMultipartMissingIV, TestDecryptB2Multipart (main_test.go:395, the named regression), TestDecryptB2MultipartCorrupted — all passing. b2BackendFactory injection (main.go:669) allows testing the B2 path without credentials. The ARMOR-server-is-gone DR path now exists for large objects. Residual nit tracked separately.

title: Admin API (MEK export/rotate) is unauthenticated and bound to 0.0.0.0 in every deployment
description: Verified in code 2026-07-19: server.go registers /admin/key/verify, /admin/key/rotate and /admin/key/export on the admin mux with NO authentication - the only gate on export is ?confirm=yes. All fleet deployments set ARMOR_ADMIN_LISTEN=0.0.0.0:9001 (needed for probes/dashboard), so ANY pod on the cluster pod network can (a) exfiltrate the MEK with a single GET to /admin/key/export?confirm=yes, or (b) POST /admin/key/rotate with an attacker-supplied MEK, silently re-wrapping every DEK to a key the attacker knows while ARMOR keeps serving normally. The entire security model (public ciphertext bucket) rests on MEK secrecy - this is the highest-severity gap in ARMOR. Fix: (1) require a bearer token (new env ARMOR_ADMIN_TOKEN, constant-time compare) on ALL /admin/* routes; keep /healthz,/readyz,/armor/canary,/metrics token-free for probes/scraping but move them off the admin-privileged surface if simpler; (2) make export additionally require the token even with confirm=yes; (3) audit-log every admin call (remote addr, route, outcome); (4) add the token to deployment manifests via the existing armor secrets when this ships (ops half - note on bf-4qq1 fleet-bump). Tests: all admin routes 401 without token, work with it; probes unaffected. Do NOT print the MEK in any test or log.

title: Optional pre-encryption compression (zstd) for non-columnar objects
description: ARMOR encrypts every PUT (internal/crypto/encryptor.go) but never compresses. Parquet is already compressed so this is a no-op there, but litestream WAL/SQLite snapshots, tar.gz DR fixtures, and JSON manifests/provenance objects stored under .armor/ (internal/manifest, internal/provenance) would shrink meaningfully with zstd applied before encryption (compressing after encryption is useless — ciphertext doesn't compress). Add an opt-in ARMOR_COMPRESS env var (default off, matches ADR-006's opt-in pattern) that zstd-compresses the plaintext stream before it hits internal/crypto/encryptor.go, and records a compressed flag in the envelope/metadata (see crypto/envelope.go version-byte dispatch pattern) so GetObject knows to decompress after decrypt. Ties into the Cost Model table in README.md — real storage cost reduction for compressible payloads.

title: Pipeline block fetches on the read path (ADR-013)
description:
Read throughput through the ARMOR service is ~1.5 MB/s, against ~7.9 MB/s available on the same Cloudflare path and ~38 MB/s direct to B2. Measured 2026-08-08 from an iad-ci pod against production: 169MB in 141s and 154MB in 86s.

ARMOR is not CPU-throttled (peaked 464m of a 1000m limit, ~46%). The cause is internal/backend/b2.go GetRangeWithHeaders issuing ONE HTTP ranged GET per 64KiB block with no pipelining. Against a measured 74ms RTT to us-west-002 that bounds throughput at blockSize/RTT = 65536/0.074 = ~0.89 MB/s serial; ~1.5 MB/s observed implies 1-2 blocks in flight.

Writes are unaffected because 64MiB multipart parts amortise 1024 blocks into one streamed PUT (~27% overhead vs ~80% loss on reads).

Fix: issue N ranged GETs concurrently (configurable, default 8-16) and reassemble in order. Confined to GetRangeWithHeaders and callers; does NOT touch the stored format, so it applies to every object already written.

Expected: ~5x, taking an 8.7GB restore through the service from ~1.6h to ~18min.

Care needed: preserve ordering on reassembly; a partial failure must fail the whole read rather than leave a hole (per-block HMACs catch corruption, but a truncated read must not look like a short object). Memory cost is N x blockSize = 1MiB at N=16, negligible against the 1Gi limit.

See docs/adr/013-read-throughput-unpipelined-block-fetches.md
close_reason: Implemented bounded pipelined ranged reads with ordered reassembly and whole-read failure handling; added ARMOR_READ_CONCURRENCY (default 16), focused concurrency/failure tests, caller wiring, and documentation. Targeted tests and race checks pass; pushed commit 1c708a99 to origin/main.

title: Add handler-level PUT→GET zstd compression round-trip tests
description:
Verify and lock in the already-wired (uncommitted) single-object compression path before extending it. Writer side: internal/server/handlers/handlers.go ~L354 (in-memory PUT) and ~L582 (streaming PUT) zstd-compress plaintext then header.SetCompressed(); main GET path ~L913 IsCompressed check + ~L957 crypto.Decompress. The ONLY tests today are unit tests in internal/crypto/compress_test.go — no handler-level proof that a real PUT with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true round-trips through a real GET.

Add integration tests driving the HTTP PUT+GET paths with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true, asserting:
- Compressible payload (manifest-like JSON, repetitive WAL/SQLite bytes) round-trips byte-identical AND the stored envelope reports IsCompressed()==true with a data region strictly smaller than plaintext.
- Incompressible payload (crypto/rand bytes) round-trips byte-identical AND is stored UNcompressed (opportunistic pass-through, IsCompressed()==false), matching internal/config/config.go ~L62-67.
- Legacy object written with ARMOR_COMPRESS off GETs correctly, IsCompressed()==false.
- Streaming PUT path (object above in-memory threshold) round-trips byte-identical when compressed.

Acceptance:
- New test compiles and passes under go test ./internal/...
- All four cases pass against current code; if any reveals a bug in existing wiring, fix it within this child.
- This child is the verified baseline the rest build on — no intended behavior change.

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
SPLIT by auto-dispatch after this bead failed 3x. Investigation before splitting found the real failure cause, which the original description hid: the streaming PUT path (putObjectStreaming, handlers.go L462-651) has NO compression wired today. It never calls crypto.CompressStream, never sets the compressed flag, and omits the metadata Compressed field, so a >10MB PUT is always stored uncompressed even with ARMOR_COMPRESS=true. Therefore the streaming round-trip case cannot pass against current code, and the blanket no-behavior-change line only holds for the already-wired in-memory path.

Split into three children along that seam:
(1) bf-4587bf - harness plus in-memory compressible baseline. Pure test; wiring already present. The verified baseline.
(2) bf-pcnwzc - incompressible pass-through plus legacy-uncompressed. Pure test; no production change.
(3) bf-5dvq22 - wire streaming PUT zstd compression plus streaming round-trip test. Deliberate behavior change; the missing feature that was sinking this bead.

Chain: 1 blocks 2 blocks 3. This umbrella is blocked by 3 (the last child). Do not work this parent as a single task; work the children in order.

title: Implement out-of-order multipart parts: uniform-part-size contract (ADR-005)
description: Implement docs/adr/005-out-of-order-multipart-uniform-part-size.md. Sidecar HMAC absolute indices unchanged. ACCEPTANCE (all must exist as tests, HTTP-handler layer like multipart_routing_test.go): shuffled/concurrent part arrival at >=44MB byte-verified round-trip; retried part mid-upload; short final part arriving before some middle parts; short-final-part-arriving-FIRST hard-fails poisoned with no stored object; non-block-aligned P rejected; all existing sequential multipart tests still green. go test -race green. title: armor-decrypt cannot use the Cloudflare path — offline restore always bills egress
description:
cmd/armor-decrypt builds an S3 client from ARMOR_B2_ENDPOINT and has no Cloudflare branch at all. The ARMOR service reads via ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN and falls back to direct S3 only when it is empty (internal/backend/b2.go GetRangeWithHeaders), so the service gets free Bandwidth Alliance egress while the break-glass tool always spends billed B2 egress.

Measured 2026-08-08 on one 154MB object: Cloudflare ~7.9 MB/s (free), direct B2 S3 ~38 MB/s (billed).

Not a correctness issue and arguably the right trade in a real emergency (a multi-GB restore costs cents, and speed matters more), but it should be a deliberate choice rather than a silent one. Now documented in docs/disaster-recovery.md.

The two are NOT interchangeable: ARMOR_CF_DOMAIN fronts B2's native download API (/file/<bucket>/<key>) with a different auth scheme, not the S3 API — so this needs a real code path, not a config flag.

Worth doing if offline restores become routine rather than exceptional.

2a. forgejo-postgres | secret/rs-manager/iad-ci/armor/forgejo-postgres | ACL "iad-ci:forgejo/cnpg/"

comments.author: cli
comments.text:
## Guide: table-driven pattern in TestShareGET_CompressionBehavior

File: internal/server/share_decompress_test.go (lines ~177-318). This is a table-driven subtest that validates decompression behavior across object types. Each row becomes its own `t.Run(tc.name, ...)` subtest with an isolated FS backend.

### 1. The testCases struct fields (lines 180-186)

- `name string` — REQUIRED, must be unique across rows. Two mechanical uses: (a) the subtest name via `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`, and (b) the stored object key is built as `"test-key-" + tc.name`. Duplicate names collide on the object key.
- `data []byte` — REQUIRED. The ORIGINAL plaintext payload. This is what the round-trip must reproduce, regardless of compression.
- `compressed bool` — REQUIRED. Controls two things: (a) whether `compressData()` is applied before encryption, and (b) the value written into `armorMeta.Compressed` by `encryptTestData`. It is also the value asserted against `armorMeta.Compressed` at the end of each row.
- `wantDecompression bool` — REQUIRED. Selects the direction of the dual assertion (see §3). NOTE: in all five existing rows `wantDecompression == compressed`; keep them aligned unless you deliberately want to test a divergence.
- `description string` — human-readable purpose; included in every error message in §3. Not mechanically required but every row should have one for failure triage.

### 2. Per-row flow (what each row goes through, lines 224-316)

1. `setupTestEnvironment(t)` → fresh temp dir.
2. `backend.NewFSBackend(...)` → isolated filesystem backend.
3. `loadTestConfig(t, tmpDir)` + `NewWithBackend(cfg, fsBackend)` → server under test.
4. `srv.presigner = presign.NewSigner(...)` → token signing (NewWithBackend skips this).
5. Prepare `dataToEncrypt` from `tc.data`:
   - `tc.compressed == true`  → `dataToEncrypt = compressData(tc.data)` (zstd).
   - `tc.compressed == false` → `dataToEncrypt = tc.data` (verbatim).
6. `encryptTestData(t, srv, dataToEncrypt, tc.compressed)` → returns `(encryptedData, hmacTable, armorMeta)`. The 4th arg sets `armorMeta.Compressed`.
7. `storeTestObject(..., objectKey, ...)` → builds the ARMOR envelope (header + encrypted + HMAC table) and PUTs it.
8. `generateTestToken(...)` → presigned share token for `("test-bucket", objectKey)`.
9. GET: `httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/share/"+token, nil)` → `srv.handleShare(w, req)`.
10. Assert status 200; read body into `retrievedData`.

### 3. The dual assertion + metadata flag (lines 287-315)

Three checks run for every row:

(a) Round-trip correctness (line 287): `bytes.Equal(retrievedData, tc.data)`. The bytes that come OUT must equal the ORIGINAL `tc.data`, NOT `dataToEncrypt`. For a compressed row this proves decompress ran; for an uncompressed row it proves passthrough.

(b) Decompression-direction check (lines 295-309), branching on `wantDecompression`:
   - `wantDecompression == true`  → assert `retrievedData != dataToEncrypt`. Since (a) guarantees `retrievedData == tc.data`, this is really asserting `tc.data != compressData(tc.data)` — i.e. the test data was genuinely compressed (bytes changed). If you pick compressed-row data that compresses to itself, this fails. Use highly-redundant text or large random blobs (zstd framing always differs).
   - `wantDecompression == false` → assert `retrievedData == dataToEncrypt`. In this branch `dataToEncrypt == tc.data`, so this is IDENTICAL to (a) — a redundant-but-harmless confirmation that decompression was bypassed. No additional coverage.

(c) Metadata flag (lines 312-315): `armorMeta.Compressed == tc.compressed`. The Compressed flag stored in metadata must equal the row's `compressed` field. Guards that `encryptTestData` wired the flag through correctly.

### 4. Exactly what a new row needs

Add one struct literal to the `testCases` slice. Populate:

- `name` — unique, kebab-case; becomes both the subtest label and `test-key-<name>`.
- `data` — the original plaintext `[]byte`. Use `[]byte("...")` for text, `strings.Repeat("...", n)` for compressible repetitive text, or `generateRandomData(size)` for binary.
- `compressed` — `true` = compress-before-encrypt + set flag (expect decompression); `false` = verbatim + unset flag (expect bypass).
- `wantDecompression` — set it EQUAL to `compressed` for normal rows. The current data has no row where they differ.
- `description` — short note on what the row validates; surfaces in failure output.

Choice rules:
- New compressed case → `compressed: true, wantDecompression: true`, and make sure `compressData(data) != data` (assertion (b) requires it). Random/binary data is fine — zstd framing differs even on incompressible input.
- New uncompressed/bypass case → `compressed: false, wantDecompression: false`; `data` can be anything.
- Legacy variant → mechanically identical to uncompressed (`compressed: false, wantDecompression: false`); the "legacy" distinction is semantic here. (The explicit `armorMeta.Compressed = false` reset lives in the standalone TestShareGET_LegacyObject, not in this table.)

Example new row (large compressed text):
```
{
    name:              "compressed_large_repeating_text",
    data:              []byte(strings.Repeat("ARMOR compression row ", 2000)),
    compressed:        true,
    wantDecompression: true,
    description:       "compressed large repeating text - should decompress",
},
```
No helper changes, no new setup — drop it into the slice and the flow in §2 handles it.

title: Verify ListMultipartUploads prefix handling matches ListObjectVersions pattern
description: The ListMultipartUploads handler (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go:2835) already wires prefix handling in the working tree: backendPrefix := h.applyPrefix(prefix) is passed to h.backend.ListMultipartUploads (line 2846), and h.stripPrefix is applied to upload keys (line 2889) and NextKeyMarker (line 2880). Verify this is correct and consistent with the ListObjectVersions sibling handler, which uses the same applyPrefix/stripPrefix pattern (handlers.go:2940). Acceptance criteria: confirm the wiring is correct vs the sibling; if correct, document findings in a comment on this bead and close it as a no-op with no code change. If a real discrepancy is found, fix it to match the sibling exactly.
close_reason:
DISCREPANCY FOUND: ListMultipartUploads does NOT pass key-marker to backend, unlike ListObjectVersions.

Current state:
- Backend interface: ListMultipartUploads(ctx, bucket, prefix) - NO key-marker/upload-id-marker params
- Handler (line 2877): calls h.backend.ListMultipartUploads(ctx, bucket, backendPrefix) - marker never passed
- Handler only echoes key-marker in response (line 2909) but doesn't use it for backend call

Sibling ListObjectVersions pattern (CORRECT):
- Backend interface: ListObjectVersions(..., keyMarker, versionIDMarker, ...) - HAS marker params  
- Handler (lines 2957, 2971): reads key-marker, applies prefix: backendKeyMarker := h.applyPrefix(keyMarker)
- Handler (line 2973): passes backendKeyMarker to backend

This is a real bug preventing pagination from working when ARMOR_PREFIX is configured. The fix requires:
1. Add keyMarker/uploadIDMarker params to backend.ListMultipartUploads interface
2. Update B2, filesystem, nil backend implementations
3. Update handler to read and pass markers to backend

This is a non-trivial change requiring backend interface updates, not just a handler fix.

title: Gate image publish on unit tests: run go vet + go test in Dockerfile build stage
description:
GAP: docs/plan/plan.md 'Testing Strategy' defines unit tests as the first line of defense, and the repo has 24 *_test.go files, but nothing runs them before an image ships. CI is the armor-build Argo WorkflowTemplate (declarative-config repo) which does a docker build + push of ronaldraygun/armor; GitHub Actions are disabled org-wide. The Dockerfile builder stage only runs 'go build' — a commit with failing unit tests still publishes an image and auto-bumps VERSION.

FIX (repo-local, no CI-template change needed): in the Dockerfile builder stage, after COPY . ., add a test gate before the binary build, e.g.:
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go vet ./... && CGO_ENABLED=0 go test ./...
Notes:
- tests/integration is guarded by env/skip conditions for real B2+Cloudflare (see tests/integration/README.md) — confirm those tests self-skip without credentials inside the container build; if any do not, scope the gate to ./cmd/... ./internal/... instead
- Keep the runtime stage (FROM scratch) unchanged
- Consider GOFLAGS=-buildvcs=false if the .git dir is not in build context

ACCEPTANCE:
- docker build fails when a unit test fails (verify by temporarily breaking a test locally — do not commit the breakage)
- docker build succeeds on clean HEAD with no B2/Cloudflare credentials available
- Build time increase is acceptable (<~2 min extra); document the gate in a Dockerfile comment

title: iad-acb ARMOR stuck on 0.1.1901 (Insufficient cpu) — old pre-fix SHA-tag pod still serving ungated admin API
description:
iad-acb (ai-code-battle ns) armor rollout to 0.1.1901 (declarative-config cf97de03/bf-3ab3) is stuck: new pod armor-7999bf96f7-* Pending ~163min, scheduler reports '0/2 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu, preemption: no victims'. The 2-node acb Spot cluster is CPU-saturated. Meanwhile the OLD pod (armor-55d8bd55cc-*) keeps serving on image ronaldraygun/armor:fcbf6d3 — a bare SHA tag (~23d old, late June), which (a) violates the declarative-config no-SHA-tag/semver-only rule, and (b) pre-dates the 0.1.1901 (07-19 admin gating, 0c6fc813), so iad-acb's ARMOR admin API (0.0.0.0:9001) is likely STILL UNGATED — a pod on the acb network could GET /admin/key/export?confirm=yes and exfil the acb-bucket MEK. Exposure is cluster-internal (acb armor is not externally routed).

FIX: free CPU on iad-acb so the 0.1.1901 pod schedules — reduce requests/replicas of a heavy acb workload via declarative-config, or add a spot node pool via the Rackspace Spot UI (node pools are not in declarative-config). Do NOT kubectl-patch live. After it schedules, confirm the old fcbf6d3 pod is gone and admin API returns 403. This is a known-troubled cluster (ai-code-battle combat epic). Lower stakes than the externally-routed iad-kalshi (already fixed), but the admin hole is still open here.

title: Wire zstd compression into the multipart upload path
description:
Feature-completeness gap and the most design-sensitive piece. The multipart PUT path (internal/server/handlers/handlers.go ~L2550 NewEncryptor + EncryptWithStartingCounter) never calls crypto.Compress or header.SetCompressed. Multipart uploads bypass compression entirely, so large multi-part objects get no storage savings; and if a multipart object were ever marked compressed, CTR part-offset math (ADR-005: part N starts at block (N-1)*P/BlockSize) would break because zstd framing is variable-length, not block-aligned.

Depends on child 1's round-trip harness and child 2's reader fixes; extend the harness to multipart.

Decide and implement the composition of compression with multipart. Two viable designs:
(a) Compress each part independently before EncryptWithStartingCounter and record per-part compressed sizes so the CTR block-alignment invariant holds on the COMPRESSED byte stream (part N startBlockIndex from cumulative compressed bytes — requires recording each part's compressed length in upload state); OR
(b) Fail closed at CreateMultipartUpload when ARMOR_COMPRESS=true (reject/disable compression on the multipart path), documenting that multipart objects are stored uncompressed while single-PUT objects still benefit.

Pick (a) ONLY if it preserves ADR-005's idempotent-retry byte-identical-ciphertext property; otherwise pick (b) as the safe default. Record the decision + tradeoff for child 4 (ADR-007).

Acceptance:
- Multipart upload under the chosen design round-trips byte-identical via multipart GET.
- ADR-005 out-of-order / idempotent-retry invariants preserved (existing internal/crypto/multipart_*_test.go tests still pass).
- Decision captured for child 4 to document.
- go test ./internal/... passes.

title: Implement ARMOR variable-part-size multipart accommodation for barman (ADR-010)
description:
## Context

ADR-010 (`docs/adr/010-barman-multipart-incompatibility.md`, revised
2026-08-07) decided: **add an opt-in variable-part-size multipart mode to
ARMOR**, not route `queue-db`/`forgejo-postgres` through Garage. This is the
implementation bead for that decision. Read ADR-010's Decision section in
full before starting — it is not a placeholder anymore, it is the spec.

barman-cloud-backup 3.19.1 produces multipart parts sized
`chunk_size + N×512` (N from the PostgreSQL backup stream's write pattern,
not controllable via any barman config) — never a multiple of ARMOR's 65536
-byte encryption block size. `bf-38uhih`'s root-cause analysis
(`docs/research/barman_armor_root_cause_analysis.md`) proved no client-side
fix exists. This bead makes ARMOR accommodate that, for opted-in clients
only, without weakening ADR-005's guarantee for anyone else.

## What to build

1. **Explicit, narrow opt-in signal** on `CreateMultipartUpload` (e.g. a
   dedicated request header) that this upload will use variable-size,
   non-block-aligned parts. Must not be inferable/defaulted from anything
   else about the request. Additionally scope it to the specific
   credential/bucket-prefix `queue-db`/`forgejo-postgres` actually use — a
   client without both the header AND the scoping must fall through to the
   existing ADR-005 uniform-part-size contract unchanged.
2. **Reject any part that arrives out of order.** Track next-expected
   `partNumber` server-side per upload; a part with any other number is
   rejected outright (poison-detection posture, matching ADR-005's own
   pattern, just enforcing sequence instead of size uniformity). This is
   what makes tracking a true cumulative offset tractable — you never have
   to guess at a part you haven't seen yet.
3. **Track true cumulative byte offset from actual part sizes**, persisted
   in the upload's existing server-side state (alongside the ADR-003
   per-part HMAC table), instead of the current
   `(partNumber-1) × partSize` formula.
4. **Handle blocks that straddle a part boundary.** Part sizes are no
   longer guaranteed multiples of the 64 KiB encryption block, so a block
   can now span the tail of one part and the head of the next. The current
   code assumes every part starts/ends on a block boundary — that
   assumption breaks here. Buffer an incomplete trailing block's plaintext
   across the `UploadPart` HTTP boundary until enough bytes arrive to
   complete it. This buffered state must either survive a process restart
   within the upload's lifetime, or the upload must fail loudly on restart
   (return an error on the next part / on Complete) — silently dropping
   buffered bytes on restart reintroduces exactly the silent-corruption
   class ADR-002/003/005 already fought and fixed once. Pick whichever is
   actually achievable given ARMOR's existing upload-state persistence and
   say explicitly which one you built.
5. **`CompleteMultipartUpload` and GET/Range-read paths** must both work
   against objects written this way — a variable-part-size object must
   decrypt and HMAC-verify identically to a uniform-part-size one from the
   client's perspective. Range GETs that land inside a straddled block need
   to read whichever parts are needed to reconstruct that block.

## Non-negotiables (this project's own history, not hypothetical)

- Opt-in only. No change in behavior for any client that doesn't set the
  new signal — verify with a regression test that an ordinary uniform-part
  upload is byte-identical in behavior before/after this change.
- A real end-to-end crypto-path test at production scale is required, not
  a mock-backend test and not a toy-sized one. This project's bead history
  (bf-28rb and others, see ARMOR's git/bead history for the ADR-002 saga)
  has repeatedly had "passing" multipart tests that never touched the real
  failure mode — don't repeat that. Build a test that reproduces the exact
  observed pattern: parts sized `chunk_size + N×512` for varying N, at
  least one part boundary that splits a 64 KiB block, upload → download →
  byte-identical plaintext, HMAC verification passes on every block
  including the straddled one.
- Do not close this bead on a single passing test run. This exact saga has
  had multiple "fixed, still corrupts" cycles (see
  `reference_armor_multipart_corruption_bug` history if available, or
  ADR-002's own incident list) — run the reproduction multiple times with
  varying part-size patterns before treating this as done.
- `go test -race ./...` green.

## Acceptance criteria

- New opt-in variable-part-size mode implemented per the "What to build"
  list above.
- Ordinary (non-opted-in) multipart uploads provably unaffected (regression
  test).
- Real-crypto-path test reproducing barman's actual part-size pattern
  (chunk_size + N×512, N a multiple of 512 but not 65536) at a scale that
  crosses at least one 64 KiB block boundary mid-part, passing consistently
  across multiple runs with varied sizes — not a single lucky pass.
- `CompleteMultipartUpload`, full-object GET, and Range GET across a
  straddled block all verified against a variable-part-size object.
- ADR-010 updated (short addendum, not a rewrite) with what actually
  shipped: the exact opt-in mechanism (header name, scoping method), and a
  pointer to the test(s) proving it.
- No cluster/`declarative-config` access needed or used here — deploying
  this to iad-ci and pointing barman's CNPG config at the new opt-in mode
  is `bf-496anl` (separate, ops-gated).
close_reason: Superseded by bf-57kgrx. ADR-011 (which supersedes ADR-010, written by a concurrent worker on this same board) found a better-scoped fix than the variable-part-size mode I speced here: the alignment check was over-broad (part 1 and the presumed-final part never needed alignment at all — shipped fc6c1a86/1f6e6934), which already resolves the immediate outage since both queue-db and forgejo-postgres fit in a single part. The durable fix for when they grow past one part is bf-57kgrx (per-part cumulative offsets + CTR seek + boundary-block HMAC backfill at Complete) — a cleaner design than the cross-part streaming-buffer approach I wrote into this bead's description. Do not implement this bead's spec; it's here for history only.

title: Disaster-recovery runbook: MEK backup/escrow, restore drill, rotation-failure recovery
description:
WHY: ARMOR exists because of a 2026-03-27 data-loss incident, and other infrastructure (an archive-to-B2 pipeline) is blocked on ARMOR being trustworthy as a backup target. The single most catastrophic failure mode — losing the MEK — has no documented mitigation. docs/ has cloudflare-setup.md and dashboard.md but no DR/operations doc. The admin API already provides the needed primitives (README.md 'Admin API': /admin/key/verify, /admin/key/rotate, /admin/key/export?confirm=yes; canary at /armor/canary).

WORK: write docs/disaster-recovery.md covering:
1. MEK backup/escrow procedure: exporting via /admin/key/export, where escrow copies should live conceptually (offline/secret manager — describe properties, NOT actual locations or key values), and the rule that a MEK must never be rotated without first verifying escrow of the old MEK (per-file DEKs wrapped by a lost MEK are unrecoverable)
2. Restore drill: step-by-step recovery when the ARMOR deployment/config is lost but MEK + B2 bucket survive — fresh instance with same env config, /admin/key/verify against the canary, spot-check decrypt; reference the offline decrypt CLI (bead bf-16vq) as the server-less path
3. Key-rotation failure recovery: rotation is resumable via .armor/rotation-state.json (plan.md 'Key Rotation'); document how to detect a half-rotated bucket and resume, and the implication that bucket versioning is OFF so CopyObject overwrites in place
4. Multipart caveat: objects with sidecar HMAC tables at .armor/hmac/<sha256-of-key> — recovery must preserve the .armor/ tree, never 'clean it up'
5. What is NOT recoverable: data written after last backup, objects whose wrapped DEK metadata was destroyed

ACCEPTANCE:
- docs/disaster-recovery.md exists and is linked from README.md Documentation section
- Every step names the exact endpoint/env var/file it uses; no placeholder hand-waving
- Contains no real key material, bucket names, tokens, or hostnames — generic examples only
- A restore drill was walked through at least on paper against the current code (endpoints verified to exist in internal/server)

title: Decompress compressed objects served through the share/range GET path
description:
Correctness gap. The single-object GET in handlers.go honors the compressed flag (~L913 IsCompressed, ~L957 Decompress), but the share/range/seekable GET path in internal/server/server.go (~L1053 NewDecryptor, and handleShareRangeRequest) never checks IsCompressed or calls crypto.Decompress. With ARMOR_COMPRESS=true, any object fetched via a share link or byte-range (DuckDB seekable) request is served raw zstd bytes after decrypt — silently corrupt for compressed objects. Uncompressed/legacy objects only work because Decompress is never reached.

Depends on child 1's round-trip harness, which is extended here to cover the share/range path.

Extend the server.go decrypt sites to honor the flag: after decrypt, if armorMeta.Compressed / envelope IsCompressed() is set, zstd-decompress the plaintext stream before writing the response. For full-object share GETs this is straightforward. For byte-range requests over a compressed stream, compression destroys fixed-offset seeking (zstd is variable-length), so range-over-compressed must FAIL CLOSED with a clear explicit error (e.g. 416/400: range reads unsupported on compressed objects) rather than silently returning wrong bytes — record this as a deliberate limitation for child 4.

Acceptance:
- Compressed object fetched through the share GET path round-trips to original bytes.
- Range request over a compressed object fails closed with a clear error, not corrupt data.
- Uncompressed/legacy objects through the share/range path byte-identical to before.
- go test ./internal/... passes.

title: restore-verifier historical sampling picks last-N objects, not a random sample
description: Plan Phase 6 goal (docs/plan/plan.md, ADR-004) is to prove backups are CONTINUOUSLY restorable across the whole bucket. internal/restoreverifier/verifier.go getHistoricalSample() (around line 873-908) lists up to 1000 objects via a single unsorted backend.List() call, then does NOT randomly sample them despite the function name and the comment on it: it just slices candidates[len(candidates)-sampleCount:] (last N of whatever order List() returned), with an explicit TODO at line ~904: "Simple random sample (in production, use proper random sampling)" / "For now, just take the last N objects". Practical effect: verification systematically favors whatever objects land at the tail of one List page and can permanently starve older or differently-prefixed objects of ever being restore-verified, undermining the whole restorability guarantee Phase 6 exists to provide. Fix: implement real random sampling (e.g. reservoir sampling or crypto/math-rand shuffle+slice) across the full candidate set, and if the bucket has more than one List page worth of objects, paginate through ListObjects (using continuationToken) rather than sampling from only the first 1000-object page. title: Phase 6: Build dual-path restore-verification harness
description:
## Summary
Build the restore-verification harness from plan.md Phase 6: a long-running verifier (Deployment with an internal scheduling loop -- per the no-CronJobs convention, not a Job/CronJob) that, per bucket, restores (a) the most recent backup object set and (b) a random sample of historical objects, through two independent paths:

1. The normal ARMOR read path (S3 GetObject through the running server)
2. armor-decrypt directly against raw B2 ciphertext with the escrowed MEK (bypassing ARMOR entirely -- proves the "ARMOR server is gone" recovery path works, not just that the server currently works)

Verify plaintext SHA-256 against manifest/provenance records on both paths, and that the two paths agree with each other.

## Why this matters now
bf-1v6skf / bf-24sxh7 (P0, found 2026-07-14/15) proved that a real backup can look completely healthy (object exists, right size, canary green) while being unrestorable. Nobody would have caught this without a human manually running litestream restore. This harness is what makes that kind of discovery automatic and continuous instead of accidental.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deployment (not Job/CronJob) with an internal ticker/scheduling loop, one per configured bucket or shared across buckets with per-bucket state
- Restores most-recent generation + a random historical sample on each run
- Both paths implemented: ARMOR read path (real S3 client) and armor-decrypt direct-to-ciphertext
- Plaintext SHA-256 compared against manifest/provenance records; mismatch or restore failure is a hard failure, not a warning
- Runs against all in-scope buckets: armor-apexalgo, ord-devimprint, iad-ci, iad-kalshi, rs-manager

## Related
- bf-1v6skf, bf-24sxh7 (the concrete bug this would have caught)
- bf-2t1f (Phase 5 version-drift check -- this harness should be able to correlate failures against deployed version)
- Phase 6 genesis

title: Map high-patch armor tags to source git commits via VERSION history
description:

CONTEXT: HEAD = 43dcd14f68959544461b334a2a280d1b8111e223 (from bf-3jq7hy; NOT clean — internal/server/server.go has +12/-1 uncommitted). VERSION at repo root = 0.1.1905. The armor-build resolve-version quirk means a re-trigger computes patch+1 from the PRIOR VERSION rather than reading VERSION, so tags like 0.1.1906 can be the SAME source as VERSION=0.1.1905.

TASK:
- Walk the VERSION file history (git log -p -- VERSION) and the main branch log to determine, for tags 0.1.1905, 0.1.1906, 0.1.1923: which git commit was main-HEAD when each was built. Use commit timestamps vs the tags' last_updated (from bf-n1g61w: 0.1.1906 pushed 2026-08-09 22:40 UTC; 0.1.1923 older, ~8/7).
- For each tag, record the candidate source commit AND compute git merge-base <commit> 43dcd14f to confirm it is a true ancestor of HEAD (i.e. HEAD is at-or-ahead of that source).
- Explicitly determine: was ANY existing tag built from a commit at-or-after HEAD 43dcd14f? (Expected answer: NO — 43dcd14f was committed 00:14 UTC 8/10, after the last build at 22:40 UTC 8/9.)

ACCEPTANCE: a comment with a table: tag -> source commit -> merge-base vs HEAD 43dcd14f -> (ancestor? yes/no). Plus a one-line verdict on whether any tag is at-or-ahead of HEAD.
notes:
TAG -> SOURCE-COMMIT MAP (timestamp + merge-base proof; HEAD=43dcd14f, VERSION@root=0.1.1905)

METHOD: resolve-version auto-bumps push to the GitHub MIRROR only, so auto-bumped tags
(0.1.1906 ... 0.1.1923) are INVISIBLE in Forgejo VERSION history. Commit 95cc29b9 documents
this: "a commit that sets VERSION takes the other branch and pushes nothing." Only the manual
bump to 0.1.1905 lands at 892bd314 (0.1.1903 -> 0.1.1905, skipping 0.1.1904). So tags are mapped
to source commits by correlating each push time to main-HEAD-at-that-instant; ancestry is then
PROVEN by merge-base.

| tag      | source commit | src commit time (UTC) | VERSION carried | merge-base vs 43dcd14f | ancestor of HEAD? |
|----------|---------------|-----------------------|-----------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| 0.1.1905 | 892bd314      | 2026-08-07 14:09:42   | 0.1.1905        | 892bd314 (=src)        | YES               |
| 0.1.1906 | d390fdf1      | 2026-08-09 18:42:24   | 0.1.1905        | d390fdf1 (=src)        | YES               |
| 0.1.1923 | f9b22955 *    | 2026-08-08 00:37:37   | 0.1.1905        | f9b22955 (=src)        | YES               |

title: Verify iad-ci consumer credential records and ACL scoping in OpenBao (data-level)
description:
ADR-012 decision 1 — VERIFICATION step (data-level). Depends on the provisioning child.

For each of the four consumer OpenBao paths, verify and record the RESULT of each check — never any credential value:
- The path exists and holds a record with access_key + secret_key + acl fields of the expected shape
- The stored acl string is well-formed (bucket:prefix[:actions]) AND matches the investigation child's documented prefix for that consumer
- CRITICAL: the acl must NOT be empty/missing, because an EMPTY ACL means FULL access in ARMOR (CheckACL returns nil when len(cred.ACLs)==0 — see internal/server/auth.go). An empty ACL is a provisioning FAILURE here, not success. This is the silent-failure mode to catch.
- restore-verifier's ACL contains exactly the consumer read-prefixes (get+list), nothing broader and no full access
- No two consumers share an identical access-key value

OUT OF SCOPE here (belongs to the cutover/deployment sibling under bf-12icmx): runtime deny-enforcement testing — i.e. proving via live ARMOR requests that own-prefix access succeeds and out-of-prefix is denied. That requires wiring ARMOR_AUTH_<NAME>_ACL env into the running deployment, which this bead family explicitly excludes. State this scope boundary explicitly in the verification record so the sibling knows runtime verification is its job.

Acceptance:
- Verification RESULT (not values) recorded for all 4 paths: shape ok; ACL matches documented prefix; ACL is non-empty and scoped (not full-access)
- restore-verifier ACL confirmed scoped to exactly the read prefixes
- Explicit note recorded that runtime deny-enforcement is deferred to the cutover sibling
- No credential value written anywhere
